27485254.Name: Glasgow-1097
27485254.bio:
[[Category:Glasgow Name Study]]
{{Estimated Date}}

== Biography ==
Archibald Glasgow was married and acquiring Glasgow burgh property by 21 May 1551. His earlier birth estimate of about 1533 would make him about eighteen at that transaction and is not record-derived. The structured estimate is therefore broadened to '''before about 1530'''; Glasgow remains an uncertain birthplace.

=== Marriage and property ===
On 21 May 1551 Elizabeth Beith sold a fore-and-back tenement on the north side of the street running from the South Port to the Clyde bridge to Archibald Glasgow and [[Newlands-647|Isobell Newlands]], explicitly described as spouses. Robert Glasgow was one of six witnesses.<ref>Robert Renwick, ed., ''Abstracts of Protocols of the Town Clerks of Glasgow'', vol. 1, protocol 84, printed p. 31, 21 May 1551, [https://archive.org/details/abstractsprotoc07robegoog/page/n59/mode/2up scan].</ref> The transaction directly proves the couple, their property acquisition, and Archibald's survival to that date.

The witness may have been [[Glasgow-1096|Robert Glasgow]] of the same burgh, but the protocol gives no occupation, spouse or patronymic that makes the identification certain. His presence supports a family or civic association, not a stated brotherhood.

== Research Notes ==
=== Property succession and probable parentage ===

[[Glasgow-1098|William Glasgow]] is the leading and '''probable''' father of Archibald, but the relationship remains marked uncertain because no record explicitly calls Archibald his son. The conclusion is based on a short, unusually specific property sequence rather than chronology alone.

In 1551 Archibald and Isobell acquired the fore-and-back parcel immediately east of Thomas Bargill; [[Glasgow-1096|Robert Glasgow]] witnessed the purchase. By 31 January 1554/55 the property immediately east of Bargill's back tenement belonged to [[Glasgow-1093|John Glasgow]], who is independently documented as William's son. John's east boundary remained unchanged in 1556 and 1557.<ref name="BargillSequence">Renwick, ''Abstracts of Protocols'', vol. 1, protocol 205, [https://archive.org/details/abstractsprotoc07robegoog/page/n97/mode/2up 31 January 1554/55], printed p. 69; vol. 2, protocol 307, [https://archive.org/details/abstractsprotoc08scogoog/page/n29/mode/2up 5 August 1556], and protocol 402, [https://archive.org/details/abstractsprotoc08scogoog/page/n57/mode/2up 22 November 1557].</ref> A 1575 boundary then calls John deceased and carries the same rear title forward.<ref name="P2241">Renwick, ''Abstracts of Protocols'', vol. 7, protocol 2241, [https://archive.org/details/abstractsprotoc00robegoog/page/n145/mode/2up 23 December 1575].</ref>

The most economical genealogy is that Archibald belonged to William's household and that the parcel passed to his elder brother John by sale, settlement or succession. Robert's presence at the acquisition, followed by Robert's own repeated property and fisher association with John, reinforces a close three-man family group. A transfer to a cousin or unrelated namesake remains possible because the 1551-54 conveyance has not survived in the published abstracts. William should therefore remain an uncertain rather than confident father. Esbell Brade is William's documented wife and mother of John, but no record identifies her as Archibald's mother; her attachment also remains uncertain.

No reviewed record identifies a child of Archibald and Isobell. The attached [[Glasgow-3026|Isabella Glasgow]] and [[Glasgow-1156|Robert Glasgow I]] therefore remain uncertain children. Earlier compilations also proposed sons Andrew and John, but no primary record currently supports those placements.

[[Glasgow-1093|John Glasgow]] and Robert Glasgow occupied the same South Port and Bridgegait network. Their association supports the probable household reconstruction above but does not by itself establish exact kinship.

Archibald's date and proved place of death are unknown. The retained structured death estimate and Bridgegate location remain uncertain; protocol 84 proves only that he was alive on 21 May 1551.

=== Validator chronology note ===
WikiTree's warning that Archibald died before [[Glasgow-1156|Robert Glasgow I]] was born is not a valid reading of the structured data. Archibald's death is recorded as '''after 1560''', an open lower boundary rather than a death in 1560. Robert's 1582 birth is an uncertain estimate, and their father-son relationship is itself marked uncertain. No source currently proves when Archibald died or that Robert was his son.

== Sources ==
<references />

Spouses.Name: Newlands-647
Spouses.bio:
== Biography ==

'''Hysbel Newlandis''', also recorded as '''Hisbell Newlandis''' and modernised as '''Isobell Newlands''', was a member of an established landholding family in the barony of Glasgow during the first half of the sixteenth century.

Her precise date and place of birth are unknown. A birth estimate of about 1530 has previously been used, based on her possible marriage to Archibald Glasgow by 1551. However, because she was already married to Robert Barde by February 1545, she was probably born during the 1520s or early 1530s.

=== Name ===

Contemporary records use the forms:

* Hysbel Newlandis — 14 January 1538/39
* Hisbell Newlandis — 26 February 1544/45

The forms Isobell Newland and Isobell Newlands are modernised spellings.

=== Parents and family ===

Hysbel was the daughter of:

* '''William Newlandis''', who died before 17 October 1534; and
* '''Margaret Love''', whose surname appears in the records as Loif or Loyf.

William Newlandis was himself a son of '''Robert Newlandis'''. This relationship is stated in a Glasgow diocesan rental entry dated 17 October 1534 concerning William's widow, Margaret Loif.<ref name="Rental1534">Joseph Bain and Charles Rogers, eds., ''Liber Protocollorum M. Cuthberti Simonis, Notarii Publici et Scribae Capituli Glasguensis, A.D. 1499–1513; also Rental Book of Diocese of Glasgow, A.D. 1509–1570'', vol. 1 (London: Grampian Club, 1875), p. 104, entry dated 17 October 1534; Margaret Loif, widow of the late William Newlandis, was permitted to marry Andrew Plemyng while retaining the lands held under arrangements involving William and “Robert Newlandis, his father.” [https://archive.org/details/liberprotocollor01bain/page/104/mode/2up View page at Internet Archive].</ref>

William had previously been entered, on 26 February 1527/28, in the rental of two merk lands of Cheddylstoun, now Shettleston, in the barony of Glasgow.<ref name="Rental1528">Bain and Rogers, ''Liber Protocollorum'', vol. 1, p. 89, entry dated 26 February 1527/28; William Newlandis entered in two merk lands of Cheddylstoun. [https://archive.org/details/liberprotocollor01bain/page/89/mode/2up View page at Internet Archive].</ref>

After William's death, Margaret Love obtained permission on 17 October 1534 to marry '''Andrew Plemyng''', or Fleming, while retaining William's two merk lands at Shettleston under the stated rental conditions.<ref name="Rental1534" />

Hysbel had at least one known sister:

* '''Margaret Newlandis''', living on 14 January 1538/39.

On 14 January 1538/39, Patrick Newlandis was entered in the 16-shilling and 8-penny land of Carrynduff Hill with the consent of:

> Margaret Newlandis and Hysbel Newlandis, daughters of the late William Newlandis and Margaret Loyf, their mother.

On the same day, David Newlandis, son of Patrick, was entered in the same land with the consent of the same persons.<ref name="Rental1539">Bain and Rogers, ''Liber Protocollorum'', vol. 1, p. 113, entries dated 14 January 1538/39; Patrick Newlandis and his son David were successively entered in land at Carrynduff Hill with the consent of Margaret and Hysbel Newlandis, daughters of the late William Newlandis and Margaret Loyf. [https://archive.org/details/liberprotocollor01bain/page/113/mode/2up View page at Internet Archive].</ref>

The record does not state Patrick Newlandis's exact relationship to Hysbel. He was evidently connected with the family's landholding, but he should not presently be identified as her brother, uncle or other specific relative without further evidence.

The proven family can therefore be represented as:

* Robert Newlandis
** William Newlandis, died before 17 October 1534 married Margaret Love or Loif
*** Margaret Newlandis, living 14 January 1538/39
*** Hysbel or Hisbell Newlandis, living 26 February 1544/45

=== Marriage to Robert Barde ===

By 26 February 1544/45, Hysbel was the wife of '''Robert Barde'''.

On that date Patrick Barde was entered in twenty-shilling lands at Conflat with the consent of his father, Robert Barde. Patrick received one half of the property immediately, while Robert Barde and “Hisbell Newlandis, his wife” retained the other half during their respective lifetimes.<ref name="Rental1545">Bain and Rogers, ''Liber Protocollorum'', vol. 1, p. 129, entry dated 26 February 1544/45; Robert Barde and Hisbell Newlandis, his wife, retained a liferent interest in half of the twenty-shilling lands at Conflat when Robert's son Patrick was entered in the property. [https://archive.org/details/liberprotocollor01bain/page/129/mode/2up View page at Internet Archive].</ref>

Patrick Barde is expressly described as Robert Barde's son. The entry does not describe him as Hysbel's son. He may have been her son or stepson, but no parent-child relationship between Hysbel and Patrick should be created from this record alone.

The Rental Book's index lists:

> Newlandis, Hysbel, 113, 129

This index entry connects the woman identified as William and Margaret's daughter on page 113 with the wife of Robert Barde on page 129.<ref name="RentalIndex">Bain and Rogers, ''Liber Protocollorum'', vol. 1, index, “Newlandis, Hysbel, 113, 129.” [https://archive.org/details/liberprotocollor01bain/page/249/mode/2up View index at Internet Archive].</ref>

No record of Robert Barde's death has yet been identified.

=== Possible later marriage to Archibald Glasgow ===

An '''Isobell Newlands''' is currently associated with '''Archibald Glasgow''', who was active in Glasgow by 21 May 1551.

This Isobell has previously been estimated to have been born about 1530 and to have married Archibald before 21 May 1551. Hysbel Newlandis, daughter of William Newlandis and Margaret Love, is a strong candidate for that woman because:

* the name and surname agree;
* Hysbel belonged to a documented family in the Glasgow barony;
* she was of marriageable age by 1545;
* the chronology permits a later marriage by 1551; and
* her family's possession of rental lands is consistent with the established social and property network of the Glasgow family.

The identification has not yet been proved. Hysbel was still Robert Barde's wife on 26 February 1544/45. For her to have married Archibald Glasgow by May 1551, Robert must have died or the marriage must otherwise have ended during the intervening six years.

The complete record dated 21 May 1551 should therefore be located and transcribed before Archibald Glasgow is treated as a certain second husband.

The likely source is:

* Robert Renwick, ed., ''Abstracts of Protocols of the Town Clerks of Glasgow'', vol. 1, ''First Protocol Book of William Hegait, 1547–1555'' (Glasgow: Carson & Nicol, 1894). [https://archive.org/details/abstractsofproto01glas View volume at Internet Archive].

Until the original entry is checked, the relationship to Archibald Glasgow should be marked uncertain.

=== Possible children with Archibald Glasgow ===

The following children have been associated with Archibald Glasgow and Isobell Newlands:

* Isabella Glasgow, born about 1560, later wife of John Howe.
* Robert Glasgow, reportedly born about 1582 and died 17 January 1647.

Neither relationship has yet been established by a contemporary source.

Robert's estimated birth in 1582 occurred approximately thirty-one years after the 1551 reference to Archibald and Isobell. This is biologically possible but raises a substantial chronological concern. His birth estimate may be wrong, he may belong to a later generation, or he may have been the son of another couple.

No child should presently be treated as proved from the available records.

=== Death ===

Hysbel was alive on 26 February 1544/45, when she was recorded as Robert Barde's wife.

If she was the Isobell Newlands associated with Archibald Glasgow, she was alive on or shortly before 21 May 1551. That later date remains conditional on proving that the two women were the same person.

Her date and place of death are unknown.

== Research Notes ==

=== Social and property status ===

The records establish that Hysbel belonged to a locally established Newlandis family holding rental lands under the Archbishopric of Glasgow.

Known family land associations included:

* Shettleston, held by William Newlandis;
* Carrynduff Hill, in which Margaret and Hysbel possessed an interest sufficient for their consent to be required; and
* Conflat, where Hysbel held a liferent interest with Robert Barde.

This supports the view that she came from a family with recognised property interests and local standing. It does not establish nobility, royal descent or membership of a titled house.

=== Patrick and David Newlandis ===

Patrick Newlandis and his son David were closely involved with the Carrynduff Hill property in 1539.<ref name="Rental1539" />

A later John Newlandis of Glendufhill was identified in records from the 1590s as the eldest son of a David Newlandis. This may represent a later generation of the same local family. Further work is required to establish whether the David of Glendufhill was identical with Patrick's son David and how Patrick was related to William Newlandis.

No exact relationship should yet be assigned.

=== Possible Newland–Anderson connections ===

Unsourced FamilySearch profiles identify:

* [https://www.familysearch.org/en/tree/person/details/K8FR-S7D Johne Newland], reportedly born in 1548 and died in 1604;
* [https://www.familysearch.org/en/tree/person/details/KCB8-DWZ Marie Andersone], reportedly born in 1552;
* [https://www.familysearch.org/en/tree/person/details/MD8B-2QJ Jonet Newland], reportedly born in 1580.

The profiles claim that Johne Newland and Marie Andersone married about 1579 in Lanarkshire and were parents of Jonet. No historical source is attached to those claims.

A contemporary John Newlandis of Glendufhill, eldest son of David Newlandis, is documented around 1595–1600, but his recorded wife in 1600 was Margaret Cors. He may or may not be the man represented by the FamilySearch profile.

An Alexander Newlandis also witnessed an Andersone family marriage transaction in Glasgow in March 1600. This shows a genuine social or legal association between the Newlandis and Andersone families, but does not prove the proposed marriage between Johne Newland and Marie Andersone.

These profiles should remain research leads only.

=== Claimed English or House of Newland ancestry ===

Several online family trees attempt to connect Scottish Newlands families with English Newland or Newlande families.

One proposed ancestor is:

* [https://www.familysearch.org/en/tree/person/details/GK7Z-Y9S Sir John Kingswell Newlande], reportedly born about 1496.

Other potentially connected FamilySearch profiles include:

* [https://www.familysearch.org/en/tree/person/details/LDM6-GH1 FamilySearch profile LDM6-GH1]
* [https://www.familysearch.org/en/tree/person/details/97SZ-MHP Agnes Glasgow or Newland]
* [https://www.familysearch.org/en/tree/person/details/K8GQ-PN3 Newlands]

No record has been identified connecting Hysbel, William or Robert Newlandis of Glasgow with any of those profiles.

The Kingdom of Newland website presents a claimed medieval and English pedigree for the surname:

* [https://kingdomofnewland.blogspot.com/p/our-history.html Kingdom of Newland: Our History]
* [https://kingdomofnewland.blogspot.com/p/our-history.html Current site (replacement for retired archive.is snapshot NhgXu)]

The pedigree does not name Hysbel or Isobell and supplies no documentary chain connecting its claimed English line to the Newlandis family of sixteenth-century Glasgow. It should not be used as evidence for her parentage.

The contemporary Glasgow records already provide a stronger and more direct ancestry:

* father: William Newlandis;
* mother: Margaret Love or Loif;
* paternal grandfather: Robert Newlandis.

=== Further research ===

# Locate and transcribe the complete Glasgow protocol dated 21 May 1551 concerning Archibald Glasgow and Isobell Newlands.

# Determine whether the entry expressly calls Isobell Archibald's wife or merely associates her with the same property.

# Search for Robert Barde's testament, death, property settlement or later appearance between February 1545 and May 1551.

# Search Glasgow diocesan rentals and protocols for further references to Robert Barde and Hysbel Newlandis.

# Determine Patrick Newlandis's relationship to William, Margaret and Hysbel.

# Establish whether David Newlandis, son of Patrick in 1539, was the David later associated with Glendufhill.

# Investigate the documented John Newlandis, eldest son of David, without relying on unsourced FamilySearch dates.

# Verify every proposed child of Archibald Glasgow and Isobell Newlands from contemporary records.

# Search under variant spellings including Newland, Newlands, Newlandis, Newlan, Newlane, Nieland and Nielands.

== Sources ==

Cuthberti Simonis, Notarii Publici et Scribae Capituli Glasguensis, A.D. 1499–1513; also Rental Book of Diocese of Glasgow, A.D. 1509–1570''. Vol. 1. London: Grampian Club, 1875. [https://archive.org/details/liberprotocollor01bain Complete volume at Internet Archive].
* Renwick, Robert, ed. ''Abstracts of Protocols of the Town Clerks of Glasgow''. Vol. 1, ''First Protocol Book of William Hegait, 1547–1555''. Glasgow: Carson & Nicol, 1894. [https://archive.org/details/abstractsofproto01glas Complete volume at Internet Archive].

27485372.Name: Glasgow-1101
27485372.bio:
{{Notables Sticker}}

== Biography ==

'''Archibald Glasgow''' was baptised on '''19 June 1614''' at Glasgow High Kirk. He was recorded as the lawful son of [[Glasgow-1099|George Glasgow]] and [[Stewart-65226|Margaret Steuart]]. William Howie, Michael Broune and Andrew Mylne were named in the baptismal entry.<ref>Glasgow High Kirk Baptisms 1609–1777, vol. 1/1329.</ref>

He graduated '''Master of Arts''' from the University of Glasgow in '''1635'''.<ref>University of Glasgow, University Story, “Archibaldus Glasgua,” graduate, Master of Arts, 1635. https://universitystory.gla.ac.uk/people?search=&surname=Glas&forename=</ref>

== Probable Identification in County Donegal ==

A series of Irish records concerns a clergyman named '''Archibald Glasgow''' who was active in County Donegal between approximately 1641 and 1677.

The records form a geographically and chronologically coherent clerical career and probably concern one man. The uncommon name, chronology and clerical background also create a strong circumstantial case that this was the Archibald Glasgow baptised in Glasgow in 1614 and educated at the University of Glasgow.

No inspected Irish record, however, explicitly identifies the Donegal clergyman as:

* the son of George Glasgow and Margaret Steuart;
* a native of Glasgow;
* the man baptised at Glasgow High Kirk in 1614; or
* the University of Glasgow graduate of 1635.

The identification should therefore be treated as probable rather than conclusively proved.

Records concerning the Irish Archibald include:

* An '''Archibald Glasgow''' serving as rector of '''Killea, County Donegal''', in or before 1641, with later restoration in 1661.<ref>Ulster Plantation and Migration project, person record for Archibald Glasgow. https://ulster-settlers.maynoothuniversity.ie/people/32084</ref>
* A clergyman of that name associated with '''Faughanvale''' in 1654 and '''Taboyne''' in 1660.<ref>Ulster Plantation and Migration project, person record for Archibald Glasgow. https://ulster-settlers.maynoothuniversity.ie/people/32084</ref>
* An Archibald Glasgow possibly mentioned in a 1657 disciplinary record concerning drunkenness.<ref>Virtual Record Treasury of Ireland. https://www.virtualtreasury.ie/item/IMC-AH-15-1944-MacLysaght</ref>
* A cleric named '''Archibald Glasgow''' appointed rector and vicar of '''Clondevadock, Tullyfern and Aughnish''' in County Donegal in April 1661.<ref>James Seaton Reid, ''A History of the Presbyterian Church in Ireland'', 1853, p. 278. https://en.geneanet.org/archives/ouvrages?action=detail&book_type=livre&livre_id=6279357&page=278</ref>
* An '''Archibald Glasgow''' appearing in a County Donegal Hearth Money Roll dated 1665.<ref>Virtual Record Treasury of Ireland, TCD MS 6232. https://www.virtualtreasury.ie/item/TCD-MS-6232</ref>
* '''Archibald Glasgow of Ramelton, County Donegal''', named as obligee in a bond from William Dutton of Greenforte dated 1675/76.<ref>Public Record Office of Northern Ireland, D1825/A/2, bond from William Dutton of Greenforte to Archibald Glasgow of Ramelton, 1675/76.</ref>
* '''Archibald Glasgow of Rathmalton, County Donegal, clerk''', whose prerogative will was proved in '''1677'''.<ref>Sir Arthur Vicars, ''Index to the Prerogative Wills of Ireland, 1536–1810'', entry for Archibald Glasgow, clerk, Rathmalton, County Donegal, 1677. https://archive.org/details/indextoprerogati00vica</ref>
* A separate probate-index transcription records '''Archibald Glascoe of Rathmatton, County Donegal''', in '''1679'''.<ref>Irish probate index transcription supplied July 2026, entry for Archibald Glascoe, Rathmatton, County Donegal, 1679.</ref>

“Rathmalton” was an historical spelling associated with Rathmelton or Ramelton. “Rathmatton” in the 1679 transcription is probably a spelling or transcription variant of the same place. These names should not be confused with Rathmullan.

The Archibald named in the 1675/76 Ramelton bond and the Rathmalton clergyman whose will was proved in 1677 were almost certainly the same person. The uncommon name, occupation, place and close dates strongly support that conclusion.

The 1679 entry probably represents a duplicate index entry, a later probate action or a transcription of the same estate rather than a second local Archibald Glasgow. The two-year discrepancy has not been resolved and should not be silently merged into a single probate date.

If the Donegal clergyman was the man baptised in Glasgow in 1614, he died before probate was granted in 1677, aged approximately 62 or 63. Ramelton was his recorded residence, but it has not been established as his place of death.

== Wife and Children ==

No wife or child has yet been identified from an inspected primary record.

The existence of Archibald’s 1677 prerogative will is potentially important. The original will was probably among the records destroyed in Dublin in 1922, but a pre-destruction genealogical abstract may survive in the notebooks compiled by Sir William Betham.

Such an abstract may identify:

* Archibald’s wife;
* sons or daughters;
* married daughters or sons-in-law;
* siblings;
* executors;
* other legatees; or
* property inherited by his heirs.

The separate 1679 entry should also be investigated to determine whether it represents a duplicate, a later grant, an administration or another action concerning the same estate.

Until a will abstract or another direct record is examined, no spouse or child should be attached to this profile.

== Possible Connection to Thomas Glasgow ==

No record has been found proving that Archibald was the father, brother or other close relative of Thomas Glasgow of Ballindrait, Shannon or Lifford.

Thomas Glasgow was described as being of '''Lifford, County Donegal''', and as an esquire, in connection with the 1689 attainder proceedings. His transactions also place him within the same broad Donegal landholding network as Abraham and James Creighton.

The chronology allows Thomas to have been Archibald’s son, nephew or younger brother, but this is speculation. Archibald’s 1675/76 bond names only Archibald Glasgow and William Dutton and gives no family relationship.

Neither the 1677 nor the 1679 probate-index entry supplies the contents of Archibald’s will or names any beneficiary.

The PRONI catalogue descriptions for Thomas Glasgow’s known transactions likewise name Thomas, Abraham Creighton and James Creighton, but do not identify Thomas’s parents, wife, children, heirs or siblings:

* D1939/18/8/1
* D1939/18/1/3
* D1939/18/3/25
* D1939/18/7/1
* D1939/18/11/16

The full deeds may contain witnesses, recitals, endorsements or inheritance language omitted from the catalogue descriptions.

== Possible Connection to Nathaniel Glasgow ==

No record has been found proving that Archibald was an ancestor or other relative of [[Glasgow-1137|Nathaniel Glasgow]].

The proposed descent:

Archibald Glasgow
|
?
|
Thomas Glasgow of Ballindrait/Shannon/Lifford
|
?
|
Nathaniel Glasgow

remains chronologically and geographically possible, but unsupported by direct kinship evidence.

Neither Archibald’s bond nor the available descriptions of Thomas’s transactions name Nathaniel. Nathaniel’s university record also names no father.

== Other Proposed Relationships ==

A possible relationship with [[Glasgow-992|William Glasgow (1614–)]], who married Bessie Howie, has previously been suggested because the surname Howie appears in Archibald’s baptismal entry.

The presence of the same surname is insufficient to establish that Archibald and William were brothers or cousins. William Howie was named in Archibald’s baptismal entry, but the record does not state that he was a relative.

A connection with [[Glasgow-1097|Archibald Glasgow (c.1533–)]], a burgess and property owner in Glasgow, has also been proposed. The suggested great-uncle and grand-nephew relationship depends upon several reconstructed parent-child links that have not been established from contemporary records.

These relationships should remain research hypotheses.

== Research Priorities ==

The most important unresolved record is the genealogical abstract of Archibald’s 1677 will, if it survives among the Betham notebooks.

Other useful records would include:

* the underlying source for the 1679 Archibald Glascoe probate-index entry;
* records explaining whether the 1679 entry was a duplicate, later grant or administration;
* the complete document for PRONI D1825/A/2;
* complete copies of Thomas Glasgow’s five D1939 transactions;
* Raphoe diocesan probate and administration records;
* marriage bonds and licence indexes;
* parish registers for Killea, Ramelton and neighbouring areas;
* property records naming Archibald’s heirs after 1677; and
* original Glasgow baptismal records for other possible children of George Glasgow and Margaret Steuart.

== Research Conclusion ==

The Donegal records from 1641 to 1677 probably document the career of one clergyman, culminating in the 1675/76 Ramelton bond and the probate of the will of Archibald Glasgow of Rathmalton in 1677.

The 1679 entry for Archibald Glascoe of Rathmatton is probably connected with the same estate, but its precise nature remains unresolved.

Identity with the Archibald Glasgow baptised in Glasgow in 1614 and awarded an M.A. in 1635 is a strong chronological and occupational fit. It remains circumstantial because no inspected Irish record names his Scottish parents, birthplace or university.

No spouse, child or proved line of descent to Thomas Glasgow or Nathaniel Glasgow has been identified.

== Sources ==

<references />

* Glasgow High Kirk Baptisms 1609–1777, vol. 1/1329.
* University of Glasgow graduate records.
* Ulster Plantation and Migration project, person record 32084.
* Public Record Office of Northern Ireland, D1825/A/2.
* Sir Arthur Vicars, ''Index to the Prerogative Wills of Ireland, 1536–1810''.
* Irish probate index transcription, entry for Archibald Glascoe of Rathmatton, 1679.
* Old Parish Records.
* Edinburgh Commissary Court, CC8/8/70.

27858104.Name: Glasgow-1136
27858104.bio:
== Biography ==

'''Nathaniel Glasgow''' was described in the University of Glasgow records as a '''Scoto-Hibernus''', indicating a Scot associated with Ireland. He graduated '''Master of Arts''' from the University of Glasgow in '''1707'''. The university entry does not identify his father or establish that he was born in Glasgow city.<ref>University of Glasgow, University Story, “Nathaniel Glasgow.” [https://www.universitystory.gla.ac.uk/people?search=&surname=glasgow&forename=nathaniel  Nathaniel Glasgow, Graduate]</ref><ref>''Publications'', entry for Nathaniel Glasgow, p. 42. https://www.google.co.uk/books/edition/Publications/hp0gAQAAMAAJ?hl=en&gbpv=1&dq=%22Nathaniel+Glasgow%22&pg=PA42</ref>

A later scholarly study identifies him as a native of '''Keady, County Donegal'''.<ref>Rankin Sherling, doctoral dissertation, Queen’s University. https://qspace.library.queensu.ca/bitstream/1974/7622/1/Sherling_Rankin_201210_PhD.pdf</ref> The underlying evidence for that statement has not yet been examined. His precise birthplace should therefore be treated as uncertain, probably in Scotland or Ireland, rather than assigned to Glasgow solely from his surname and university attendance.

Nathaniel was ordained by the Presbytery of Monaghan in '''1719''', apparently with the intention that he would serve in America. He did not emigrate and instead entered the Presbyterian ministry in Ireland.

Later congregational histories place him at '''Ballyjamesduff''', where he is reported to have been installed on '''3 February 1721'''. The evidence for this part of his ministry is less direct than the record of his later appointment at Golan.<ref name="Killen">William Dool Killen, ''A History of the Congregations of the Presbyterian Church in Ireland'', pp. 36 and 145. https://archive.org/details/historyofcongreg00kill</ref>

On '''5 April 1732''', Nathaniel was installed as minister of '''Golan''', also written Golen, the congregation later known as '''Fintona'''.<ref name="Killen" />

Nathaniel continued in the ministry there until his death in '''April 1743'''. Contemporary records of the General Synod of Ulster report his death during that month.<ref name="Synod">''Records of the General Synod of Ulster'', vol. 2, pp. 284, 314 and 339. https://archive.org/details/recordsofgeneral02pres</ref>

The year 1732 was the year of his installation at Golan, not the year of his death or retirement.

== Probate ==

An Irish probate-index transcription records a '''Nathaniel Glasgow''' in the Diocese of Clogher in '''1746''', with the residence given as '''Cavan, Donaghcavey'''. The entry has also been indexed under Cavan, County Tyrone.<ref>Irish probate index transcription supplied July 2026, entry for Nathaniel Glasgow, Diocese of Clogher, 1746, residence Cavan, Donaghcavey.</ref>

Donaghcavey parish contains Fintona, the later name associated with Nathaniel’s Golan congregation. The uncommon name, matching locality and three-year interval after his death make this a strong identity match.

The delay between Nathaniel’s death in April 1743 and the 1746 probate entry may reflect ordinary estate administration rather than a different person. The index itself, however, does not identify an occupation, widow, child, executor or other relative. The identification should therefore be described as highly probable rather than conclusively proved.

The probate entry is evidence of post-death estate proceedings. It does not prove that Nathaniel died at Donaghcavey, Cavan or Fintona, and his place of death remains uncertain.

== Wife and Children ==

No record has yet been found that identifies Nathaniel’s wife or children by name.

The records of the General Synod refer after Nathaniel’s death to a poor widow named '''Glasgow'''. In 1748, the Synod granted assistance to “the children of Mr Glasgow, deceased.”<ref name="Synod" />

These entries establish that Nathaniel left:

* an unnamed widow; and
* at least two unnamed children.

The plural wording “children” supports a minimum of two children, but the surviving Synod minutes do not give their names, ages, sexes or places of residence.

The 1746 probate record may be particularly important. A surviving copy, abstract, administration bond or related diocesan record could identify:

* Nathaniel’s widow;
* his children;
* executors or administrators;
* guardians acting for minor children;
* relatives or sureties; or
* property belonging to the estate.

No spouse or child should be created or attached without a record naming that person.

== Family and Relationship Research ==

No inspected record conclusively identifies Nathaniel’s parents or siblings.

A descent from Thomas Glasgow of Ballindrait, Shannon or Lifford remains chronologically and geographically possible, but no record examined to date names Nathaniel as Thomas’s son.

There is likewise no proven relationship between Nathaniel and:

* [[Glasgow-1101|Archibald Glasgow M.A. (1614–bef.1677)]];
* [[Glasgow-3410|Jacob or James Glasgow M.A. (1700–)]];
* Thomas Glasgow of Ballindrait, Shannon or Lifford; or
* any other identified Glasgow family in seventeenth-century Donegal.

The proposed descent:

Archibald Glasgow
|
?
|
Thomas Glasgow of Ballindrait, Shannon or Lifford
|
?
|
Nathaniel Glasgow
|
unnamed widow
|
at least two unnamed children

is a research hypothesis only. Each question mark represents an unproved relationship.

Nathaniel’s description as ''Scoto-Hibernus'' supports an association with both Scotland and Ireland. It does not prove:

* birth in Glasgow;
* descent from the Glasgow family of that city;
* descent from Archibald Glasgow of Ramelton;
* descent from Thomas Glasgow of Lifford; or
* any specific Scottish birthplace.

Geography, chronology, education and surname similarity are useful research leads but are insufficient to attach parents or siblings.

== Research Notes ==

A publication issued in 1725 under the name “Nathaniel Glasgow” should not be attributed to this Nathaniel. The catalogue identifies the author as '''“Nathaniel Glasgow (pseud.)”''', showing that the name was a pen name.<ref>Google Books catalogue, ''A Letter to the Magistrates and Town Council of Glasgow''. https://books.google.com/books?id=AIHsPQAACAAJ</ref>

A Nathaniel Glasgow recorded as a demonstrator in a dental department in 1891 was a much later person and is unrelated to this profile.

The description of Nathaniel as a native of Keady should be retained as a secondary-source statement unless the original evidence used by the author can be identified. It should not be converted into a certain birth location without further support.

== Research Priorities ==

Future research should concentrate on:

* the original or fullest surviving record behind the 1746 Clogher probate-index entry;
* Clogher diocesan wills, administrations, bonds and probate abstracts;
* Fintona, Golan or Golen congregational records;
* Presbytery of Monaghan minutes;
* Synod widow and orphan-support accounts;
* estate or guardianship records created after Nathaniel’s death;
* records identifying the person who received financial support on behalf of Nathaniel’s children;
* marriage records for Presbyterian ministers in County Tyrone and neighbouring counties;
* burial records for Fintona and Donaghcavey;
* records supporting the claim that Nathaniel was a native of Keady; and
* contemporary records naming Nathaniel’s father, siblings or other relatives.

== Research Conclusion ==

Nathaniel Glasgow was a University of Glasgow graduate and Presbyterian minister associated with Ballyjamesduff and later Golan or Fintona.

Contemporary Synod evidence establishes that he died in '''April 1743''', leaving an unnamed widow and at least two unnamed children.

The 1746 Clogher probate entry for Nathaniel Glasgow of Donaghcavey is a strong match to the deceased minister because Donaghcavey includes Fintona. It probably concerns the administration of his estate, although the index does not name relatives or explicitly identify him as a minister.

His birthplace remains uncertain. The university description ''Scoto-Hibernus'' indicates a Scottish-Irish association but does not establish birth in Glasgow city. A later study’s identification of Keady, County Donegal, should be treated as a secondary-source claim pending examination of its underlying evidence.

No parent, spouse, child or sibling has yet been identified by name. No descent from Archibald Glasgow of Ramelton or Thomas Glasgow of Lifford has been proved.

=== Widow and children ===
In 1745 relief was recorded for a poor widow Glasgow, and in 1748 the Synod referred to the children of the deceased Rev. Nathaniel Glasgow in connection with the Golen congregation, later Fintona. The children were not named, and the widow was not explicitly identified as Nathaniel's wife; the entries establish a bereaved family context but not individual identities.<ref>[https://archive.org/stream/recordsofgeneral02pres/recordsofgeneral02pres_djvu.txt Underlying record source: widow glasgow].</ref><ref>[https://archive.org/stream/recordsofgeneral02pres/recordsofgeneral02pres_djvu.txt Underlying record source: children of mr glasgow].</ref>

27920473.Name: Glasgow-1150
27920473.bio:
{{One Name Study|name=Glasgow}}

== Biography ==

'''James Glasgow''' was born before 16 June 1641, probably in Scotland. His precise date and place of birth have not been identified.

He became a weaver and burgess of Edinburgh.

=== Apprenticeship and burgess status ===

On 16 June 1641 James, explicitly described as a son of '''Robert Glasgow, servant to William Crichtoun in Wester Duddingston''', was apprenticed to William Sclaitter, weaver.<ref name="Apprentice1641">Francis J. Grant, ed., ''Register of Apprentices of the City of Edinburgh, 1583–1666'' (Scottish Record Society, 1906), printed p. 71, [https://archive.org/details/scottishrecordso28scotuoft/page/71/mode/2up scan]: “Glasgow, James, son to Robert G., servitor to William Crichtoun, in Wester Duddingston, with William Sclaitter, weaver 16 June 1641.”</ref>

James was admitted as a burgess of Edinburgh on 20 June 1649. The entry identifies him as a weaver, states that he had been apprenticed to the deceased William Sklatter, and repeats the apprenticeship date of 16 June 1641.<ref name="Burgess1649">Charles B. Boog Watson, ed., [https://www.tradeshouselibrary.org/uploads/4/7/7/2/47723681/roll_of_edinburgh_burgesses_1406_to_1700.pdf#page=218 ''Roll of Edinburgh Burgesses and Guild-Brethren, 1406–1700''] (Scottish Record Society, 1929), printed p. 208: “Glasgow, James, B., weiver, as p. to umq. Wm. Sklaitter, weiver, B. (16 June 1641) 20 June 1649.”</ref>

The matching master and exact apprenticeship date establish that the 1641 apprentice was the later Edinburgh weaver and burgess.

=== Marriages ===

James married first '''[[Whyte-2772|Bessie Whyte]]''' at Edinburgh on 6 July 1649.<ref name="EdinburghMarriages">Henry Paton, ed., [https://www.tradeshouselibrary.org/uploads/4/7/7/2/47723681/register_of_marriages_for_the_parish_of_edinburgh_1595-1700_~_1898.pdf#page=277 ''Register of Marriages for the Parish of Edinburgh, 1595–1700''] (Scottish Record Society, 1905), printed p. 267: “Glasgow, James, weaver; Bessie Whyte 6 July 1649” and “James, weaver; Agnes Duncan 11 Nov. 1653.”</ref>

He married second '''[[Duncan-16106|Agnes Duncan]]''' at Edinburgh on 11 November 1653.<ref name="EdinburghMarriages" />

The matching name, occupation and parish, together with the sequential dates, identify the bridegroom in both entries as the same James Glasgow.

=== Children ===

James's known children were:

* '''[[Glasgow-3097|Helen Glasgow]]''', daughter of Bessie Whyte;
* '''[[Glasgow-3099|Jonet Glasgow]]''', daughter of Bessie Whyte;
* '''[[Glasgow-1374|Robert Glasgow]]''', son of Agnes Duncan;<ref name="RobertBaptism">“Scotland, Births and Baptisms, 1564–1950,” database, ''FamilySearch'', [https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:VRSV-T1T Robert Glasgow, baptised 5 May 1655, Edinburgh], son of James Glasgow and Agnes Duncan.</ref>
* '''[[Glasgow-3143|Marion Glasgow]]''', daughter of Agnes Duncan;
* '''[[Glasgow-1373|Bethia Glasgow]]''', daughter of Agnes Duncan; and
* '''[[Glasgow-1057|John Glasgow]]''', son of Agnes Duncan.

The individual baptismal records should be consulted for the evidence identifying each child's mother.

Marion Glasgow married William Calder at Edinburgh on 29 June 1686.<ref name="MarionMarriage">Henry Paton, ed., [https://www.tradeshouselibrary.org/uploads/4/7/7/2/47723681/register_of_marriages_for_the_parish_of_edinburgh_1595-1700_~_1898.pdf#page=278 ''Register of Marriages for the Parish of Edinburgh, 1595–1700''] (Scottish Record Society, 1905), printed p. 268: “Glasgow, Marion; William Calder 29 June 1686.”</ref>

On the following day William Calder was admitted as a burgess through his wife Marion, who was explicitly described as a daughter of James Glasgow, weaver and burgess.<ref name="CalderBurgess">Charles B. Boog Watson, ed., [https://www.tradeshouselibrary.org/uploads/4/7/7/2/47723681/roll_of_edinburgh_burgesses_1406_to_1700.pdf#page=101 ''Roll of Edinburgh Burgesses and Guild-Brethren, 1406–1700''] (Scottish Record Society, 1929), printed p. 91: “Calder, Wm., B., weaver, be r. of w. Marion, dr. to James Glasgow, weaver, B. 30 June 1686.”</ref>

This directly establishes Marion as James's daughter.

James's date and place of death have not been identified.

== Research Notes ==

=== Birth ===

The former birth date of 19 March 1626 and birthplace of Inveresk do not belong to this James.

The only presently supported birth statement is that James was born before 16 June 1641, when he entered his apprenticeship.<ref name="Apprentice1641" />

His birthplace remains unknown.

=== Parentage ===

The apprenticeship record directly identifies James's father as '''Robert Glasgow, servant to William Crichtoun in Wester Duddingston'''.<ref name="Apprentice1641" />

'''[[Glasgow-1156|Robert Glasgow]]''' is a plausible existing-profile match for this father because of the Wester Duddingston association and chronology. The record does not, however, contain enough information to prove that the named father and the existing profile represent the same man. That relationship should therefore remain uncertain.

The record does not name James's mother.

'''[[Ivey-2264|Deborah Ivey]]''' is not identified as his mother in any inspected record. Any attachment should remain uncertain and be treated as a working hypothesis rather than an established relationship.

=== Distinct from the Inveresk James ===

This James was not '''[[Glasgow-3923|James Glasgow]]''', who was baptised at Inveresk and Musselburgh on 19 March 1626 as a son of [[Glasgow-1148|Alexander Glasgow]] and [[Clerk-296|Jannet Clerk]].<ref name="InvereskBaptism">“Scotland, Births and Baptisms, 1564–1950,” database, ''FamilySearch'', James Glasgow, baptised 19 March 1626, Inveresk and Musselburgh, son of Alexander Glasgow, [https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:VQ4V-GQW record VQ4V-GQW] (accessed 2025).</ref>

The 1641 apprenticeship names Robert Glasgow, not Alexander Glasgow, as the father of the Edinburgh weaver. The two men should remain on separate profiles.

=== Incorrect child profile ===

'''[[Glasgow-1376|James Glasgow]]''' is not a supported child of this family and should not be attached as a son born on 29 January 1657.

The cited record for that date is the baptism of Marion Glasgow and names James Glasgow as her father. It is not a birth or baptism record for a son named James.

=== Identity caution ===

This James should not be confused with '''[[Glasgow-3077|James Glasgow]]''', who married [[Clerk-460|Helen Clerk]] and was associated with [[Glasgow-3093|John Glasgow]].

The Edinburgh weaver is identified by:

* the 1641 apprenticeship naming him as a son of Robert Glasgow;
* his apprenticeship to William Sclaitter;
* his 1649 admission as an Edinburgh burgess;
* his occupation as a weaver;
* his marriages to Bessie Whyte and Agnes Duncan; and
* the 1686 burgess record identifying Marion Glasgow as his daughter.

=== Further research ===

Useful remaining records include:

* the original apprenticeship papers or incorporation records;
* records establishing whether [[Glasgow-1156|Robert Glasgow]] was the father named in the apprenticeship;
* records identifying James's mother;
* original baptism entries for each child;
* any further records establishing the children's mothers;
* a burial or testament for James;
* records identifying James's birthplace; and
* further records concerning William Calder and Marion Glasgow.

27923171.Name: Glasgow-1156
27923171.bio:
{{One Name Study|name=Glasgow}}

== Biography ==

'''Robert Glasgow''' was buried in the parish of Duddingston, Midlothian, Scotland, on '''17 January 1647'''.<ref name="RobertBurial">Church of Scotland, Old Parish Registers, Duddingston deaths and burials, burial of Robert Glasgow, 17 January 1647, parish number 684, reference 60/47, ''ScotlandsPeople''.</ref>

His date and place of birth have not been identified.

The burial entry does not state Robert's age, occupation, residence, spouse, parentage or children. It should not be assumed that every contemporary man named Robert Glasgow in Midlothian was the same person.

== Research Notes ==

=== Profile identity ===

This profile represents the '''Robert Glasgow buried at Duddingston on 17 January 1647'''.

The burial is the only record presently identified that can be assigned to this profile with reasonable certainty. Other records involving men of the same name are discussed below as possible or rejected identifications.

Because the record is a burial entry rather than an identified death entry, Robert died on or before 17 January 1647. His precise date of death is unknown.

=== Birth ===

The structured birth year of about 1582 and the Glasgow birthplace are retained as uncertain working estimates.

No inspected record states Robert's age or birthplace or supports either estimate. They should not be treated as proved facts.

Although Robert was buried in Scotland, the burial record does not establish that he was born there.

=== Possible identification at Wester Duddingston ===

On 16 June 1641 '''[[Glasgow-1150|James Glasgow]]''', son of a Robert Glasgow who was servant to William Crichtoun in Wester Duddingston, was apprenticed to William Sclaitter, weaver.<ref name="JamesApprentice">Francis J. Grant, ed., [https://archive.org/details/scottishrecordso28scotuoft/page/71/mode/2up ''Register of Apprentices of the City of Edinburgh, 1583–1666''] (Scottish Record Society, 1906), printed p. 71: “Glasgow, James, son to Robert G., servitor to William Crichtoun, in Wester Duddingston, with William Sclaitter, weaver 16 June 1641.”</ref>

The record directly proves that:

* James's father was named Robert Glasgow;
* the elder Robert was associated with Wester Duddingston in 1641;
* Robert was then a servant to William Crichtoun; and
* James was apprenticed to William Sclaitter.

The matching surname, Duddingston locality and compatible dates make the father named in 1641 a plausible candidate for the man buried there in 1647.

The identification is not proved. Neither record supplies Robert's age, wife, occupation beyond the 1641 description, or another distinguishing relationship that securely joins the two entries.

If James remains attached as a son of this Robert, the relationship should be marked uncertain.

=== James Glasgow the Edinburgh weaver ===

The apprentice named in 1641 was later admitted as a burgess of Edinburgh on 20 June 1649. The burgess entry identifies him as a weaver, names his deceased master William Sklaitter and repeats the exact apprenticeship date of 16 June 1641.<ref name="JamesBurgess">Charles B. Boog Watson, ed., [https://www.tradeshouselibrary.org/uploads/4/7/7/2/47723681/roll_of_edinburgh_burgesses_1406_to_1700.pdf#page=218 ''Roll of Edinburgh Burgesses and Guild-Brethren, 1406–1700''] (Scottish Record Society, 1929), printed p. 208: “Glasgow, James, B., weiver, as p. to umq. Wm. Sklaitter, weiver, B. (16 June 1641) 20 June 1649.”</ref>

The matching master and exact apprenticeship date establish that the 1641 apprentice and the later Edinburgh burgess were the same James Glasgow.

This evidence strengthens the identification of James but does not provide additional information identifying his father with the man buried in 1647.

=== Distinct from the Inveresk James ===

The Edinburgh apprentice was not '''[[Glasgow-3923|James Glasgow]]''', who was baptised at Inveresk and Musselburgh on 19 March 1626 as a son of Alexander Glasgow and Jannet Clerk.<ref name="InvereskJames">“Scotland, Births and Baptisms, 1564–1950,” database, ''FamilySearch'', [https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:VQ4V-GQW James Glasgow, baptised 19 March 1626, Inveresk and Musselburgh], son of Alexander Glasgow.</ref>

The 1641 apprenticeship explicitly names Robert Glasgow, not Alexander Glasgow, as the father of the Edinburgh weaver.

The two men should remain on separate profiles.

=== Possible father ===

'''[[Glasgow-1097|Archibald Glasgow]]''' is attached as Robert's uncertain father.

Archibald and his wife Isobell Neulands are documented acquiring a tenement in Glasgow on 21 May 1551.<ref name="Archibald1551">Robert Renwick, ed., ''Abstracts of Protocols of the Town Clerks of Glasgow'', vol. 1, ''First Protocol Book of William Hegait, 1547–55'' (Glasgow: Carson & Nicol, 1894), protocol 84, 21 May 1551, printed p. 31: Elizabeth Beitht sold a tenement to “Archinbald Glasgw and Isobell Neulands, spouses.” Robert Glasgw was among the witnesses.</ref>

The record does not name any children of Archibald and Isobell. It also does not state that Robert Glasgw, one of the witnesses, was Archibald's brother, son or other relative.

The proposed father-and-son relationship is chronologically possible. Archibald was married by 1551, and Robert's birth date is unknown. A son born later in the sixteenth century could have been the Robert associated with Wester Duddingston in 1641 and buried there in 1647.

There is presently no direct evidence establishing the relationship. No baptism, testament, sasine, deed or other inspected contemporary record identifies Robert as Archibald's son.

There is likewise no known record identifying a different father for Robert, and no better-supported profile has been identified as a child of Archibald.

Archibald may therefore remain attached as Robert's father with the relationship marked '''uncertain'''. The relationship should not be described as proved, probable or likely without further evidence.


=== Validator chronology note ===
WikiTree's warning that [[Glasgow-1097|Archibald Glasgow]] died before Robert was born is not a valid reading of the structured data. Archibald's death is recorded as '''after 1560''', an open lower boundary rather than a death in 1560. Robert's 1582 birth is an uncertain estimate, and their father-son relationship is itself marked uncertain. No source currently proves when Archibald died or that Robert was his son.

=== Deborah Ivey ===

'''[[Ivey-2264|Deborah Ivey]]''' has previously been attached as Robert's wife.

No Scottish marriage, baptism, testament, sasine, court record or other contemporary source has been found identifying Deborah as Robert's wife or as the mother of James Glasgow.

The attachment appears to derive from later compiled pedigrees involving Glasgow, Glasco, Glascocke or Glasscock families rather than from records concerning the Duddingston man.

Deborah should be detached from this profile.

=== Distinct from the Edinburgh cordiner ===

'''[[Glasgow-3938|Robert Glasgow]]''' married Jonet or Janet Thomsone at Edinburgh on 1 July 1652. The marriage register identifies that Robert as a cordiner.<ref name="CordinerMarriage">Henry Paton, ed., [https://www.tradeshouselibrary.org/uploads/4/7/7/2/47723681/register_of_marriages_for_the_parish_of_edinburgh_1595-1700_~_1898.pdf#page=278 ''Register of Marriages for the Parish of Edinburgh, 1595–1700''] (Scottish Record Society, 1905), printed p. 268: “Glasgow, Robert, cordiner; Janet Thomsone 1 July 1652.”</ref>

The Duddingston Robert was buried in January 1647 and therefore could not have been the bridegroom in July 1652.

The two men are conclusively distinct and should remain on separate profiles.

No evidence presently identifies the Edinburgh cordiner as a son of the Duddingston Robert.

=== Daniel Glasco ===

Daniel Glasco, husband of Mary Gamon, is documented in Lower Norfolk County, Virginia, through the will of his father-in-law John Gamon, dated 4 October 1693 and proved 15 March 1694.

No inspected record identifies Daniel as a son of the Robert buried at Duddingston.

The supposed relationship depends on unsourced submitted pedigrees and should be removed.

There is likewise no evidence that the Duddingston Robert:

* travelled to Virginia;
* had children in colonial America;
* belonged to the Glasco, Glascocke or Glasscock families;
* married Ann Johnson or Johnston; or
* participated in any Scottish-to-Virginia migration.

=== Occupation and social status ===

If the 1641 Wester Duddingston record concerns this Robert, he was described as a servant to William Crichtoun.

The term does not establish that Robert was a merchant, burgess, property owner or participant in civic government. No evidence presently supports those descriptions.

There is also no evidence that Robert migrated from the burgh of Glasgow to Edinburgh or Duddingston. His surname alone does not identify his place of origin.

=== Wife and other children ===

No inspected record identifies the wife of the Robert buried in 1647.

James Glasgow is the only proposed child supported by a contemporary record naming a father called Robert Glasgow in Wester Duddingston. Even that identification remains uncertain because the apprenticeship record does not directly connect the father to the 1647 burial.

No other children should be attached without independent evidence.

=== Further research ===

Useful remaining research includes:

* inspection and transcription of the original 1647 Duddingston burial entry;
* Duddingston baptism, marriage and burial registers;
* neighbouring parish registers, including Canongate, Liberton and Inveresk;
* Edinburgh Commissary Court testaments;
* Midlothian sasines, rentals and property records;
* records concerning William Crichtoun of Wester Duddingston;
* household, estate or employment records naming William Crichtoun's servants;
* the original apprenticeship papers for James Glasgow;
* records of the Edinburgh Incorporation of Weavers;
* evidence identifying James Glasgow's mother;
* records naming the wife or other children of the Wester Duddingston Robert;
* a testament or estate inventory for the man buried in 1647; and
* evidence directly linking or separating the 1641 and 1647 records.

27923176.Name: Glasgow-1157
27923176.bio:
{{Conflated}}
{{One Name Study|name=Glasgow}}

== Biography ==

'''Robert Glasgow''' is the name used in later compiled genealogies for the supposed husband of '''Ann Johnson''', also reported as Ann Johnston, and the alleged father of several people associated with colonial Virginia.

Robert's date and place of birth have not been identified. No inspected contemporary record names his parents, occupation, wife or children.

=== Reported marriage to Ann Johnson ===

Later family trees and compiled genealogies represent Robert as the husband of '''Ann Johnson''' or '''Ann Johnston'''.

No marriage record, deed, will, court order, parish entry, land record or other contemporary source has yet been found identifying Robert and Ann as spouses.

A 1994 compiled family history has been cited for the family, but it was written more than three centuries after the supposed marriage and does not itself constitute primary evidence.<ref name="Topping">Thomas Rudolph Topping, comp., [https://www.familysearch.org/library/books/records/item/154949-topping-latham-family-history-and-allied-families-alligood-brewer-chilton-ethridge-glasgow-satchwell-shavender-sillery-wiggins-windley-and-winstead-generation-to-generation ''Topping/Latham Family History and Allied Families: Alligood, Brewer, Chilton, Ethridge, Glasgow, Satchwell, Shavender, Sillery, Wiggins, Windley and Winstead: Generation to Generation''] (Charlotte, North Carolina: compiler, 1994), FamilySearch Digital Library book 154949. The underlying contemporary evidence for Robert's marriage, dates and children has not been identified.</ref>

The relationship to Ann should remain marked uncertain unless a contemporary record naming the couple together is found.

=== Possible identification with Robert Glascocke ===

A man recorded as '''Robert Glascocke''' was living in the Elizabeth River area of colonial Virginia during the 1630s and 1640.

On '''7 October 1635''' Robert Glascocke received a patent for 200 acres in Elizabeth City County. The land was situated on the south side of the main river, adjoining land of Lieutenant Cheeseman. The patent was granted for the transportation of four servants.<ref name="Patent1635">Nell Marion Nugent, ed., [https://archive.org/details/cavalierspioneer00nuge/page/33/mode/2up ''Cavaliers and Pioneers: Abstracts of Virginia Land Patents and Grants, 1623–1800''], vol. 1 (Richmond, Virginia: Dietz Printing Company, 1934), p. 33, abstract of Virginia Patent Book 1, p. 290: patent to Robert Glascocke, 200 acres, Elizabeth City County, 7 October 1635.</ref>

On '''10 June 1639''' Robert Glascocke received a further patent for 50 acres in Lower New Norfolk County. The property was situated up the western branch of the Elizabeth River, above the land of Jonathan Langworth. The patent was granted for the transportation of Iszabella Dixon.<ref name="Patent1639">Nell Marion Nugent, ed., [https://archive.org/details/cavalierspioneer00nuge/page/111/mode/2up ''Cavaliers and Pioneers: Abstracts of Virginia Land Patents and Grants, 1623–1800''], vol. 1 (Richmond, Virginia: Dietz Printing Company, 1934), p. 111, abstract of Virginia Patent Book 1, p. 658: patent to Robert Glascocke, 50 acres, Lower New Norfolk County, 10 June 1639.</ref>

A Lower Norfolk County court order dated '''6 July 1640''' directed that the local minister preach every other Sunday at the house of Robert Glascocke until a church could be built for the inhabitants of the Elizabeth River area.<ref name="Court1640">Edward W. James, ed., [https://archive.org/details/lowernorfolkcoun01newy/page/84/mode/2up ''The Lower Norfolk County Virginia Antiquary''], vol. 1 (1895; reprint, New York: Peter Smith, 1951), p. 84, Lower Norfolk County court order, 6 July 1640: the minister was to preach at the house of Robert Glascocke until a church was constructed.</ref>

The matching name and Elizabeth River locality make it probable that the patents and court order concern the same Robert Glascocke.

These records prove that a man named Robert Glascocke owned land and maintained a household in the Elizabeth River area between 1635 and 1640. They do not identify:

* his wife;
* any children;
* his age or birthplace;
* his parents;
* a connection with Scotland;
* a connection with Ann Johnson or Johnston; or
* a connection with Daniel Glasco.

The identity of Robert Glascocke with the Robert Glasgow represented by this profile remains uncertain. The surnames should not be treated as interchangeable without a record demonstrating that they referred to the same family.

=== Reported children ===

Later family trees have attributed several children to Robert and Ann, including:

* Edward Travis Glasgow;
* Robert Glasgow;
* Thomas Glasgow;
* Mary Glasgow, later represented as a wife of a Moncrief; and
* Daniel or William Daniel Glasgow.

No inspected contemporary record identifies any of these people as a child of Robert Glasgow and Ann Johnson or Johnston.

The reported relationships appear to derive from compiled pedigrees rather than original colonial records. They should remain uncertain or be removed unless independent evidence is found.

=== Daniel Glasco and Mary Gamon ===

A Daniel Glasco is independently documented in Lower Norfolk County during the 1690s.

The will of John Gamon, dated 4 October 1693 and proved 15 March 1694, identified Daniel Glasco as Gamon's son-in-law and named Daniel's wife as Mary. John Gamon left the couple eighty acres bordering Richford Swamp.<ref name="GamonWill">Charles Fleming McIntosh, ''Brief Abstract of Lower Norfolk County and Norfolk County Wills, 1637–1710'' (Virginia: Colonial Dames of America, 1914), p. 149, abstract of the will of John Gamon, dated 4 October 1693 and proved 15 March 1694; discussed in Legacy Tree Genealogists, [https://www.legacytree.com/wp-content/uploads/T1508095.CLIENTGlasgow1508.report.public.pdf “Research Report”] (1 March 2016), pp. 3–4.</ref>

That record proves:

* Daniel Glasco was married to Mary Gamon by October 1693;
* John Gamon was Mary's father; and
* Daniel and Mary were associated with Lower Norfolk County.

The will does not identify Daniel's parents.

A professional review of the family found that online trees commonly represented Daniel as a son of Robert Glasgow and Ann Johnson, but those trees supplied no documentary evidence for the relationship.<ref name="LegacyReport">Legacy Tree Genealogists, [https://www.legacytree.com/wp-content/uploads/T1508095.CLIENTGlasgow1508.report.public.pdf “Research Report”] (1 March 2016), pp. 3–4: the report noted that online trees asserted Daniel Glasco was a son of Robert Glasgow and Ann Johnson but provided no documentary support.</ref>

Daniel should not be attached as a certain son of Robert and Ann.

=== Unsupported birth and death information ===

Robert has previously been assigned a birth date of about 1612 in Scotland and a death date of about 1690 in Virginia.

No inspected record supports either date or place.

The earliest record belonging to the possible Virginia candidate is the 1635 patent to Robert Glascocke. This proves only that the patentee was living by 7 October 1635.

The latest presently inspected record is the Lower Norfolk County court order of 6 July 1640. If the Glascocke records concern the man represented by this profile, Robert was alive on that date.

A death date after 6 July 1640 may therefore be used only as uncertain. The former 1690 estimate should be removed.

=== Distinct from Scottish Robert Glasgows ===

This Robert should not be confused with '''[[Glasgow-3938|Robert Glasgow]]''', the cordiner who married Jonet or Janet Thomsone at Edinburgh on 1 July 1652.

The Edinburgh marriage record explicitly describes that Robert as a cordiner in Edinburgh. It contains no connection with Virginia, Ann Johnson or the colonial Glasco family.

This Robert should also not be confused with the Robert Glasgow buried at Duddingston, Midlothian, on 17 January 1647. No inspected record connects the Duddingston man with Virginia or with Ann Johnson.

Shared names and approximate chronology do not establish identity.

=== Ann's identity ===

No inspected record establishes:

* whether Ann's surname was Johnson or Johnston;
* her date or place of birth;
* her parents;
* a marriage to Robert;
* the identity of any children; or
* the reported death in James City County in 1682.

Her profile should not state these details as facts without contemporary evidence.

=== Possible Glasscock conflation ===

The Virginia records consistently identify the documented landholder as '''Robert Glascocke'''.

Separate compiled pedigrees associate a Robert Glasscock or Glascock with a wife named Deborah Ivey. Those pedigrees may have contributed to the later combination of the Glasgow, Glasco, Glascocke and Glasscock families.

No inspected record proves that:

* Robert Glascocke used the surname Glasgow;
* the Glascocke and Glasgow families were the same paternal family;
* Deborah Ivey was connected with this Robert;
* Robert married both Deborah Ivey and Ann Johnson; or
* either woman was the mother of Daniel Glasco.

Deborah Ivey should not be attached to this profile.

=== DNA evidence ===

A 2016 research report examined Y-DNA from a documented later Glasgow line. The tested line did not match the group then represented in the Glasgow surname project and instead had close matches to men bearing the Murtishaw or related surnames.<ref name="LegacyDNA">Legacy Tree Genealogists, [https://www.legacytree.com/wp-content/uploads/T1508095.CLIENTGlasgow1508.report.public.pdf “Research Report”] (1 March 2016), pp. 4–10.</ref>

The result may indicate a paternal-line break somewhere among the later descendants, or a separate paternal origin for that particular Glasgow line. It does not identify where such a break occurred and does not prove or disprove the existence of this Robert or his reported marriage to Ann.

=== Further research ===

Useful remaining research includes:

* the original 1635 and 1639 Virginia land patents;
* all surviving Lower Norfolk County court orders mentioning Robert Glascocke;
* Lower Norfolk and Elizabeth City County deeds and probate material;
* records concerning the later ownership of the Glascocke patents;
* any estate administration for Robert Glascocke;
* records identifying his wife, heirs or nearest relatives;
* evidence establishing whether Glascocke, Glasco and Glasgow were used for the same family;
* the original source used by the 1994 Topping compilation;
* records concerning Ann Johnson or Johnston;
* evidence identifying the parents of Daniel Glasco;
* records concerning the attributed children Edward, Robert, Thomas and Mary; and
* evidence connecting or separating the Virginia Glascocke and Glasco families.

== Sources ==

<references />

== Acknowledgements ==

This profile was separated from Scottish records formerly combined with the colonial Virginia family. The documented Edinburgh cordiner is now represented by '''[[Glasgow-3938|Robert Glasgow]]'''.

28110610.Name: Glasgow-1168
28110610.bio:
[[Category:Stevenston, Ayrshire]]

[[Category:Glasgow Name Study]]

== Biography ==

'''James Glasgow''' was a tenant at Corsinkell in the parish and barony of Stevenston, Ayrshire. He was probably born about 1515, although his precise date and place of birth have not been identified.

The estimate is based on the presence of an adult or near-adult son, also named James, at Corsinkell by 1559–1560. It is an approximate generational estimate rather than a date stated in any record.

=== Corsinkell ===

A reconstructed list of Cunninghame teind debtors for 1559–1560 names Katherine Campbell, James Glasgow younger and James Glasgow elder under Corsinkell in Stevenston parish.<ref name="TeindList">Margaret H. B. Sanderson, [https://aanhs.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/05/people-of-ayrshire.pdf#page=36 “The People of Sixteenth Century Ayrshire,”] ''Ayrshire Collections'' 14, no. 8 (1987), appendix, “The Cunninghame Teind Lists of 1559–60,” printed p. 331, citing Register of Acts and Decreets, vol. 22, fols. 102v–167v.</ref>

The designations “elder” and “younger” establish that two men named James Glasgow were present at the same holding. That record alone does not state their relationship.

On 9 February 1571 letters of reversion concerning an annual rent from the 40-shilling land of Corsinkell named the occupiers as James Glasgow elder, James Glasgow and John Glasgow, his sons, and Christian Campbell.<ref name="NRS1571">National Records of Scotland, Charter Chest of the Earls of Glencairn, [https://catalogue.nrscotland.gov.uk/nrsonlinecatalogue/details.aspx?reference=GD39%2F5%2F59 GD39/5/59], letters of reversion concerning annual rent from the 40-shilling land of Corsinkell, barony of Stevenston, sheriffdom of Ayr, dated 9 February 1571.</ref>

This directly establishes that James elder had sons named James and John.

=== Children ===

James's record-confirmed sons were:

* '''[[Glasgow-3921|James Glasgow, younger]]''', present with James elder at Corsinkell in 1559–1560 and explicitly identified as his son in 1571; and
* '''[[Glasgow-3193|John Glasgow]]''', the record-defined Corsinkell son explicitly identified in 1571.

[[Glasgow-3193|John Glasgow of the Kilwinning district]] remains a possible identity match for the record-defined son because Burrowland, Dalgarven and Corsinkell were all in northern Ayrshire. No reviewed deed connects those holdings, so Glasgow-3193 remains separate and his father link remains uncertain.

[[Glasgow-3178|Agnes Glasgow]] was formerly attached as a daughter, but no reviewed source identifies her parents. The 1571 record names two sons and does not address daughters.

=== Death ===

James was living on 9 February 1571.<ref name="NRS1571" />

His date and place of death have not been identified. The supported death statement is therefore '''after 9 February 1571, place unknown'''.

A death date in or after November 1580 appears to derive from conflation with a different Glasgow family and should not be applied to this profile without additional evidence.

== Research Notes ==

=== Birth estimate ===

The former estimate of about 1540 is too late.

James Glasgow younger was separately listed alongside James elder at Corsinkell in the 1559–1560 teind material.<ref name="TeindList" /> The 1571 record then directly identifies the younger James as the elder James's son.<ref name="NRS1571" />

If the younger James was at least about eighteen to twenty-one in 1559, he was born by approximately 1538–1541. Normal generational spacing would place his father's birth around 1510–1520.

About 1515 is used as an uncertain working estimate. A more conservative statement would be that James elder was born before about 1525.

=== Parentage ===

'''[[Glasgow-1098|William Glasgow]]''' is attached as James's father.

The relationship is chronologically possible, but no inspected record connects William's Glasgow burgh family with James at Corsinkell. The attachment should remain uncertain and should not be described as proved.

'''[[Brade-232|Isobel Brade]]''' is attached as James's mother. No record cited on this profile establishes that relationship. It should likewise remain uncertain.

The earlier attachment to [[Glasgow-1093|John Glasgow]] was unsupported and chronologically problematic.

=== Wife or Campbell associates ===

Katherine Campbell was listed at Corsinkell with James elder and James younger in the 1559–1560 teind material.<ref name="TeindList" />

Christian Campbell was named among the occupiers in the 1571 archival catalogue description.<ref name="NRS1571" />

Neither source states that either woman was James's wife, daughter or other relative. Katherine and Christian should not be assumed to be the same person, and neither should be attached as James's spouse without further evidence.

=== Son James ===

The younger James named at Corsinkell is represented by '''[[Glasgow-3921|James Glasgow]]'''.

The repeated holding, the elder/younger distinction and the 1571 statement of relationship make this identification well supported.

Earlier links to [[Glasgow-991|James Glasgow]] should not be restored unless separate evidence shows that profile represents the Corsinkell son.

=== Son John ===

The 1571 record directly proves that James elder had a son named John.<ref name="NRS1571" /> [[Glasgow-3193|John Glasgow]] is the surviving profile after the record-defined Corsinkell profile Glasgow-4061 was merged into it on 27 September 2026. James is directly identified as the father of the Corsinkell son named in the deed; the structured father link to this merged profile remains uncertain because its Kilwinning identity is not directly bridged.

The merger also brings the Kilwinning/Burrowland/Dalgarven records under this one profile as a probable identity match by name, generation and Ayrshire setting. No inspected deed explicitly carries the Corsinkell son to those holdings, so that part of the combined identity remains qualified. The former link to [[Glasgow-1561|John Glasgow]] should not be used.

=== Landholding context ===

Corsinkell formed part of lands held under branches of the Cunninghame family.

A charter made at Kerelaw on 4 February 1527 and confirmed on 25 May 1536 granted David Cunningham of Bertaneholme the five-merk lands of Corsinkell and Middlepart with other Stevenston lands.<ref name="Corsinkell1536">''Registrum Magni Sigilli Regum Scotorum'', vol. 3, [https://archive.org/details/registrummagnisi03scot/page/133/mode/2up no. 596, printed pp. 133–134].</ref>

A further charter dated 11 July 1537 and confirmed on 4 August 1537 included two-and-a-half merk lands of Corsinkell in a grant to David Cunningham of Robertland.<ref name="Corsinkell1537">''Registrum Magni Sigilli Regum Scotorum'', vol. 3, [https://archive.org/details/registrummagnisi03scot/page/377/mode/2up no. 1698, printed p. 377].</ref>

These charters establish the superior-title history of Corsinkell but do not name James Glasgow, identify an earlier Glasgow tenant or prove a kinship relationship with the Cunninghames.

Later marriages between people named Glasgow and Cunningham do not establish James's ancestry or his relationship to those later families.

=== Mathie and Glencairn network ===

The 1559–60 teind list also places John Mathie at Ardeer Nether, Margaret Mathie at Templemuir of Corscraig and William Mathie at Middlepart, alongside [[Glasgow-3908|Matthew Glasgow]], [[Glasgow-3911|Michael Glasgow]] and the Corsinkell Glasgows.<ref name="TeindList" /> This repeated association has a city counterpart: David Mathy and [[Glasgow-1096|Robert Glasgow]] were fellow Glasgow burgesses witnessing the same sasines in 1554.<ref name="Mathie1554">Robert Renwick, ed., Abstracts of Protocols of the Town Clerks of Glasgow, vol. 1, protocols 183–184, [https://archive.org/details/abstractsprotoc07robegoog/page/n90/mode/2up 10 May 1554, printed p. 63].</ref>

David’s son John is a plausible match for the writer admitted with the Earl of Glencairn’s burgess group in 1583. Tutory retours entered in 1607 identify the deceased John Mathie of Ibert’s full brother Matthew as a Glasgow burgess and name John’s lawful children James, David, Agnes and Margaret.<ref name="Ibert1607">Inquisitionum ad Capellam Domini Regis Retornatarum ... Abbreviatio, vol. 2, tutory retours 100–101, 20 January 1607, [https://books.google.com/books?id=PiVDAAAAcAAJ digitised volume]; underlying register, National Records of Scotland, [https://catalogue.nrscotland.gov.uk/nrsonlinecatalogue/browsetreeview.aspx?reference=C22 C22/3].</ref> This provides a credible route between Robert’s Glasgow burgh family and the Glencairn estate community at Stevenston. It makes an association between the Glasgow households more plausible, although it does not identify James elder’s father.

=== The 1571 Glasgow burgess witness ===

The 9 February 1571 Corsinkell letters of reversion name Mr Adam Wallace, explicitly a '''burgess of Glasgow''', among the witnesses, alongside the Porterfields and an earl's servant.<ref name="NRS1571" /> This places a named Glasgow civic figure at the same transaction that identifies James elder and his sons. A later Glencairn record names a Mr Adam Wallace as one of Glasgow's bailies and William Wallace as his son; the matching name and city favour the same civic officer but do not establish his relationship to the Corsinkell Glasgows.<ref>National Records of Scotland, Earls of Glencairn, [https://catalogue.nrscotland.gov.uk/nrsonlinecatalogue/details.aspx?reference=GD39%2F5%2F68 GD39/5/68], commission dated 26 April 1588 (catalogue description; original not inspected).</ref>

The 1571 witness is a direct city-to-estate legal contact, not evidence that James elder was a son of [[Glasgow-1098|William Glasgow]] or kin to Wallace. The reason Wallace witnessed this deed remains open.

=== Margaret Smith of Brekpleuch ===

The Glasgow Commissary testament index contains an entry dated 21 February 1632 for Margaret Smith, spouse of James Glasgow in Brekpleuch, parish of Stevenston.<ref name="MargaretSmith">Francis J. Grant, ed., [https://archive.org/details/scottishrecordso07scotuoft/page/460/mode/2up ''The Commissariot Record of Glasgow: Register of Testaments, 1547–1800''] (Scottish Record Society, 1901), printed p. 460.</ref>

That couple belongs to a later generation. The entry does not identify the James Glasgow of Brekpleuch as James elder, his son or another specific descendant.

=== Disputed origins ===

Online family trees have assigned James a birth in Midlothian, parents named John Glasgow and Nancy Glendinning, a wife named Margaret Edstoun, and a death in 1580.

No contemporary evidence cited on this profile supports those claims.

The 1580 testament of Margaret Glasgow, widow of John Edstoun of Croftmalloch, concerns a Midlothian family and does not establish a marriage to James of Corsinkell.

The Ayrshire and Midlothian families should be researched independently unless a record explicitly connects them.

=== Negative searches ===

No published Great Seal entry examined for Corsinkell identifies James's father, siblings or a preceding Glasgow tenant.

No relevant entry was found in the searched published Privy Seal registers under James Glasgow, surname variants or Corsinkell variants.

The printed Glasgow Commissary testament index contains no testament indexed under James Glasgow of Corsinkell.

These negative results narrow the available evidence but do not prove that no relevant record survives elsewhere or under a different spelling.

=== Further research ===

Useful remaining records include:

* the original GD39/5/59 deed, particularly its punctuation and witness clauses;
* the underlying Court of Session teind action cited for 1559–1560;
* Ayrshire sasines and rentals for Corsinkell;
* Glencairn and Cunningham estate papers;
* Stevenston parish and commissary records;
* a deed connecting the 1571 Corsinkell son John to the Kilwinning/Burrowland/Dalgarven holdings now represented on his merged profile;
* evidence for or against Agnes Glasgow as a daughter;
* records identifying Katherine and Christian Campbell; and
* any record connecting the Corsinkell family with [[Glasgow-1098|William Glasgow]] or [[Brade-232|Isobel Brade]].

=== Possible collateral households ===
The 1559-60 Stevenston teind list places [[Glasgow-3908|Matthew Glasgow]] at Ardeer Nether and [[Glasgow-3911|Michael Glasgow]] at Brakpleuch in the same estate landscape as James elder and James younger at Corsankell.<ref>Margaret H. B. Sanderson, ''The People of Sixteenth Century Ayrshire'', appendix “The Cunninghame Teind Lists of 1559-60,” [https://aanhs.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/05/people-of-ayrshire.pdf#page=36 p. 331].</ref>

Matthew is linked as James's uncertain working son, although the same evidence also permits a nephew or younger collateral. The 1571 Corsankell writ proves sons James and John but does not purport to enumerate every child.<ref>National Records of Scotland, Charter Chest of the Earls of Glencairn, [https://catalogue.nrscotland.gov.uk/nrsonlinecatalogue/details.aspx?reference=GD39%2F5%2F59 GD39/5/59], 9 February 1571.</ref> Michael was already an adult legal witness in the Glencairn network in 1549, so he is better assessed as James's probable brother or cousin rather than a son. Neither exact relationship is stated in a record.
