{{One Name Study|name=Glasgow}}

== Biography ==
Alexander Glasgow was born on 7 July 1673 and christened on 20 July 1673 at Kirknewton and East Calder, Midlothian, Scotland.<ref name="Alexander1673">''Scotland, Births and Baptisms, 1564-1950'', database, FamilySearch ([https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:VQ4K-X9V VQ4K-X9V]), Alexander Glasgow, birth 7 July 1673, christening 20 July 1673, Kirknewton and East Calder, Midlothian, Scotland; father Alexander Glasgow.</ref> His father was [[Glasgow-3118|Alexander Glasgow]]. The indexed christening record names no mother.

Alexander is currently linked as a son of [[Smith-230509|Margaret (Smith) Glasgow]], although the cited baptism record does not identify his mother. His known sibling is [[Glasgow-1312|Agnes Glasgow]].

=== Marriages ===

Alexander married [[Aikman-803|Margaret Aikman]] on 7 November 1701 at Kirknewton, Linlithgowshire, Scotland.<ref name="AikmanMarriage">''Scotland, Marriages, 1561-1910'', database, FamilySearch ([https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:XY9W-T57 XY9W-T57]), Alexander Glasgou and Margrat Aikman, marriage 7 November 1701, Kirknewton, Linlithgowshire, Scotland.</ref>

They were the parents of at least [[Glasgow-1313|Andrew Glasgow]]. Andrew's christening record explicitly names his parents as Alexander Glasgow and Margaret Aikman.<ref name="Andrew1703">''Scotland, Births and Baptisms, 1564-1950'', database, FamilySearch ([https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:VQ4K-NJB VQ4K-NJB]), Andrew Glasgow, christening 21 November 1703, Kirknewton and East Calder, Midlothian, Scotland; parents Alexander Glasgow and Margaret Aikman.</ref>

Alexander apparently married secondly [[Graham-23064|Janet Graham]] on 16 November 1705 at Kirknewton, Linlithgowshire, Scotland.<ref name="GrahamMarriage">''Scotland, Marriages, 1561-1910'', database, FamilySearch ([https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:XY9W-TYZ XY9W-TYZ]), Alexander Glasgow and Janet Graham, marriage 16 November 1705, Kirknewton, Linlithgowshire, Scotland.</ref>

The two marriages, four years apart in the same parish, together with Alexander's children recorded there, make it plausible that the 1701 and 1705 marriage records refer to the same man. The evidence presently available does not establish what happened to Margaret Aikman between Andrew's baptism in 1703 and Alexander's marriage to Janet Graham in 1705.

=== Children ===

Children currently linked to Alexander are:

* [[Glasgow-1141|Alexander Glasgow]]
* [[Glasgow-1313|Andrew Glasgow]], christened 21 November 1703.<ref name="Andrew1703" />
* [[Glasgow-1316|James Glasgow]], christened 8 September 1707.<ref name="James1707">''Scotland, Births and Baptisms, 1564-1950'', database, FamilySearch ([https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:VQ4K-6MS VQ4K-6MS]), James Glasgou, christening 8 September 1707, Kirknewton and East Calder, Midlothian, Scotland; father Alexander Glasgou.</ref>
* [[Glasgow-1315|Marion Glasgow]], christened 18 May 1711.<ref name="Marion1711">''Scotland, Births and Baptisms, 1564-1950'', database, FamilySearch ([https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:VQ4K-H54 VQ4K-H54]), Marion Glasgou, christening 18 May 1711, Kirknewton and East Calder, Midlothian, Scotland; father Alexander Glasgou.</ref>

[[Glasgow-1313|Andrew Glasgow]] can be confidently assigned to Alexander and [[Aikman-803|Margaret Aikman]], since both parents are named in his christening record.<ref name="Andrew1703" />

[[Glasgow-1316|James Glasgow]] and [[Glasgow-1315|Marion Glasgow]] were christened after Alexander's 1705 marriage to [[Graham-23064|Janet Graham]]. Their christening records name Alexander as father but do not name a mother.<ref name="James1707" /><ref name="Marion1711" /> Janet is therefore a plausible mother of both children, but the relationship should not be treated as proven solely from these records.

No source for [[Glasgow-1141|Alexander Glasgow]] as a child has yet been included in this profile.

== Research Notes ==
This profile incorporates information previously represented by two profiles for an Alexander Glasgow.

One profile gave Alexander's birth year as 1685. However, the indexed parish record identifies an Alexander Glasgow born on 7 July 1673 and christened on 20 July 1673 at Kirknewton and East Calder, with father Alexander Glasgow.<ref name="Alexander1673" /> The 1673 date is therefore used here. The origin of the 1685 date remains unclear.

The family chronology is:

* 7 July 1673 — birth of Alexander Glasgow.<ref name="Alexander1673" />
* 7 November 1701 — marriage to [[Aikman-803|Margaret Aikman]].<ref name="AikmanMarriage" />
* 21 November 1703 — christening of their son [[Glasgow-1313|Andrew Glasgow]], with both parents named.<ref name="Andrew1703" />
* 16 November 1705 — marriage of Alexander Glasgow to [[Graham-23064|Janet Graham]].<ref name="GrahamMarriage" />
* 8 September 1707 — christening of [[Glasgow-1316|James Glasgow]], father Alexander named but no mother recorded.<ref name="James1707" />
* 18 May 1711 — christening of [[Glasgow-1315|Marion Glasgow]], father Alexander named but no mother recorded.<ref name="Marion1711" />

This sequence is consistent with one Alexander Glasgow marrying Margaret Aikman in 1701 and Janet Graham in 1705. It also explains why Andrew can be assigned to Margaret while the maternity of James and Marion remains uncertain.

=== Current research ===

FamilySearch VQ4K-X9V supports Alexander's 1673 Kirknewton event and names his father Alexander. His 7 November 1701 marriage to Margaret Aikman and their children are separately indexed.

[[Glasgow-3119|Glasgow-3119]] may duplicate him, but that profile supplies no birth source. Its structured 1673 date and same-father attachment conflict with its biography's 1685 estimate. Its 1705 marriage to Janet Graham could be a second marriage or could identify another Alexander.

This assessment draws on the cited records and public source material.<ref name="ProjectSource1">[https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:VQ4K-X9V www.familysearch.org].</ref><ref name="ProjectSource2">[https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:XY9W-T57 www.familysearch.org].</ref><ref name="ProjectSource3">[https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:VQ4K-NJB www.familysearch.org].</ref><ref name="ProjectSource4">[https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:XY9W-TYZ www.familysearch.org].</ref><ref name="ProjectSource5">[https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:VQ4K-6MS www.familysearch.org].</ref>

28960239.Name: Glasgow-1376
28960239.bio:
{{Estimated Date}}
[[Category:Glasgow Name Study]]

== Biography ==
{{Notables Sticker}}
James Glasgow was born before 1657, the son of [[Glasgow-1150|James Glasgow]] and [[Duncan-16106|Agnes Duncan]].<ref name=Birth>"Scotland, Births and Baptisms, 1564-1950", database, FamilySearch (https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:X1YD-PRL : 11 February 2020), James Glesgow in entry for Marione Glesgow, 1657.</ref> He is noted in records during the tumultuous era of the Covenanter movement in Scotland.

In 1670, James appeared in legal proceedings for refusing to give his oath—a requirement aimed at suppressing illegal religious gatherings, known as field conventicles. These conventicles were organized by Presbyterians protesting government-imposed religious uniformity. James is specifically mentioned as being from a place called '''Whitecastle''', a site associated with Covenanting activities, although its exact location remains uncertain.<ref>Wodrow, Robert. ''The History of the Sufferings of the Church of Scotland from the Restoration to the Revolution.'' 1721. [https://archive.org/details/bim_eighteenth-century_the-history-of-the-suffe_wodrow-robert_1721_1/page/n795/mode/2up?q=%22James+Glasgow%22 Internet Archive]</ref>

=== Whitecastle and Covenanting Context ===
It is not clear which Whitecastle James was associated with, as many areas in 17th-century Scotland hosted field conventicles, especially in Lanarkshire and Dumfriesshire. Lanarkshire, in particular, was a stronghold of Presbyterian dissent during this period. The fragmentary nature of the source makes it difficult to identify Whitecastle precisely without further geographical or archival clues.

=== Mr. Duncan and 1671 Proceedings ===
References to a certain '''Mr. Duncan''' in July 1671 connect him to the King’s Advocate and to legal action related to nonconformist religious practices. The records do not clarify whether he was a landowner, minister, or another figure who supported or harbored Covenanters. Many individuals, including local gentry and ministers, were penalized for enabling or attending these conventicles.

== Research Notes ==
* '''James Glasgow''' (b. ~late 1600s – d. unknown) may have held a position at Edinburgh Castle in 1738, as mentioned in ''The Principal Acts of the General Assembly of the Church of Scotland.''<ref>[https://archive.org/details/bim_eighteenth-century_the-principal-acts-of-th_church-of-scotland-gene_1738/page/n19/mode/2up?q=%22James+Glasgow%22 ''The Principal Acts of the General Assembly of the Church of Scotland''], 1738 (Internet Archive)</ref>
* '''James Glasgow''' was a notable figure mentioned in legal proceedings during the turbulent times of the Covenanter movement in Scotland. In July 1670, he was fined for refusing to give his oath, alongside several others, as part of a crackdown on illegal religious gatherings known as field conventicles. These gatherings were a form of protest against the government's attempt to impose religious uniformity, particularly on those who adhered to Presbyterianism. James Glasgow is specifically noted as being from Whitecastle, a location associated with Covenanting activities during this period.<ref>[https://archive.org/details/bim_eighteenth-century_the-history-of-the-state_crookshank-william_1751_1/page/284/mode/2up?q=%22James+Glasgow%22 ''The History of the Sufferings of the Church of Scotland from the Restoration to the Revolution''], by Robert Wodrow, 1721</ref>
**From the information provided in the images and context, '''Whitecastle''' is likely a location associated with the '''Covenanter''' activities, but the specific reference does not immediately clarify which Whitecastle it is. Given the widespread nature of the Covenanter movement in '''Scotland''', '''Whitecastle''' could plausibly be located in '''Lanarkshire''', '''Dumfriesshire''', or nearby areas known for strong Covenanter sympathies during the 17th century. The '''Lanarkshire''' region, specifically, was a hotspot for religious dissent during the Covenanting times, making it a strong candidate. However, without further geographic markers or historical maps, it's challenging to conclusively identify Whitecastle's exact location just from this.
**As for '''Mr. Duncan''', the mention of his name in the July 1671 proceedings involving the '''King's Advocate''' seems to tie him to some legal action related to the suppression of religious activities or nonconformity in religious practices. Without more context from the previous or following sections of the document, it's difficult to determine exactly who '''Mr. Duncan''' was. He could have been a local landowner, minister, or someone involved in harboring or protecting Covenanters, as many individuals were targeted during this period for their association with field conventicles.
**Further research into legal records or historical sources about '''Mr. Duncan''' in 1671 and '''Whitecastle''' in Covenanting Scotland would be required to offer a more precise identification.  Note, could be any of the other James Glasgow's in this timespan. No good match for location (Whitecastle) 
* On October 11, 1680, a James Glasgow is listed as a weaver in the Back of Lindsaylands, Parish of Biggar (Lanark Commissary Court, CC14/5/10). It is unclear if he is the same individual.

=== Current research ===

The asserted 29 January 1657 birth and placement as a son of James Glasgow and Agnes Duncan are unsupported and result from a record-role error. The profile's cited FamilySearch entry is for '''Marione Glesgow'''; "James Glesgow" appears in it as her father. It is not a baptism or birth record for a son James.

Glasgow-1376 was previously attached to the household. That relationship has been removed and should not be restored unless an independent record for a son James is found. The profile does not merge this profile into the father merely from the misread citation, because its later Whitecastle/Covenanter claims have not been shown to describe the Edinburgh weaver.

The proposed merge with [[Glasgow-2682|Glasgow-2682]] is also rejected. Glasgow-2682 is a documented father with Isobell Duffe from 1677 to 1691. The false 1657 birth on this profile supplies no matching identity fact, and no record connects the Whitecastle occurrence to the Duffe household.

This assessment draws on the cited records and public source material.<ref name="ProjectSource1">[https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:X1YD-PRL FamilySearch index X1YD-PRL].</ref><ref name="ProjectSource2">[https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:X1YD-PR2 FamilySearch index X1YD-PR2].</ref><ref name="ProjectSource3">[https://www.tradeshouselibrary.org/uploads/4/7/7/2/47723681/roll_of_edinburgh_burgesses_1406_to_1700.pdf#page=101 PDF p. 101].</ref><ref name="ProjectSource4">[https://archive.org/details/bim_eighteenth-century_the-history-of-the-suffe_wodrow-robert_1721_1/page/n795/mode/2up?q=%22James+Glasgow%22 archive.org].</ref><ref name="ProjectSource5">[https://archive.org/details/bim_eighteenth-century_the-principal-acts-of-th_church-of-scotland-gene_1738/page/n19/mode/2up?q=%22James+Glasgow%22 archive.org].</ref>

28999015.Name: Glasgow-1433
28999015.bio:
[[Category:Glasgow Name Study]]

== Biography ==
Jannet Glasgow was born or baptised at Kilwinning on 1 February 1689. The indexed entry names her father as John Glasgow and gives her mother's surname as Allason.<ref>“Old Parish Registers, Births and Baptisms,” Scotland's People index entry, JANNET GLASGOW, 1 February 1689, parents JOHN GLASGOW / ALLASON, Kilwinning parish 599, frame 75.</ref>

Her father link is retained as the uncertain [[Glasgow-3375|John Glasgow]], not [[Glasgow-1073|Rev. John Glasgow M.A.]]. The two adult profiles must remain separate unless the full parish entry or another record identifies the Kilwinning father. Her mother is represented by [[Allison-6866|Barbara Allison]].

== Research Notes ==
=== Supplied parish index comparison ===

The supplied Scotland’s People index records '''JANNET GLASGOW''' on '''31/01/1689''' at Kilwinning, with parent text “JOHN GLASGOW/ ALLASON FR75 (FR75)”.<ref name="OPRBirth033">Scotland’s People, [https://www.scotlandspeople.gov.uk/ Old Parish Registers, births and baptisms], exact surname Glasgow through 1700, index text supplied 10 September 2026: JANNET GLASGOW, 31/01/1689, JOHN GLASGOW/ ALLASON FR75 (FR75), indexed gender F, Kilwinning, parish 599, reference 10 / 62. Original register image not inspected for this review.</ref>

The profile’s structured birth date is 1689-02-01, whereas this index date is 1689-01-31. The two dates remain unreconciled. The combined births and baptisms collection does not establish whether the indexed date is a birthday or a baptism date. The mother’s forename is not supplied; Allason alone does not establish that she was Barbara Allison.

28999020.Name: Glasgow-1434
28999020.bio:
== Biography ==
John Glasgow was born or baptised on 6 July 1679 in Kilwinning parish, Ayrshire, Scotland. The indexed entry names his parents as John Glasgow and Barbara Alason. His father link is retained as the uncertain [[Glasgow-3375|John Glasgow]] rather than [[Glasgow-1073|Rev. John Glasgow M.A.]]; the two adult profiles must remain separate pending an identifying record. His mother is represented by [[Allison-6866|Barbara Allison]].<ref name="John1679">"Old Parish Registers, Births and Baptisms," ''Scotland's People'', index entry for JON GLASGOW, 6 July 1679, son of JON GLASGOW and BARBARA ALASON, Kilwinning, Ayrshire, parish number 599, frame 44.</ref>

The surname of John's mother appears as '''Alason''' in the indexed record. Allison and Allason are possible spelling variants, but Alason should be retained as the recorded form unless the original image gives a different reading.

John may have moved from Kilwinning to the neighbouring parish of Stevenston as a young man. He is believed to have been the John Glasgow who had at least two sons with [[Cowan-5106|Margaret Cowan]]:

* John Glasgow, born or baptised in Stevenston in 1701;<ref name="John1701">"Scotland, Births and Baptisms, 1564-1950," database, FamilySearch (https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:XYZK-MY7 : accessed 11 February 2020), John Glasgow, 1701.</ref>
* Adam Glasgow, born or baptised in Stevenston in 1706.<ref name="Adam1706">"Scotland, Births and Baptisms, 1564-1950," database, FamilySearch (https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:XYZV-BNR : accessed 11 February 2020), John Glasgow in entry for Adam Glasgow, 1706.</ref>

No confirmed record has yet been found for John's marriage, occupation or death.

== Kilwinning ==

John's baptism was entered in the register of Kilwinning parish. At that time the former chancel of Kilwinning Abbey was being used as the parish church. It remained in use until the present Abbey Church was built in 1775.<ref name="KilwinningSession">National Records of Scotland, catalogue entry CH2/591, "Records of Kilwinning / Kilwinning Abbey Church, Kirk Session," 1656–1956 (https://catalogue.nrscotland.gov.uk/nrsonlinecatalogue/browseDetails.aspx?reference=CH2/591 : accessed 20 July 2026).</ref>

Kilwinning kirk-session records survive from 1656. These records may contain further references to John's parents or other members of the Glasgow family, but they have not yet been fully examined.

== Research Notes ==

=== Identification with the Stevenston family ===

The identification of the child baptised at Kilwinning in 1679 with the later father of John and Adam Glasgow in Stevenston is plausible but has not been proved by a record explicitly naming his parents.

The chronology is consistent. The John born or baptised in 1679 would have been about twenty-one or twenty-two when the younger John was born in 1701, and about twenty-six or twenty-seven when Adam was born in 1706.

A secondary account of the Stevenston kirk-session records states that a '''John Glasgow of Pipers-Heugh''' appeared before the session in April 1700. He requested a testimonial, which was initially refused after he was accused of stealing a goose on a Sunday and being drunk the preceding Saturday. He was publicly rebuked and was then granted the testimonial.<ref name="Piperheugh">"Piperheugh," ''Wikipedia'', section "Micro-history" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piperheugh : accessed 20 July 2026), citing the Stevenston kirk-session records of April 1700.</ref>

This man was living in Stevenston shortly before the baptism of John Glasgow in 1701 and is a possible match for the John born in Kilwinning in 1679. The original kirk-session minute must be examined before treating the two men as identical.

=== Possible confusion with the minister of Kilbirnie ===

John's father has sometimes been identified as Rev. John Glasgow, minister of Kilbirnie. That relationship is not supported by the currently available evidence.

The published account of the minister states that he married first Jean Cunningham and secondly Margaret Scott. His recorded children were Robert, James, Margaret, William, Samuel, Janet, Elizabeth and Jean. Neither Barbara Alason nor a son John is included.<ref name="Fasti">Hew Scott, ''Fasti Ecclesiae Scoticanae: The Succession of Ministers in the Church of Scotland from the Reformation'', new edition, volume 3, Synod of Glasgow and Ayr (Edinburgh: Oliver and Boyd, 1920), 103, entry for John Glasgow, minister of Kilbirnie (https://archive.org/details/fastiecclesiaesc03scot/page/102/mode/2up).</ref>

The elder John Glasgow named in the 1679 baptism should therefore be treated as a separate, otherwise unidentified man unless additional evidence establishes a connection with the Kilbirnie minister.

=== Further research ===

Records still to be examined include:

* the original image of John's 1679 baptism, particularly any residence, occupation or witnesses omitted from the index;
* Kilwinning kirk-session records, NRS reference CH2/591, around 1678–1681;
* the Ayrshire hearth-tax roll for the division of Cunninghame, particularly the Kilwinning and Stevenston entries;
* the original April 1700 Stevenston kirk-session minute concerning John Glasgow of Pipers-Heugh;
* marriage records for John Glasgow and Margaret Cowan in Kilwinning, Stevenston, Ardrossan, Irvine, Kilbirnie and nearby parishes;
* baptisms of any additional children of John Glasgow and Margaret Cowan under the spellings Glasgow, Glasgo, Glascow and Glassgow.

29004968.Name: Glasgow-1473
29004968.bio:
== Biography == 

John Glasgow was born about 1695–1700, likely in Irvine, Ayrshire, Scotland. He was probably the son of [[Glasgow-3018|John Glasgow (abt.1675-)]], skipper and merchant in Irvine.

He appears in the public records as "John Glasgow younger," a skipper active in Irvine in the early 1720s.

On 12 January 1720, John Glasgow younger was named as the creditor in a bond for 400 merks granted by Thomas Gray, merchant, and his father John Gray, late Bailie of Irvine.<ref>GD1/500/56, National Records of Scotland. [https://catalogue.nrscotland.gov.uk/nrsonlinecatalogue/details.aspx?reference=GD1/500/56&st=1&tc=y&tl=n&tn=n&tp=n&k=John+Glasgow&ko=p&r=&ro=s&df=&dt=&di=y]</ref>

On 23 January 1720, he was again mentioned in an instrument of resignation and sasine alongside Barbara Stewart, widow of Neil Gray, involving a property in Irvine.<ref>GD1/500/57, National Records of Scotland. [https://catalogue.nrscotland.gov.uk/nrsonlinecatalogue/details.aspx?reference=GD1/500/57&st=1&tc=y&tl=n&tn=n&tp=n&k=John+Glasgow&ko=p&r=&ro=s&df=&dt=&di=y]</ref>

In 1719, a John Glasgow was recorded as the father of Grizal Glasgow at her baptism.<ref>[FamilySearch Entry for Grizal Glasgow, 1719](https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:XBLH-YP6)</ref> Based on timing, this is likely the same John Glasgow younger.

On 23 September 1737, John Glasgow was awarded a bursary from the Dundonald Mortification, indicating a pursuit of education or professional advancement later in life.<ref>GB 248 GUA 02848, [University of Glasgow Collections](https://www.gla.ac.uk/collections/#/details?irn=542052&catType=C&referrer=/results&q=%22John+Glasgow%22)</ref>

Between 1736 and 1746, John Glasgow & Co. of Irvine appeared in business correspondence dealing with international trade, particularly with merchants in St. Petersburg and Königsberg.<ref>GB 248 UGD 042/2/1, [University of Glasgow Collections](https://www.gla.ac.uk/collections/#/details?irn=679589&catType=C&referrer=/results&q=%22John+Glasgow%22)</ref>

== Research Notes ==
* Estimated birth between 1695 and 1700 based on adult activities beginning by 1720.
* Likely son of John Glasgow elder (c.1675–aft.1740), though direct proof is pending.
* His appearance as "younger" confirms there was an elder John Glasgow living at the same time.
* Further research could clarify his marriage, death, and any other children beyond Grizal.

John was born in 1693. He is the son of [[Glasgow-3018|John Glasgow]] and [[Martine-274|Agnes Martine]].

29026946.Name: Glasgow-1494
29026946.bio:
[[Category:Stevenston, Ayrshire]]

== Biography ==
'''Jonet Glasgow''' was born before 1610, likely around 1600, in Ayrshire, Scotland. She lived in the parish of Stevenston, where she was married to George Logane.

The primary record of her life is her testament, which confirms she died in or before September 1628. Her Testament Dative and Inventory was recorded in the Glasgow Commissary Court on 2 September 1628, just six months after that of her sister, Agnes.<ref name="Testament1628">''The Commissariot Record of Glasgow, Register of Testaments, 1547-1800'', Vol. 7, ed. by Francis J. Grant (Edinburgh: Scottish Record Society, 1901), citing the testament of Jonet Glasgw, spouse to George Logane in Steinstoun. National Records of Scotland, Reference CC9/7/22.</ref>

The term "Testament Dative" signifies that Jonet died without a formal will, and the court appointed an executor to settle her estate.

=== A Tale of Two Sisters ===
The testament records from 1628 paint a poignant picture of two sisters, Jonet and [[Glasgow-3178|Agnes Glasgow]]. Both were married to Logan men in the small parish of Stevenston, and tragically, both died in the same year.

Agnes's testament, as the spouse of Johnne Logane, was recorded in March 1628. Jonet's testament followed in September. This remarkable coincidence strongly suggests the two sisters married two brothers, George and Johnne Logane, and may have succumbed to the same illness or event.

== Research Notes ==

The currently attached father [[Glasgow-1557|Edward Glasgow]] is marked uncertain. The cited 1628 testament index identifies Jonet’s spouse but supplies no father; Edward’s attachment is a working hypothesis.

* The central fact of Jonet's life is her death in 1628. The birth year of 1610 found on some trees is an estimate and is likely incorrect, as she was married and established enough to have an estate by this time. A birth year closer to 1600 is more probable.
* The primary research goal is to find the parents of Jonet and Agnes Glasgow. A search of baptismal records in the Stevenston parish registers (or nearby parishes like Kilwinning or Irvine) from roughly 1590-1610 is the most promising next step.
* Locating the marriage records for both couples (Jonet to George Logan, and Agnes to Johnne Logan) prior to 1628 would further solidify the family structure.

== Biography ==
'''Katherine Glasgow''' lived in the parish of Stevenston, Ayrshire, and was married to [[Weir-4172|Thomas Weir]]. The Glasgow Commissary Court calendar identifies her as Thomas's spouse and records her testament on 9 May 1605, so she died before that date.<ref name="Testament">Francis J. Grant, ed., ''The Commissariot Record of Glasgow: Register of Testaments, 1547-1800'' (Edinburgh, 1901), [https://archive.org/details/scottishrecordso07scotuoft/page/196/mode/1up p. 196], entry for Katherine Glasgow; underlying register NRS CC9/7/4.</ref>

== Research Notes ==
Katherine's birth about 1580 is an unsourced estimate and remains uncertain. The testament calendar does not name her parents or children.

[[Glasgow-3921|James Glasgow younger of Corsankell]] is retained only as an uncertain father because the generation and Stevenston locality are compatible; no reviewed record states the relationship. WikiTree may flag Katherine's estimated 1580 birth as occurring after James's death. This is not a chronological conflict: 9 February 1571 is the last date on which James is documented alive, and his death field is marked “after,” not as an exact death date.

The indexed record establishes Katherine's spouse, parish and death boundary. It does not support the former speculative narrative about an insolvent inventory, unidentified administrators, “Sir Dafnes,” Stafford or guardianship. The underlying Glasgow Commissary Court reference CC9/7/4 is retained, but those interpretations should not be restored without verified images and a reliable transcription.

The date 9 May 1605 is the testament date, not a marriage date. Stevenston is in Ayrshire, not Lanarkshire.

Spouses.Name: Weir-4172
Spouses.bio:
{{Estimated Date}}
[[Category:Stevenston, Ayrshire]]

== Biography ==
'''Thomas Weir''' lived in the parish of Stevenston, Ayrshire. The original
testament of [[Glasgow-1495|Katherine Glasgow]] explicitly identifies her as
his wife and states that she died in January 1603.<ref name="KatherineWill">National
Records of Scotland, Glasgow Commissary Court, testament dative and inventory
of Katherine Glasgow, CC9/7/4, images 6–7; original register inspected through
[https://www.scotlandspeople.gov.uk/search-records/legal-records/wills Scotland's
People] and working transcription supplied 8 September 2026.</ref>

William, James and probably Jonet Weir were appointed as three minor executors, and
Thomas acted in their names.<ref name="KatherineWill" /> Their surname,
minority and Thomas's representation of them make them very probably the
children of Thomas and Katherine, although the surviving passage does not
explicitly call Thomas their father or Katherine their mother.

The manuscript confirmation date appears to be '''[26?] May 1605'''. Grant's
printed calendar and the Findmypast transcript instead give '''9 May
1605'''.<ref name="KatherineWill" /><ref name="Grant">Francis J. Grant, ed.,
''The Commissariot Record of Glasgow: Register of Testaments, 1547–1800''
(Edinburgh, 1901), [https://archive.org/details/scottishrecordso07scotuoft/page/196/mode/1up
p. 196], entry for Katherine Glasgow.</ref><ref name="FMP">Findmypast,
[https://www.findmypast.co.uk/transcript?id=SCOT%2FWILLS%2F057453&tab=this
Scotland, Will and Testament Index 1481–1807], Katherine Glasgow,
SCOT/WILLS/057453, citing the Glasgow Commissary Court register.</ref> The
confirmation occurred in May 1605, but its exact day remains unresolved.

== Research Notes ==
=== Current evidence assessment ===

The record is a testament, not a marriage entry. Neither possible confirmation
day is a marriage date, and Stevenston is the family's documented parish.

A full working transcription, modern-English rendering and record-boundary
analysis is maintained at [[Space:Kathereine Glasgow: Will and testament
translation]].

An older FamilySearch index entry is retained as a derivative lead, but it
does not override the original testament.<ref>FamilySearch,
[https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:XY6J-CQS indexed record].</ref>

Thomas's exact birth, parents and death are not established. The birth date is
only an estimate based on his adult role in the testament. [[Weir-4172]] is
The established profile for Katherine's Stevenston husband; its former,
incompatible 1590 Aberdeen identity should not be restored.

Complete local and fully paged live WikiTree duplicate audits on 8 September
2026 found no compatible profile for William, James or Jonet Weir. Distinct
profiles may therefore be created, with both parent links and the inferred
Stevenston birthplaces marked uncertain. Jonet's forename must also remain
uncertain.

29027429.Name: Glasgow-1498
29027429.bio:
{{Notables Sticker}}

== Biography ==
John Glasgow (about 1650 – ?) was one of the Covenanter prisoners aboard the ship '''Croune of London''' when it wrecked near the Mull of Deerness in Orkney on 10 December 1679. The vessel was transporting 257 Scottish Presbyterian Covenanters, captured at the Battle of Bothwell Bridge, to forced labor in the American Plantations. Locked below deck, many perished, but John was listed under Cavers Parish, Roxburghshire, among the survivors. The source also names a William Glasgow under Cavers, but gives no kinship, parents or later destination; identifying that man as [[Glasgow-1605|William Glasgow]] remains unproved.<ref>William Glasgow, ''The History of the Reformed Presbyterian Church in America, with Sketches of all her Ministry, Congregations, Missions, Institutions, Publications, etc.'' (Baltimore: Hill & Harvey, Publishers, 1888), 245. [https://drmarkjardine.wordpress.com/2016/12/10/beyond-orkneys-fatal-shore-the-wreck-of-the-croune-10-december-1679-history-scotland/ Dr. Mark Jardine’s article on the wreck of the Croune]</ref>

The Covenanters were a 17th-century Scottish Presbyterian sect who opposed attempts by Charles II to impose an episcopal structure on the Scottish Church. Many were fined, imprisoned, or exiled for their religious convictions. A contemporary source depicted the Covenanters as swearing to defend “their bodies, property and consciences against all attacks; to defend Christ’s gospel and the purity of the Church; to submit to no ruler who would not submit to Christ, and to defend their liberty from fears without and within.”

== Genealogical Note ==
* No reviewed record identifies John's father. [[Glasgow-3331|John Glasgow]] remains attached only as an uncertain working father.
* [[Glasgow-2249|Janet Glasgow]] remains an uncertain daughter; the prisoner list does not name a child, take John to Ireland, or supply any family relationship.
* The same list's William Glasgow is not proved to be John's relative or [[Glasgow-1605|William Glasgow]].  
* The only other Glasgow recorded in Roxburghshire at an earlier date is [[Glasgow-3023|Alan Glasgow (1550–1594)]], but no documentary link to John Glasgow has been established.

29027866.Name: Glasgow-1502
29027866.bio:
{{Estimated Date}}

== Biography ==

'''Robert Glasgow''' was associated with the Presbyterian congregation of Larne and Kilwaughter, County Antrim, Ireland, by 1699.

A published transcript of the congregation's early records identifies Robert as a stipend bondsman in 1699. He was appointed to carry the stipend bonds to Presbytery and, during 1700, participated in arrangements concerning congregational land, ploughing and work on the minister's meeting-house property.<ref name="Porter1863">Classon Porter, “Congregational Memoirs: Larne and Kilwaughter,” ''The Christian Unitarian'', vol. 2 (1863), pp. 409–414; [https://archive.org/details/christianunitari0002unse Internet Archive].</ref>

These responsibilities indicate that Robert was already an adult congregational representative in 1699. His birth is therefore estimated as occurring before about 1678. His precise birth date and birthplace have not been established.

Robert is attached as an uncertain son of [[Glasgow-1081|James Glasgow]], who was documented in Kilwaughter by the 1669 Hearth Money Roll and was active in the same Presbyterian congregation in 1700 and 1722.<ref name="timeline">[https://web.archive.org/web/20101124184247/http://lifesweaving.com/Glasgow/Kilwaughter/Timeline.html “Kilwaughter Timeline,”] ''lifesweaving.com'', archived 24 November 2010.</ref> James is a plausible father based on his earlier presence, compatible age and association with the same small community. However, no reviewed record explicitly identifies Robert as James's son, and the relationship remains unproved.

Robert's activities in 1700 are the last records that can presently be assigned to him with reasonable confidence. His marriage, children, occupation outside the congregation, date of death and place of death remain unknown.

== Research Notes ==

=== Possible father ===

[[Glasgow-1081|James Glasgow]] is retained as Robert's uncertain father because he belonged to an earlier generation of Glasgows established at Kilwaughter and appears beside Robert in congregational activity during 1700.

This attachment is circumstantial. It is not supported by a baptism, marriage record, will, deed or church entry naming Robert as James's son.

James was also not the only possible older relative in the district:

* [[Glasgow-3913|John Glasgow]] was recorded with James in the 1669 Hearth Money Roll for Kilwaughter.
* [[Glasgow-1078|Robert Glasgow]] was recorded at nearby Larne in 1653.

Any of these men could have been related to the Robert active in 1699–1700. The available records do not establish the precise relationship.

James's will was reportedly proved in 1727. Locating the original or a surviving abstract may help determine whether Robert was one of his children.<ref name="timeline" />

=== Separation from the younger Robert Glasgow ===

This Robert should not be conflated with [[Glasgow-1143|Robert Glasgow]], who was born about 1710, married in 1729 and was still living in 1772.

The man serving as a congregational bondsman and representative in 1699 must have belonged to an earlier generation. Evidence concerning the Robert living in 1772 should therefore remain attached to Glasgow-1143 and should not be used to extend the lifespan of this profile.

=== Later session and discipline records ===

A published continuation of the Larne and Kilwaughter congregational records contains a session list naming a Robert Glasgow and marking him as “turned out.” An entry dated 17 May 1747 explains that a former session member named Robert Glasgow had refused to make public satisfaction following an accusation of fornication.<ref name="Porter1864">Classon Porter, “Congregational Memoirs: Larne and Kilwaughter,” ''The Christian Unitarian'', vol. 3 (1864); [https://archive.org/details/christianunitari0003unse Internet Archive].</ref>

It has not been established whether the man in the later session and discipline records was:

* this older Robert, active in 1699–1700;
* [[Glasgow-1143|Robert Glasgow]], born about 1710; or
* another man of the same name.

The 1747 entry should not presently be used as evidence that this Robert was still living at that date.

=== Possible descendants and other relatives ===

The following Glasgow men appear in Kilwaughter records during the early eighteenth century:

* [[Glasgow-1499|Hugh Glasgow]]
* [[Glasgow-1504|James Glasgow]]
* [[Glasgow-1505|William Glasgow]]
* [[Glasgow-1143|Robert Glasgow]]

A secondary account suggests that their similar estimated ages may indicate that some were brothers.<ref name="EarlyGlasgows">[https://web.archive.org/web/20101124184247/http://lifesweaving.com/Glasgow/Kilwaughter/TheirStory2.html “The Early Glasgows,”] ''lifesweaving.com'', archived 24 November 2010.</ref> It does not establish that they were sons of this Robert, sons of James Glasgow or members of any particular nuclear family.

No parent-child relationships involving these men should be treated as proved solely from estimated ages, naming patterns or their residence in the same parish.

The proposed connection with [[Glasgow-591|William Glasgow]] and the family sometimes described as the “Melanchthon branch” also remains unproved.


=== William and Hugh Glasgow lease ===

A Registry of Deeds memorial records a lease dated 10 March 1736 from the Earl of Antrim to William and Hugh Glasgow of Larne for several Newtown of Larne tenements.<ref name="ROD1736WilliamHugh">Registry of Deeds, memorial of lease dated 10 March 1736, Earl of Antrim to William and Hugh Glasgow of Larne. [https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSN1-FXR2 FamilySearch image].</ref> The memorial supplies no kinship term, and its measuring lives were members of the royal family rather than Glasgow relatives. It therefore does not prove that William or Hugh was Robert's son. Their attachments remain working hypotheses.

29028532.Name: Glasgow-1512
29028532.bio:
== Biography ==
'''Robert Glasgow''' was likely born in Ayrshire, Scotland, before 1652. This birth estimate is based on his marriage and the birth of his known children in the early 1670s.

He married '''Margaret Donald'''. Together, they had at least two sons who were baptised in the parish of Ayr, Ayrshire:
* '''[[Glasgow-1513|Robert Glasgow]]''', born on 6 June 1670 and christened on 9 June 1670.<ref>"Scotland, Births and Baptisms, 1564-1950", database, FamilySearch (https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:XY8Z-L28 : 11 February 2020), Robert Glasgow in entry for Robert Glasgow, 1670.</ref>
* '''[[Glasgow-1514|Ralph Glasgow (bef.1671-)]]''', born on 3 December 1671.<ref>"Scotland, Births and Baptisms, 1564-1950", database, FamilySearch (https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:XY8Z-22X : 11 February 2020), Robert Glasgow in entry for Ralph Glasgow, 1671.</ref>

Both birth records name Robert Glasgow as the father and Margaret Donald as the mother. The family was living in Ayr, Ayrshire, at the time of these events.

Further details regarding his life, including his parentage and death, are not yet known.

29033410.Name: Glasgow-1521
29033410.bio:
== Biography ==
'''William Glasgow''' is represented by a profile whose baptism details have not yet been resolved. Scotland's People separately indexes WILLIAME GLASGOW on 28 September 1648 in Glasgow parish, with parents WILLIAME GLASGOW and BESSIE HOWIE (OPR 644/1, reference 40/156).<ref name="SP1648">National Records of Scotland, Church of Scotland Old Parish Registers, births and baptisms, Glasgow parish 644/1, reference 40/156, WILLIAME GLASGOW, indexed 28 September 1648, parents WILLIAME GLASGOW and BESSIE HOWIE; Scotland's People index, original register page not inspected.</ref> A separate 24 October 1641 entry for William, son of [[Glasgow-992|William Glasgow]] and [[Howie-1119|Bessie Howie]], belongs to [[Glasgow-1497]]. The 1648 index supports this child's event and recorded parent names, but does not distinguish a birthday from a baptism date or establish later life or the exact identities of the attached parent profiles. The attached [[Glasgow-1497|William Glasgow]] is retained as a possible older sibling, but the claim that he died before this William's birth depends on the unresolved 1648 identification.

=== Early Life in Scotland ===
William's profile belongs in the context of mid-17th-century Scotland, a period of political and religious upheaval. No record inspected so far details his early life, proves that his family were Covenanters, or proves that he migrated to Ulster. The 1648 index places a child of this name and parent names in Glasgow parish, but the original page has not been inspected for a more precise location or context.


=== Possible connection to the Tyrone family ===

A late family history says that an ancestor named William Glasgow came from Scotland in connection with the 1689 relief of Londonderry and remained in northern Ireland.<ref name="WMG">William Melanchthon Glasgow, ''History of the Glasgow Family'', [https://www.wikitree.com/photo/pdf/Glasgow-590 PDF attached to Glasgow-590].</ref> It does not name that William's parents, baptism, exact Scottish parish or military unit. It also does not mention Glasgow High Kirk, Cavers, the 1679 prisoner transport or the Orkney wreck.

No parish, military, land, testament or other contemporary record has been found connecting the child represented by this profile to [[Glasgow-591]], [[Glasgow-551]] or the Tyrone family. The identification is therefore an unproved hypothesis, not a biography fact.

=== Two indexed entries ===

An earlier footnote wrongly combined this child's 1648 entry with the 1641 entry assigned to [[Glasgow-1497]]. Scotland's People lists the children separately: 24 October 1641, Glasgow OPR 644/1, reference 30/298, and 28 September 1648, Glasgow OPR 644/1, reference 40/156. The 1641 FamilySearch citation has been removed from this profile. The asserted “Vol. 3/3621” wording and guardians John Stewart and Michael Leckprivick still require the original 1648 register page; those details are not established by the index.

== Research Notes ==

* The 28 September 1648 date is independently indexed, but the index alone does not say whether it is a birth or baptism date. The structured birth date remains marked uncertain.
* The 1648 index names William Glasgow and Bessie Howie as parents of the indexed child. The exact identities of the attached parent profiles and any connection to the later Tyrone man remain unproved.
* The disputed 1648 note gives reference “Vol. 3/3621” and names John Stewart and Michael Leckprivick, but those details remain unverified.
* The only evidence offered for migration to Ireland is the late family narrative, which does not identify this child.
* Future research should locate the complete Glasgow High Kirk index entry or original register image before pursuing Tyrone records.

=== Quothquan testament, 1673 ===

A William Glasgow “in Quodquen” (Quothquan), Libberton parish, Lanarkshire, had a testament entered in the Lanark Commissary Court on 9 April 1673, register CC14/5/9.<ref name="Quothquan1673">Francis J. Grant, ed., ''The Commissariot Record of Lanark: Register of Testaments, 1595–1800'' (Edinburgh: Scottish Record Society, 1903), printed p. 38, entry “Glasgow, William, in Quodquen,” [https://www.tradeshouselibrary.org/uploads/4/7/7/2/47723681/the_commissariot_record_of_lanark__register_of_testaments__1595-1800_~_1903.pdf#page=50 digital copy]. The original testament, NRS CC14/5/9, images 24–26, was reviewed on 10 September 2026; the surviving selective reading finds no securely identified kin.</ref> He had died by that date. The index does not state his age, occupation, spouse, children or parents.

The former [[Glasgow-3912]] represented this Quothquan man and was merged into this profile as the leading existing-profile identification. A person baptised at Glasgow in 1648 could have lived at Quothquan and died by 1673, and no closer same-name candidate has been identified in the reviewed local cluster. The index gives no direct link to this profile's 1648 baptism or William and Bessie Howie. The combined identity is therefore a working inference, not a proved parent-to-testator chain. The original testament was reviewed on 10 September 2026. Its partly obscured opening and selective reading have not yielded a secure kin bridge to the 1648 Glasgow baptism; further reading may test the match. This Lanark record supplies no evidence of migration to Tyrone.

29042221.Name: Glasgow-1557
29042221.bio:
== Biography ==  
{{One Name Study|name=Glasgow}}

'''Edward Glasgow''' has no identified birth or baptismal record. The structured estimate of about 1570 and the broad birthplace Scotland are retained as uncertain family-tree traditions. The often-repeated estimate of about 1583 is a narrower inference from his appearance as the father of a child baptised in 1615, not a recorded birth year. Either estimate is chronologically possible; his documented connection to Inveresk and Musselburgh begins with the 1615 baptism and does not prove that he was born there.

Edward is currently attached to [[Glasgow-3921|James Glasgow]] as an '''uncertain''' son. No identified birth, baptismal, testamentary or other relational record names Edward's father. Earlier prose proposed [[Glasgow-1168|James Glasgow (abt.1540–)]] from naming and locality alone; that stale proposal is not evidence for changing the current uncertain attachment.

=== Known Children ===

Edward appears in the Inveresk and Musselburgh parish register as the father of:

* '''Edward Glasgow''' – christened 6 June 1615  
** ''Scotland Births and Baptisms, 1564–1950'':  [https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:XTRN-75P FamilySearch Record]

The 1615 baptism proves that a man named Edward Glasgow was the child's father. It permits, but does not prove, an estimated birth in the later sixteenth century; it does not resolve the competing about-1570 and about-1583 estimates.

=== Context and Possible Family Connections ===

* [[Glasgow-994|Eduard Glasgow (1609–)]] is another individual baptized in the same parish, potentially a nephew or cousin.
* Edward’s activity in the Inveresk and Musselburgh area aligns him with a broader cluster of Glasgow family members recorded in early 17th-century Midlothian. This includes [[Glasgow-1148|Alexander Glasgow (abt.1600–bef.1700)]] and his documented sons and daughters born between 1626 and 1637.

== Research Notes ==
* Although Edward is not yet linked to a specific spouse in surviving records, further review of Inveresk OPR marriage entries from 1600–1620 may clarify this connection.
* Edward’s potential relationship to the Alexander Glasgow–Janet Clerk family should be explored via sasines and wills, if available.

== Biography ==
'''Johne Glasgow''' was recorded at Duddingston on '''4 April 1639''', with parents '''Johne Glasgow''' and '''Margaret Sluman'''. He is attached to [[Glasgow-1088|Johne Glasgow]] and [[Sluman-45|Margaret Sluman]].<ref name="John1639">[https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:X1TP-WYF FamilySearch], indexed Duddingston child record; the source citation on this profile reads MARGARET SLUMAN, Duddingston, 1639, and JOHNE, 04-04-1639, JOHNE GLASGOW/MARGARET SLUMAN, FR48, parish 684. Original image not inspected.</ref>

He is a possible match for '''Jon Glasgow''' in the Duddingston deaths and burials index on '''23 August 1641''', parish 684, reference 60/24. The other-details field reads '''JON GLASGOW''', but the index gives neither age nor an explicit kin term.<ref name="Jon1641">National Records of Scotland, Old Parish Registers, deaths and burials, Duddingston, parish 684, reference 60/24, 23 August 1641, JON GLASGOW, Parents/Other details JON GLASGOW, age blank, gender M; [https://www.scotlandspeople.gov.uk/ Scotland's People], exact-surname Glasgow search to 1700, index extract supplied 10 September 2026. Original image not inspected.</ref>

[[Glasgow-3014|John Glasgow]], recorded in the same parish in January 1638, is another chronological candidate. That child also has a probable, unproved match to a January 1638 deaths-and-burials entry. The originals must distinguish the two children before the 1641 event is assigned to either. This 1639 child cannot be the subject of the earlier 1638 event. No exact death date is established here.

29042292.Name: Glasgow-1561
29042292.bio:
'''⚠️ Paleographic Warning:'''

This profile is based on a testament written in 16th-century Secretary Hand. Due to the ornate and inconsistent handwriting style, all names, places, and relationships should be considered '''tentative''' and subject to '''revision''' pending further document comparison or corroboration. Interpretations are paleographically informed but speculative.

== Biography ==  
'''John Glasgow''' was born about 1590, likely in Linlithgowshire, Scotland. This estimate is based on the 1613 baptism of his daughter, [[Glasgow-3055|Jean Glasgow (bef.1613–)]]<ref>https://www.familysearch.org/tree/person/sources/MG7J-6GM</ref>.

He appears in multiple parish records as the father of children baptized in the town of Linlithgow between 1613 and 1622, suggesting he resided there for at least a decade and was part of the established Glasgow family in the area.

=== Children ===  
The following children are documented in the ''Scotland Births and Baptisms, 1564–1950'' database, all born in Linlithgow, Linlithgowshire:

* '''Jean Glasgow''' – christened 17 July 1613<ref>https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:X1RX-HPB</ref>  
* '''John Glasgow''' – christened 14 September 1617<ref>https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:X1RV-T8R</ref>  
* '''George Glasgow''' – christened 20 January 1622<ref>https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:X1RN-XV7</ref>  

== Research Notes ==

* The geographic setting (Linlithgowshire) and naming patterns suggest possible descent from [[Glasgow-1099|George Glasgow (abt.1580–)]] or [[Glasgow-1168|James Glasgow (abt.1540–1580)]], both associated with the greater Lanarkshire–Ayrshire–Lothian area.
* His son may have been [[Glasgow-991|James Glasgow (abt.1585–)]], also later found in Linlithgow.
* [[Glasgow-1103|Thomas Glasgow (1612–abt.1675)]], whose records also place him in the region, may be another child of John, though further documentation is needed.
* The surname in these records appears as ''Glesgow'', a common early spelling variation.


=== Parentage and generation ===
[[Glasgow-3163|Andrew Glasgow]]'s operative 1598 testament expressly names four children—Marioune, James, Andrew, and William—but does not name John.<ref>National Records of Scotland, Edinburgh Commissary Court, testament of Andrew Glasgow, CC8/8/32; printed index: [https://archive.org/details/scottishrecordso01scotuoft/page/n117/mode/1up ''Scottish Record Society'', p. 108].</ref> John was alive and parenting children in Linlithgow from 1613 to 1622, so this omission conflicts with treating him as Andrew's proved direct son.

The existing links to Andrew and [[Anderson-103463|Jonet Anderson]] are retained as '''uncertain working parents''', not as proved relationships. The Lothian geography could instead place John one generation lower or on a collateral line through one of Andrew's documented sons, but the evidence does not identify an exact parent. [[Glasgow-3608|John Glasgow]] is also an unproved same-name duplicate candidate; no merge is proposed.

29125246.bio:
== Biography ==
Hugh is currently estimated to have been born about 1600 and is associated with Ayrshire. Both the estimate and the geographic association derive from the cited online tree and remain uncertain.

== Research Notes ==
No reviewed record yet proves Hugh's identity, birth, father, or son. The existing links to [[Glasgow-991|James Glasgow]] as father and [[Glasgow-1604|John Glasgow]] as son are retained as '''uncertain scaffold relationships'''.

James Glasgow's documented household is centred on Calder and Inveresk in Midlothian, while this profile's working hypothesis is Ayrshire; that geographic mismatch makes the present father attachment especially tentative. A more plausible broad route may lie in the Corsankell–Stevenston–Kilwinning cluster beneath [[Glasgow-1098|William Glasgow]], but no source identifies Hugh's exact place in it.

A 1571 record names James elder of Corsankell and his sons James and John, but does not name Hugh.<ref>National Records of Scotland, [https://catalogue.nrscotland.gov.uk/nrsonlinecatalogue/details.aspx?reference=GD39%2F5%2F59 GD39/5/59], 1571.</ref> The Glasgow commissary testament index also identifies John at Montfoid (1610), James at Brekpleughe (1632), and Ninian at Brigend of Eglinton (1634).<ref>Francis J. Grant, ed., [https://archive.org/details/scottishrecordso07scotuoft ''Commissariot Record of Glasgow: Register of Testaments, 1547–1800''], surname index.</ref> These records establish nearby candidate households and may indicate a missing generation or conflated placeholder; they do not prove Hugh. He could be a son or grandson of [[Glasgow-3193|John Glasgow]], but no direct attachment should be made without a record.

A 1677 printed Register of Deeds index lists “Hugh, preacher of the gospel” under Glasgow. The same row calls him grantee (“Ge.”) in a deed indexed as “Transl.”, recorded 8 March 1677 at the Durie Office, volume 42, page 148 (NRS RD3/42, p. 148). This is a possible match only: the index gives no locality or relatives, and it does not identify the man with this profile. 8 March is the date the deed was recorded, not a death date. The underlying deed must be examined before changing this profile's dates or family links.<ref>FamilySearch, ''Scotland. == Biography ==

John Glasgow is retained as an uncertain Ayrshire-generation profile. His approximate 1626 birth in Ayrshire and approximate 1664 death at Kilwinning come from online family trees, not an identified contemporary record. No independent original record currently establishes those dates or identifies his parents.

== Research Notes ==

=== Attached relationships ===

The attached father [[Glasgow-1603|Hugh Glasgow]] and three sons are uncertain working relationships. Records for the sons' own adult households do not name this John as their father:

* [[Glasgow-3375|John Glasgow]] and Barbara Alason were parents at Kilwinning in 1679 and 1689. Whether this John was the father of that man remains unproved. Glasgow-3375 is also a possible identity match for [[Glasgow-1073|Rev. John Glasgow M.A.]].
* [[Glasgow-1512|Robert Glasgow]] and Margaret Donald had sons at Ayr in 1670–71; the baptism records do not name Robert's father.
* [[Glasgow-1066|Hew Glasgow]] married Margaret Lachland in 1676 and had children at Kilwinning; those records do not name Hew's father.

=== Former duplicate and parentage routes ===

Glasgow-3145 also represented a John Glasgow with an estimated birth about 1626 in Scotland and no independent life event. The profiles were merged into this ID on 27 September 2026 as duplicate imported-tree scaffolds, with no record identifying two different Johns. The former profile was attached, uncertainly, to [[Glasgow-991|James Glasgow]] and [[Bie-55|Christina Bie]], while this profile's uncertain route runs through Hugh Glasgow. Neither route is proved. The former parentage is preserved here as a research hypothesis; these alternatives must not be combined into a single asserted couple.

The source of the supposed 1664 Kilwinning death has not been identified. Its date and place remain uncertain research leads.

29125564.Name: Glasgow-1605
29125564.bio:
== Biography ==

'''[[Glasgow-1605|William Glasgow]]''' was baptised on 4 April 1658 at Polwarth, Berwickshire, with his father recorded only as William Glasgow.<ref name="PolwarthBirths" /> This profile represents that child.

No reviewed source connects the Polwarth child with the currently attached [[Glasgow-2462|father]], [[Glasgow-4138|the Cavers Covenanter]], the attached children [[Glasgow-3370|Isabell Glasgow]] and [[Glasgow-3587|William Glasgow]], or the later [[Glasgow-591|William Glasgow]] and [[Glasgow-2731|William Glasgow]] profiles. These links are retained as uncertain working hypotheses. A separate early derivative prisoner list names a William Glasgow of Cavers as a Covenanter, transportee and survivor of the wreck of the ''Croune of London'' near Deerness, Orkney, on 10 December 1679; that same-name man is not proved to be the Polwarth child. The 1679 Cavers deposition, survivor list and 1684 Ormistoun record are gathered on [[Glasgow-4138]]; those records also do not identify the Polwarth child.<ref name="Cloud1714">''A Cloud of Witnesses, for the Royal Prerogatives of Jesus Christ'' (1714), Appendix, "A List of the Banished," printed pp. 274–276. The list states that men who escaped the wreck were marked with a star and records "Will. Glasgow" under Cavers with that mark. [https://archive.org/details/cloudofwitnesses00edin Internet Archive scan]. A clearer reset of the list appears in John H. Thomson's 1871 edition, p. 523. [https://archive.org/details/cloudofwitnesses00thom/page/523/mode/1up Page 523].</ref><ref name="BrownDiary">A. Francis Steuart, ed., ''Diary of Thomas Brown, Writer in Kirkwall, 1675–1693'' (Kirkwall: William Peace, 1898), p. 10. Brown's contemporary entry for 10 December 1679 records the ''Croun'', carrying about 250 men taken at Bothwell Bridge and intended for Virginia, wrecked at or near the Mull Head of Deerness at about nine in the evening. [https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=hvd.32044081269342&seq=24 HathiTrust image]. Brown does not name William.</ref>

=== Same-name hypothesis: Covenanter and survivor of the ''Croune'' ===

Following Bothwell Bridge, hundreds of Covenanter prisoners were confined at Edinburgh. Colonial transportation was explicit government policy. A royal instruction of 29 June 1679 supported sending three or four hundred prisoners to the colonies; it is recorded in the Secretary for Scotland's warrant book as National Records of Scotland reference SP4/5, folios 174–175.<ref name="RoyalTransportation">Joseph Wagner, ''Scottish Colonization before Darien: Opportunities and Opposition in the Union of the Crowns'' (PhD thesis, University of St Andrews, 2020), pp. 157–158 and note 66, citing NRS SP4/5, Charles II to the Scottish Privy Council, 29 June 1679, fols. 174–175. [https://doi.org/10.17630/sta/47 University of St Andrews thesis]. National Records of Scotland, SP4/5, "Warrant book of Secretary for Scotland," 16 October 1678–30 April 1680. [https://catalogue.nrscotland.gov.uk/nrsonlinecatalogue/details.aspx?df=&di=y&dt=&k=&ko=a&r=SP4&reference=SP4%2F5&ro=s&st=1&tc=y&tl=n&tn=n&tp=n NRS catalogue]. The original letter was not available digitally for this review.</ref><ref name="Wodrow">Robert Wodrow, ''The History of the Sufferings of the Church of Scotland from the Restoration to the Revolution'', vol. III, pp. 130–131. [https://books.google.co.uk/books?id=eEwsAAAAYAAJ&pg=PA130 Google Books].</ref>

The 1714 ''Cloud of Witnesses'' states that about 250 prisoners taken at Bothwell were sent for banishment, that about 200 drowned near Orkney, and that the names of those who escaped were marked with a star. Under Cavers it records a William Glasgow with that survivor mark.<ref name="Cloud1714" /> This is the principal evidence for the Cavers man, but it does not identify him with the subject of this profile.

Thomas Brown's contemporary diary independently confirms the prisoner group, intended destination, date and approximate place and time of the wreck.<ref name="BrownDiary" /> Later Covenanter accounts state that many prisoners remained confined below deck as the ship broke apart and give totals of roughly two hundred dead and forty to fifty survivors.<ref name="Blackadder">John Blackadder, ''Memoirs of the Rev. John Blackader'' (Edinburgh, 1826), pp. 230–232. The published work preserves an account said to have been obtained from a survivor of the wreck. [https://archive.org/details/memoirsrevjohnb00blacgoog Internet Archive].</ref><ref name="Wodrow" /> Those details derive from partisan or survivor-based accounts rather than an official inquiry and should be attributed accordingly.

A post-wreck petition by William Paterson, the merchant directing the transportation, survives in the published Privy Council register. Paterson alleged that English and Scottish dissenters had influenced the captain or crew and intended to land the prisoners in England or Ireland. Paterson had an obvious financial and legal interest in assigning responsibility for the failed voyage. His petition documents the dispute following the wreck but does not prove that the loss was deliberate.<ref name="PatersonPetition">P. Hume Brown, ed., ''The Register of the Privy Council of Scotland'', Third Series, vol. VI, 1678–1680 (Edinburgh: H. M. General Register House, 1914), pp. 415–417, particularly p. 416. [https://books.google.com/books?id=00_aKojSqGIC&pg=PA416 Google Books]. Wagner, ''Scottish Colonization before Darien'', pp. 158–159, discusses Paterson's petition and his interest in blaming others. [https://doi.org/10.17630/sta/47 Thesis].</ref>

The 1714 prisoner list is an early derivative source rather than a surviving government passenger manifest, and the manuscript from which its names were compiled has not been identified. Comparison with surviving Privy Council material nevertheless shows that numerous people in the list can be independently found among those taken after Bothwell and selected for banishment, supporting its general reliability.<ref name="Jardine">Mark Jardine, "Beyond Orkney's Fatal Shore: The Wreck of The Croune, 10 December 1679," ''Jardine's Book of Martyrs'', 10 December 2016. Jardine compares the 1714 list with Privy Council material, identifies corroborated prisoners and discusses the list's unknown provenance. [https://drmarkjardine.wordpress.com/2016/12/10/beyond-orkneys-fatal-shore-the-wreck-of-the-croune-10-december-1679-history-scotland/ Article].</ref> No separate government entry naming William individually was identified in the published material examined.

=== Cavers survivors and the Ulster question ===

The Cavers group in the 1714 list comprised James Leydon, [[Glasgow-1498|John Glasgow]], William Glasgow, John Greenshields, Richard Young, Samuel Douglas, James Young and James Hopkirk. The survivor notation applies to James Leydon, [[Glasgow-1498|John Glasgow]], William Glasgow and James Young.<ref name="Cloud1714" />

No relationship between [[Glasgow-1498|John Glasgow]] and the Cavers William is stated. Their appearance together establishes only that both were assigned to the same Cavers parish group.

The earliest source located during this review that specifically places William after the wreck is Joseph A. Waddell's 1886 first edition of ''Annals of Augusta County, Virginia''. Waddell reproduced part of the banished-prisoner list, explained that the survivors' names were printed in italics, included John and William "Glascow" under Cavers, and then stated that all fifty survivors made their way to northern Ireland.<ref name="Waddell1886">Joseph A. Waddell, ''Annals of Augusta County, Virginia'' (Richmond: Wm. Ellis Jones, 1886), p. 5, note 1. Waddell includes John and William "Glascow" under Cavers and states that the fifty survivors reached northern Ireland. His note cites ''A Cloud of Witnesses'' for the prisoner list but does not identify a source for the destination statement. [https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Page:Annals_of_Augusta_County.djvu/21 Page image and transcription].</ref>

This is direct support for a northern-Ireland destination, but it was published 207 years after the wreck and is unsupported by a stated contemporary source. It cannot by itself prove William's migration.

Waddell materially recast the passage in his revised 1902 edition. He then wrote only that "some" of the prisoners who escaped made their way to Ulster and supplied ten names: John Thomson, William Waddell, John Gardner, Thomas Miller, Thomas Thomson, Andrew Thomson, Hugh Montgomery, John Martin, Andrew Clark and James Young. Neither [[Glasgow-1498|John Glasgow]] nor the Cavers William appears in that shorter list.<ref name="Waddell1902">Joseph A. Waddell, ''Annals of Augusta County, Virginia, from 1726 to 1871'', 2nd ed., revised and enlarged (Staunton, Virginia: C. Russell Caldwell, 1902), p. 8. The edition says that "some" escapees made their way to Ulster and names ten survivors, including James Young but neither Glasgow. [https://archive.org/stream/annalsofaugustac00wadd/annalsofaugustac00wadd_djvu.txt Internet Archive full text].</ref>

The omission does not disprove William's migration because the 1902 list is expressly introduced as only "some" of the survivors. It does, however, prevent the 1886 blanket statement from being accepted without qualification. Waddell did not explain the change or identify his evidence for either version.

Rob Close preserved another version of the Ulster tradition in 2004. He reported that nine survivors were believed to have escaped to Ulster, citing J. Thomson's ''A Cloud of Witnesses'' as quoted by Robert B. Miller.<ref name="AyrshireUlster">Rob Close, "Deerness Covenanter Memorial," ''Ayrshire Notes'', no. 28 (Autumn 2004), p. 15, note 17. The note states that nine survivors were believed to have escaped to Ulster, citing J. Thomson's ''A Cloud of Witnesses'' as quoted by Robert B. Miller. [https://aanhs.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/04/an28.pdf PDF].</ref> Close also stated that his account of the wreck owed much to Miller's research, a copy of which had been deposited at the Orkney Library and Archive.<ref name="AyrshireUlster" />

The corresponding archive catalogue entry has now been located. It describes a 1993 letter from Robert B. Miller of Richmond, Virginia, enclosing a list of survivors from the wreck of the ''Crown'' together with his sources.<ref name="MillerDossier">Orkney Library and Archive, catalogue entry, "The Wreck of 'The Crown'," 1993: letter from Robert B. Miller, Richmond, Virginia, enclosing a list of survivors from the wreck with his sources. [https://yourscottisharchives.com/catalogues/598d9888-6456-3c76-8c19-128ffce82a4b?component-id=fb62ec54-9931-3921-b3ea-9b4b94ddcdb6&terms=%22Songs%22 Catalogue entry]. The dossier was located but could not be inspected because no digital copy was available.</ref> Until that dossier is examined, it is not possible to determine whether Miller included William among the nine, what evidence he used, or whether Close and Waddell ultimately depended on the same tradition.

A modern study by Lawrence Holden and Mark Thompson gives a ten-person group of wreck survivors said to have fled to Ulster. It includes '''James Young of Teviotdale'''. The same study documents an active post-Bothwell refugee route: officials watched the ports of Larne and Donaghadee, while about fourteen open boats reportedly carried Covenanters from Irvine to Carrickfergus.<ref name="UlsterSurvivors">Lawrence Holden and Mark Thompson, "The Covenanters in Ulster," Part Six, "1666–1679, A Kirk Divided," pp. 6–7, Ulster-Scots Community Network. The study names ten wreck survivors said to have fled to Ulster, including James Young of Teviotdale, and describes the post-Bothwell refugee route from Irvine to Carrickfergus and government watch at Larne and Donaghadee. [https://ulster-scots.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/USCN-Covenanters-in-Ulster-Tabloid.pdf PDF]. This is a modern secondary study; its evidence for each named destination requires verification.</ref>

The description "James Young of Teviotdale" fits the James Young marked as a survivor in William's Cavers group. The matching name, regional description and survivor status make it probable that the two references concern the same man. If so, a member of William's exact parish cohort reached Ulster. This is stronger evidence than the general fact that unrelated Covenanters used the route, but it still does not prove that William travelled with him.

The Ulster evidence is therefore assessed as follows:

* '''Plausible and supported by substantial late evidence:''' Waddell's 1886 statement directly includes William among survivors said to have reached northern Ireland.
* '''Corroborating route and associate evidence:''' a probable member of William's exact Cavers survivor group, James Young, is repeatedly included among the Ulster fugitives.
* '''Important evidential tension:''' Waddell's revised 1902 list omits both Glasgows and limits its claim to "some" survivors.
* '''Not proved:''' no contemporary record examined identifies the Polwarth child as the Cavers prisoner, a survivor of the ''Croune'', or any William found in Ireland.
