== Research Notes ==

* The established identity on this profile is the child baptised at Polwarth on 4 April 1658. The Cavers Covenanter and ''Croune'' survivor is a same-name hypothesis, not an established identification.
* The Cavers heading establishes a parish association. It does not establish William's birthplace, exact residence or later home.
* For the Cavers same-name man, the Ulster hypothesis is now assessed as '''plausible rather than merely possible'''.
** Waddell's 1886 statement directly includes William among survivors said to have reached northern Ireland.<ref name="Waddell1886" />
** Waddell's 1902 revision narrows the claim and omits both Glasgows, but expressly lists only "some" survivors.<ref name="Waddell1902" />
** Close preserves a nine-survivor tradition derived through Robert B. Miller.<ref name="AyrshireUlster" />
** A probable member of William's exact Cavers survivor group, James Young, is repeatedly named among those who fled to Ulster.<ref name="UlsterSurvivors" />
** None of these sources is contemporary evidence of William's own arrival or settlement.
* The 1658 Polwarth baptism is the sourced identity for this profile. It remains only a candidate for the Cavers man because the chronology fits and another adult Glasgow household can be documented in the same district.
** No record connects the Polwarth child with Cavers, Bothwell Bridge, [[Glasgow-1498|John Glasgow]] or the wreck.
** The father named in the index is simply William Glasgow. The index does not identify him with [[Glasgow-2462|William Glasgow]] of Inveresk.
** [[Glasgow-3107|James Glasgow]] of Polwarth/Gordon is a stronger local kinship lead than the unattached Inveresk theory, but no relationship has been proved.
* The current attachments of [[Glasgow-3370|Isabell Glasgow]] and [[Glasgow-3587|William Glasgow]] as William's children are not established by their indexed records. Those entries prove later Glasgow activity at Cavers, not parentage.
* The attached father and children are retained as uncertain relationship hypotheses pending an original record or other evidence that bridges the identities.
* [[Glasgow-1498|John Glasgow]] was another Cavers survivor, but the prisoner list states no relationship between John and William.
* Cavers and Hawick were separate adjoining parishes in Roxburghshire. Polwarth and Gordon were separate parishes in Berwickshire.<ref name="Places">Scotland's People place and record pages: [https://www.scotlandspeople.gov.uk/place-page/Cavers/GAZ00352/- Cavers]; [https://www.scotlandspeople.gov.uk/place-page/Hawick/GAZ00597/REX01605 Hawick]; [https://www.scotlandspeople.gov.uk/virtual-volumes/volume-images/volume_data-OS1-29-14/REX01692 Hawick parish description, identifying Cavers on its eastern boundary]; and [https://www.scotlandspeople.gov.uk/place-page/Polwarth/GAZ00924/REX00785 Polwarth].</ref>
* The earlier description of Cavers as the same place as Hawick or as part of the Polwarth/Duns locality should not be retained.

=== Research completed for this revision ===

* '''Profile and record audit'''
** All mapped records for [[Glasgow-1605|William Glasgow]], his currently attached relatives and the relevant same-name Scottish and Irish candidates were compared.
** No source-backed parent, spouse or child relationship was found for William.
** No additional source-backed pre-1690 Glasgow occurrence at Cavers was identified beyond [[Glasgow-1498|John Glasgow]] and a William Glasgow in the prisoner list.

* '''Ulster source chain'''
** Waddell's 1886 first edition was checked against his 1902 revised edition.
** The 1886 edition directly places the fifty survivors, including William, in northern Ireland; the 1902 edition materially narrows the statement.
** Close's cited nine-survivor tradition was retained and traced to Robert B. Miller's deposited research.
** Miller's 1993 archive dossier was located in the Orkney catalogue, but no digital images or transcript were available.<ref name="MillerDossier" />
** The named survivor lists were compared with the Cavers group. James Young of Teviotdale is the strongest associate-level bridge.

* '''Published Scottish testament indexes'''
** The published Lauder commissary testament index was searched for Glasgow, Glasgo, Glascow, Glasco and Glassgow without finding a relevant entry.<ref name="LauderTestaments">Francis J. Grant, ed., ''The Commissariot Record of Lauder: Register of Testaments, 1561–1800'' (Edinburgh: Scottish Record Society). [https://archive.org/details/commissariotreco18laud Internet Archive]. Absence from a published index does not prove that no testament or related paper existed.</ref>
** The available published Peebles testament material for 1681–1699 was also searched without finding a relevant Glasgow entry.<ref name="PeeblesTestaments">Scottish Record Society, published Peebles commissary testament material covering 1681–1699. [https://archive.org/details/scottishrecords10scot Internet Archive]. This is a limited chronological and jurisdictional search.</ref>
** [[Glasgow-3912|William Glasgow]] of Quothquan was excluded because his testament was recorded before 1679.<ref name="QuothquanTestament" />

* '''Irish probate index'''
** Sir Arthur Vicars's index to Irish Prerogative wills was searched for William and surname variants. No William Glasgow was found.
** The index does contain an Archibald Glasgow, clerk, associated with Rathmullan or Ramelton, County Donegal, in 1677. This confirms another pre-wreck Ulster occurrence but supplies no relationship to William.<ref name="IrishPrerogativeWills">Sir Arthur Vicars, ''Index to the Prerogative Wills of Ireland, 1536–1810'' (Dublin, 1897). [https://archive.org/download/indextoprerogati00vica/indextoprerogati00vica.pdf PDF]. The Prerogative index is not a complete index to local diocesan probate records.</ref>

* '''Hearth-tax and archival identification'''
** The relevant surviving Scottish hearth-tax rolls were identified as NRS E69/5/1 for Berwickshire, including Polwarth and Gordon, and E69/21/1 for Roxburghshire, including Cavers and Hawick.
** Digital images of those rolls were not accessible in this review, so their contents have not been claimed or inferred.<ref name="HearthTax">National Records of Scotland, "Hearth Tax, 1691–1695." [https://www.nrscotland.gov.uk/learning-and-events/research-guides/taxation-records/?section=hearth-tax-1691-1695 Research guide]. FamilySearch catalogue, Scottish hearth-tax records. [https://www.familysearch.org/en/search/catalog/212753 Catalogue].</ref>
** The surviving Polwarth kirk-session, Marchmont estate, Kerr of Cavers, Reformed Presbyterian and Kilwaughter estate collections were identified, but the relevant documents are not available as open digital images.

=== Remaining Priority Research ===

* '''Robert B. Miller's survivor dossier'''
** Obtain a copy of the 1993 letter and enclosed survivor list from Orkney Library and Archive.<ref name="MillerDossier" />
** Determine whether Miller included the Cavers William among the nine Ulster fugitives.
** Record every source Miller supplied and establish whether Close, Holden/Thompson and Waddell depend on the same earlier account.
** This is currently the single highest-value unresolved Ulster source.

* '''Original Polwarth registers'''
** Inspect and transcribe the original baptismal entries for [[Glasgow-3362|Elizabeth Glasgow]] on 17 August 1656 and William Glasgow on 4 April 1658.
** Record the full wording, residence, occupation, mother's name, witnesses, sponsors and marginal notes.
** Search immediately before and after both entries for additional children of the same father.
** Inspect the original 1663 marriage of [[Glasgow-3107|James Glasgow]] and [[Watt-5185|Agnes Watt]] and the six Gordon baptisms.
** Compare residences and witnesses to test whether James and the father William were relatives.

* '''Polwarth kirk session and Marchmont estate'''
** Search Polwarth kirk-session minutes, NRS CH2/721, which include minutes for 1652–1668, for Glasgow, Glasgo, Glascow, Glasco and Glassgow.<ref name="PolwarthSession">National Records of Scotland, CH2/721, Polwarth kirk-session records. [https://catalogue.nrscotland.gov.uk/nrsonlinecatalogue/browseTreeview.aspx?reference=CH2%2F721 Catalogue]. Scotland's People, Polwarth kirk-session record page. [https://www.scotlandspeople.gov.uk/place-page/Polwarth/GAZ00924/REX00785/REX00785 Record page].</ref>
** Search the Hume of Polwarth and Earls of Marchmont papers for rentals, tacks, estate accounts, removals, testaments and lists of tenants.<ref name="Marchmont">National Records of Scotland, GD158, "Papers of the family of Hume of Polwarth, Earls of Marchmont." [https://catalogue.nrscotland.gov.uk/nrsonlinecatalogue/details.aspx?reference=GD158 Catalogue].</ref>
** These sources offer the best prospect of identifying the father of the 1656 and 1658 children or tracing the household out of Polwarth.

* '''Scottish hearth-tax rolls'''
** Inspect NRS E69/5/1 for Glasgow variants in Polwarth, Gordon and neighbouring Berwickshire parishes.
** Inspect NRS E69/21/1 for Glasgow variants in Cavers, Hawick, Kirkton, Hobkirk, Stitchel and neighbouring Roxburghshire parishes.
** A William or John Glasgow heading a household in 1691–1695 could distinguish continued Scottish residence from the Ulster hypothesis.<ref name="HearthTax" />

* '''Original Cavers and Hawick registers'''
** Inspect the original entries behind the 1692 Hawick baptism, the 1694 Cavers record and the 1709 Cavers marriage.
** Establish whether the 1694 entry names parents, residence, occupation or witnesses.
** Reconstruct every Glasgow household in Cavers, Hawick, Kirkton, Hobkirk and Stitchel from about 1650 to 1720.
** Compare witnesses and residences rather than merging same-name men.
** The surviving Cavers kirk-session minutes begin only in 1758 and cannot directly answer the 1679 question.<ref name="CaversSession">Scotland's People, "Cavers Church of Scotland kirk session." [https://www.scotlandspeople.gov.uk/place-page/Cavers/GAZ00352/-/REX01122 Record page].</ref>

* '''Kerr of Cavers estate records'''
** Search rentals, tacks, accounts, legal papers, correspondence and tenant lists in GD1/461.
** Search the 1666–1669 cash book in GD1/78 for Glasgow variants and for the other Cavers prisoners.<ref name="KerrCavers">National Records of Scotland, GD1/461, "Papers of the Kerr Family of Cavers, 1561–1820." [https://catalogue.nrscotland.gov.uk/nrsonlinecatalogue/browseDetails.aspx?reference=GD1%2F461 Catalogue]; GD1/78, cash book of Sir Andrew Ker of Cavers, 1666–1669. [https://catalogue.nrscotland.gov.uk/nrsonlinecatalogue/browseDetails.aspx?reference=GD1%2F78 Catalogue].</ref>
** Estate records may establish whether William or [[Glasgow-1498|John Glasgow]] was a tenant, servant or tradesman at Cavers before Bothwell.

* '''Original Bothwell and transportation records'''
** Search the Privy Council acts, decreets, warrants, petitions, bonds and transportation papers for Glasgow, Glasgo, Glascow, Glasco and Glassgow.
** Search the Cavers William as part of the complete Cavers cluster: James Leydon, [[Glasgow-1498|John Glasgow]], John Greenshields, Richard Young, Samuel Douglas, James Young and James Hopkirk.
** Search post-wreck petitions, indemnity records and forfeiture material for any survivor described by parish, occupation, relative or destination.<ref name="PrivyCouncilGuide">National Records of Scotland, "Privy Council Records." [https://www.nrscotland.gov.uk/learning-and-events/research-guides/privy-council-records/ Research guide].</ref>

* '''Post-Revolution Covenanter records'''
** Search the Reformed Presbyterian subscription rolls and related papers for 1689–1712 in NRS GD1/465.
** Search William, [[Glasgow-1498|John Glasgow]], James Young and the remaining Cavers prisoners together.
** A shared congregation, locality, witness or subscription entry could provide the missing post-wreck Scottish bridge.<ref name="CameronianRolls">National Records of Scotland, GD1/465, papers concerning the Reformed Presbyterian Church, 1689–1712, including Covenant subscription rolls. [https://catalogue.nrscotland.gov.uk/nrsonlinecatalogue/browseDetails.aspx?reference=GD1%2F465 Catalogue].</ref>

* '''James Young and the Ulster survivor cluster'''
** Establish whether James Young of Teviotdale was the James Young listed under Cavers.
** Trace all ten people named by Waddell and Holden/Thompson in Presbyterian, land, probate, military and court records.
** Identify their earliest Ulster locations, congregations, landlords and repeated associates.
** Search for the Cavers William and [[Glasgow-1498|John Glasgow]] in the same localities and networks.
** A cluster around one destination would materially strengthen the migration case even if William's own entry remains indirect.

* '''Original east-Ulster records'''
** Inspect the original 1669 County Antrim hearth roll, PRONI T/307/A, rather than relying solely on the modern transcription.
** Search Connor diocesan probate material for every Glasgow/Glascho testator from about 1650 to 1730; the Prerogative index does not cover most local estates.
** Search original Larne, Kilwaughter, Glenarm, Carrickfergus and Belfast Presbyterian material for admissions, removals, testimonials, marriages, baptisms, communion rolls and disciplinary cases.
** Search the Agnew family's Kilwaughter estate papers, particularly GD154/505–534 for 1636–1712, for leases, rentals, accounts and correspondence naming the Glascho householders.<ref name="AgnewEstate">National Records of Scotland, GD154, "Papers of the Agnew Family of Lochnaw," including GD154/505–534 concerning the Irish estate at Kilwaughter, County Antrim, 1636–1712. [https://catalogue.nrscotland.gov.uk/nrsonlinecatalogue/details.aspx?di=y&k=Agnew+Estate&ko=a&reference=GD154&ro=s&st=1&tc=y&tl=n&tn=n&tp=n Catalogue].</ref>
** A valid Ulster identification should require a Scottish parish of origin, named relative, fellow prisoner, repeated associate, occupation or migration record. Surname and Presbyterian affiliation alone are insufficient.

== Biography ==

Janet Glasgow is represented on WikiTree as the wife of James Woodside. Her reported dates and Irish birthplace have not been established by a reviewed original record.

== Research Notes ==

[[Glasgow-1498|John Glasgow]] is documented as a survivor of the 1679 ''Croune of London'' wreck under Cavers parish, Scotland. That prisoner list names no parents or children and gives no later Irish destination. It therefore does not prove that Janet was his daughter; the father link is retained only as uncertain pending a better placement.

An earlier profile version placed Janet's death at Elgin, Illinois, in 1775. This is impossible because Elgin was founded in 1835; the city history is retained below as evidence for excluding that location. The generic baptism collection and memorial previously cited do not supply an original record proving Janet's Irish birth or her father.

39499897.Name: Glasgow-2682
39499897.bio:
== Biography ==
The parentage and birth date for James Glasgow are not yet known. Based on the birth of his first known child in 1677, he was likely born by about 1657.

He was married to [[Duffe-18|Isobell Duffe]]. Her name is recorded as "Issobell Duff" or "Issobell Duffe" in the christening records of most of their children.

James and Issobell had the following children, all christened in Edinburgh Parish, Midlothian, Scotland:
* [[Glasgow-3088|Jean Glasgow]], christened 13 April 1677.<ref name="Jean1677">"Scotland, Births and Baptisms, 1564-1950", database, FamilySearch (https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:XTPF-7YB : 11 February 2020), James Glasgow in entry for Jean Glasgow, 1677.</ref>
* [[Glasgow-3103|James Glasgow]], christened 16 March 1679.<ref name="James1679">"Scotland, Births and Baptisms, 1564-1950", database, FamilySearch (https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:VQC9-Q9J : 11 February 2020), James Glasgow in entry for James Glasgow, 1679.</ref> (See Research Notes regarding mother's name on this record).
* [[Glasgow-3368|James Glasgow]], christened 18 April 1680.<ref name="James1680">"Scotland, Births and Baptisms, 1564-1950", database, FamilySearch (https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:VQC9-8S4 : 11 February 2020), James Glasgow in entry for James Glasgow, 1680.</ref> The christening of a second son with the same name strongly suggests the first James died in infancy.
* [[Glasgow-3284|Mary Glasgow]], christened 23 April 1682.<ref name="Mary1682">"Scotland, Births and Baptisms, 1564-1950", database, FamilySearch (https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:VQCM-LLH : 11 February 2020), James Glasgow in entry for Mary Glasgow, 1682.</ref>
* [[Glasgow-3285|Thomas Glasgow]], christened 13 November 1684.<ref name="Thomas1684">"Scotland, Births and Baptisms, 1564-1950", database, FamilySearch (https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:VQC9-N9X : 11 February 2020), James Glascow in entry for Thomas Glascow, 1684.</ref>
* [[Glasgow-2681|Margaret Glasgow]], christened 20 March 1691.<ref name="Margaret1691">"Scotland, Births and Baptisms, 1564-1950", database, FamilySearch (https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:FM3W-XBN : 11 February 2020), James Glasgow in entry for Margarett Glasgow, 1691.</ref>

The date and place of James's death are unknown, but he was alive as of March 1691.
== Research Notes ==
'''Identifying the parents of James Glasgow is a top research priority.''' Several contemporary men named James Glasgow who were also having children in Edinburgh at the same time have been investigated and ruled out as being the same person, though they are likely relatives (e.g., brothers or cousins). These include:
*   '''[[Glasgow-3098|James Glasgow (b. 1631)]]''', who was married to Bessie Whyte.
*   '''[[Glasgow-3077|James Glasgow (b. bef. 1640)]]''', who was married to Helen Clerk.
*   '''[[Glasgow-3337|James Glasgow (b. ca. 1640)]]''', who was married to Annapill Glessie.

Since our James was consistently recorded with his wife, [[Duffe-18|Isobell Duffe]], it is highly unlikely he is the same person as any of the men listed above.

*   '''Parentage is Unknown:''' The parents of James are not yet confirmed. The original profile suggested he might descend from the Midlothian line of [[Glasgow-1168|James Glasgow (abt.1540-1580)]], perhaps as a son of [[Glasgow-1151|Johne Glasgow (1632-)]] or [[Glasgow-1084|John Glasgow (bef.1616-)]]. This is speculative and requires further research to find a primary source linking him to a father.
*   '''Conflicting Mother's Name:''' The 1679 christening record for his son [[Glasgow-3103|James]] lists the mother's name as "Elizabeth Duffe" instead of "Issobell". As all other children's records name her as Issobell, and given the commonality of clerical errors, it is most likely that "Elizabeth" was a mistake by the parish clerk.
*   '''Future Research:''' The highest priority is to find a marriage record for James Glasgow and Issobell Duffe in the Edinburgh parish registers, likely dated before April 1677. A search for burial records for both James and Issobell after March 1691 should also be conducted.

39831137.Name: Glasgow-2731
39831137.bio:
== Biography ==

William Glasgow's origins, including his precise birth date, location, and parentage, are currently unknown. Based on the christening date of his daughter Margaret in 1692, he was likely born before about 1675, perhaps placing his birth somewhere between 1650 and 1672.

He is documented as residing in Hawick, Roxburghshire, Scotland, in early 1692, when his daughter was christened there.

=== Family ===

The name of William's spouse, the mother of Margaret, is not recorded in the available christening record and remains unknown.

Known child:
*  [[Glasgow-2730|Margaret Glasgow (abt.1692-)]], christened 7 February 1692 in Hawick, Roxburghshire, Scotland.<ref name="MargaretChr">"Scotland Births and Baptisms, 1564-1950", database, FamilySearch (https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:X11X-46N : 12 February 2020), William Glasgo in entry for Margaret Glasgo, 1692.</ref> (Note the spelling "Glasgo" in the record for both father and daughter).

It is possible William had other children, but further research is needed to identify them.

=== Death ===

William's death date and place are unknown.

=== Research Notes ===

*   The estimate for William's birth year is speculative, based solely on being a father in 1692.
*   The spelling "Glasgo" appears in the source record for both William and Margaret. Research should consider variations like Glasgow, Glascoe, etc.
*   Further research is needed to find:
**   William's birth/christening record (potentially in Roxburghshire or surrounding counties).
**   A marriage record for William Glasgow (likely before 1692, potentially in Roxburghshire).
**   Birth/christening records for other potential children in the Hawick area.
**   Records placing William in Hawick or Roxburghshire at other times (e.g., kirk session, land, tax records).
**   A death or burial record for William Glasgow.


* [[Glasgow-1605|William Glasgow (bef.1658-)]] and [[Glasgow-2731|William Glasgow (abt.1670-)]] may represent the same person because;
** [[Glasgow-1605|William Glasgow (bef.1658-)]] is based on the Crowne Shipwreck, 1679, it lists William and John from Cavers (same place as Hawick, near Polwarth, Duns)
** [[Glasgow-2731|William Glasgow (abt.1670-)]] is based on the birth of his daughter [[Glasgow-2730|Margaret Glasgow (abt.1692-)]] in Hawick. 



=== Corrected assessment ===

=== Parentage and identity ===

Margaret's baptism establishes William only as her named father. It supplies no evidence that he was the son of [[Glasgow-3331|John Glasgow]], whose biography independently reports no confirmed children. That attachment should be treated as uncertain pending direct evidence.

No record connects this Hawick father with [[Glasgow-1605|William Glasgow (bef.1658-)]], who is associated with Polwarth and the 1679 Crowne shipwreck/Cavers material. Similar names and broad regional proximity do not establish identity; no merge is supported.

44189451.Name: Glasgow-3011
44189451.bio:
== Biography ==

'''Robert Glasgow''' was baptised or born at Glencorse on 29 December 1676, a son of [[Glasgow-3012|John Glasgow]] and [[Currie-4998|Margaret Currie]].<ref name="Robert1676">Scotland's People, Church of Scotland old parish registers, Robert Glasgow, 29 December 1676, parents John Glasgow and Margaret Currie, Glencorse parish 687, reference 10/8.</ref>

== Research Notes ==

An exact Scotland's People search for Robert Glasgow baptisms at Glencorse from 1640 through 1690 returns only this entry. A Robert Glasgow married [[Davidson-20783|Margaret Davidson]] in the same parish on 8 June 1704, when this Robert would have been twenty-seven.<ref name="Marriage1704">Scotland's People, Church of Scotland old parish registers, marriage of Robert Glasgow and Margarett Davidson, 8 June 1704, Glencorse parish 687, reference 20/53.</ref> The unique indexed local candidate, matching parish and chronology, makes this Robert a strong candidate for that groom and the couple's children. The marriage index gives no age, parents or occupation, so the identity remains unproved and no spouse or children are attached here yet.

An exact Scotland's People wills-and-testaments search for Robert Glasgow from 1690 through 1760, repeated under Glasgo, Glascow, Glaskow and Glassgow, returned no result. Targeted inspection of the Glencorse kirk-session testimonial register found no Robert Glasgow or Margaret Davidson on the pages covering 1704, 1708, 1710 and 1720.<ref>National Records of Scotland, Glencorse kirk session, CH2/181/1, testimonials (1685–1728), targeted pages for 1704, 1708, 1710 and 1720, [https://www.scotlandspeople.gov.uk/virtual-volumes/volume-images/volume_data-CH2-181-1/REX00185 Scotland's People Virtual Volumes].</ref> These are limited negatives: neither source is a population list, and spelling variation or register gaps may conceal relevant evidence.

This Robert was seventeen in October 1694 and is also chronologically capable of being the Robt Glasgow then listed as a servant in Alexander Ainslie's North Leith glass-manufactory household.<ref>National Records of Scotland, E70/4/10, North Leith poll tax, 3 October 1694, image 11, [https://www.scotlandspeople.gov.uk/virtual-volumes/volume-images/volume_data-E70-4-10/REX01666?image_number=11 Scotland's People Virtual Volumes].</ref> On 16 July 1694 a Robert Glasgow gave a receipt in Ainslie's name for bottles supplied to the Earl of Breadalbane.<ref>National Records of Scotland, Breadalbane Muniments, GD112/15/59, item 24, 16 July 1694, [https://catalogue.nrscotland.gov.uk/nrsonlinecatalogue/details.aspx?reference=GD112%2F15%2F59 catalogue description].</ref> The shared employer and year make him almost certainly the October servant and prove a functional glassworks-business role, but neither record identifies him with the Glencorse child.

Neither possible continuation identifies this man as [[Glasgow-2867|Robert Glasgow]], master of the ''John and Archibald'' in 1754.

Holloman's biography of his son describes the reverend as a native of Scotland; this secondary statement supports only a cautious, uncertain Scottish origin, not a specific birthplace.Charles R. After adopting the Westminster Confession of Faith, Patrick was ordained and installed at the Manokin Presbyterian congregation in Maryland in 1736. [[Category:Glasgow Name Study]]

== Biography ==
John Glasgow was christened in 1649 in the parish of Kirknewton and East Calder, Midlothian, Scotland. He was the son of [[Glasgow-3610|John Glasgow]].<ref name="Birth1649">"Scotland, Births and Baptisms, 1564-1950", database, FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:VQ4K-X6G : 16 September 2021), Johne Glasgow, 1649.</ref> His known siblings included [[Glasgow-3112|Margaret Glasgow]] and [[Glasgow-3118|Alexander Glasgow]].{{Citation needed }}

He married '''[[Currie-4998|Margaret Currie]]''' in 1673 in Kirknewton.<ref name="Marriage1673">"Scotland, Marriages, 1561-1910", database, FamilySearch (https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:XY9W-J5Q : 11 February 2020), Johne Glasgow, 1673.</ref>

Sometime after their marriage, the family moved to the neighboring parish of Glencorse, Midlothian, where their known children were christened.

John and Margaret had the following children:
* [[Glasgow-3011|Robert Glasgow]], christened 29 December 1676 in Glencorse.<ref name="Robert1676">Old Parish Registers, Baptisms, Glencorse, Midlothian. Ref: 687/ FR11.</ref>
* [[Glasgow-3013|William Glasgow]], christened 26 December 1680 in Glencorse.<ref name="William1680">Old Parish Registers, Baptisms, Glencorse, Midlothian. Ref: 687/ FR16.</ref>
* [[Glasgow-3085|Margaret Glasgow]], christened 13 April 1684 in Glencorse.<ref name="Margaret1684">"Scotland, Births and Baptisms, 1564-1950", database, FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:VQ4J-FXD : 16 September 2021), John Glaskow in entry for Margarat Glaskow, 1684.</ref>
* [[Glasgow-2917|Charles James Glasgow]], christened 3 October 1686 in Glencorse.<ref name="Charles1686">"Scotland, Births and Baptisms, 1564-1950", database, FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:VQ4J-JJK : 16 September 2021), John Glesgowe in entry for Charles Glesgowe, 1686.</ref>

== Research Notes ==
Sources are needed to confirm these sibling relationships.

'''Spelling Variations'''
The parish records show variations in the spelling of the family's names. The father is recorded as John Glaskow and John Glesgowe, and the mother as Margaret Corrie. These phonetic spellings were common due to varying literacy and local dialects.

'''Marriage and Residency'''
The marriage record places the couple in Kirknewton in 1673, while the baptismal records for all known children place them in the neighboring parish of Glencorse from 1676 onward. This indicates a move shortly after their marriage.

=== Supplied parish index comparison ===

The supplied Scotland’s People index records '''JOHNE GLASGOW''' on '''22/04/1649''' at Kirknewton and East Calder, with parent text “JOHNE GLASGOW/ FR15 (FR15)”.<ref name="OPRBirth046">Scotland’s People, [https://www.scotlandspeople.gov.uk/ Old Parish Registers, births and baptisms], exact surname Glasgow through 1700, index text supplied 10 September 2026: JOHNE GLASGOW, 22/04/1649, JOHNE GLASGOW/ FR15 (FR15), indexed gender M, Kirknewton and East Calder, parish 690, reference 10 / 14. Original register image not inspected for this review.</ref>

The profile’s structured birth date is 1649-04-04, whereas this index date is 1649-04-22. The two dates remain unreconciled. The combined births and baptisms collection does not establish whether the indexed date is a birthday or a baptism date. A parent’s name alone does not uniquely identify an attached historical person, and the index does not establish an unnamed parent.

44189562.Name: Glasgow-3018
44189562.bio:
== Biography ==

'''John Glasgow''' was born about 1675 and is associated with Irvine, Ayrshire, Scotland. Both the date and place are part of a reconstruction and remain uncertain. This profile currently combines at least three same-name propositions which have not been proved to represent one man.

=== 1693 father proposition ===

An Irvine baptism dated '''8 October 1693''' records a son John to a father named John Glasgow and Agnes Martine.<ref name="Baptism1693">“Scotland Births and Baptisms, 1564–1950,” FamilySearch, John Glasgow and Agnes Martine, baptism of son John, 8 October 1693, Irvine 595/ M.</ref> This record proves that a couple with those names had a son John; it does not identify the father as the 1725 skipper or the 1740 bailie. [[Martine-274|Agnes Martine]] and [[Glasgow-1473|John Glasgow]] are retained on this combined profile as uncertain relationship candidates.

=== 1725 skipper proposition ===

In 1725, '''John Glasgow elder''', skipper in Irvine, purchased a one-sixteenth share of the ship ''Janet'' of Irvine, commanded by James Miller, for £7 sterling.<ref name="IrvineCatalogue">Irvine Burgh catalogue, 1725 ship-share entry. The catalogue PDF link formerly supplied by Ayrshire Archives returned HTTP 410 Gone when checked 26 August 2026; the source title and entry detail are retained pending recovery of a stable archive catalogue URL.</ref> The word “elder” distinguishes him from a younger namesake. It does not by itself prove that the younger John was his son, identify Agnes Martine as his wife, or connect him to the 1693 baptism family.

=== 1740 bailie proposition ===

A 1740 Irvine record names John Glasgow as a bailie in a legal summons against Elizabeth Cunninghame, widow of Robert Montgomerie of Broomland.<ref name="IrvineCatalogue" /> The shared name and Irvine setting make the 1725 skipper and 1740 bailie possible matches, but the cited records do not supply an occupation, family relationship or other bridge proving they were the same man.

=== Comparison with Glasgow-1434 ===

[[Glasgow-1434|John Glasgow]], baptised in 1679 at Kilwinning and later associated with Stevenston, remains an open candidate for part of this reconstruction. He would have been only about fourteen when the son John was baptised in 1693, which weighs against—but does not by itself disprove—the father proposition. The alleged duplicate-son conflict is not decisive because the skipper, bailie and family identifications on this profile are themselves reconstructed. The profiles should not be merged or detached without burgh or parish evidence linking the Kilwinning/Stevenston man to Irvine.

John's death remains unknown. If the 1740 bailie was the same person represented here, he was alive in that year; that equation is not proved.

== Research Notes ==

* The 1693 father, 1725 skipper and 1740 bailie are three separate propositions.
* The attached spouse Agnes Martine and son John are retained as uncertain links, not proved members of the skipper/bailie household.
* “Elder” proves only that a younger namesake existed, not that the younger man was his son.
* The possible relationship to [[Glasgow-1406|Michael Glasgow]] remains unproved.
* Compare witnesses, occupations and residences in Irvine burgh and shipping records before considering a merge with Glasgow-1434.

* A 1721 Irvine prize bond lists “John Glasgow for one” among subscribers pledging a half crown toward an annual shooting prize. The name and town make this a possible earlier occurrence of the 1725 skipper, but the bond gives no occupation, kin or identifying description.<ref>''Muniments of the Royal Burgh of Irvine'', vol. II (1891), p. 133, no. 78, “Bond by Residenters in Ayrshire for payment of stakes for the Prize to be shot for yearly at Irvine,” 1721, [https://electricscotland.com/history/gazetteer/MunimentsoftheroyalburghofIrvine02.pdf#page=160 digitised page].</ref>
* A separate Irvine town account covering 1669–70 records the provost with a John Glasgow “ffor stones to the bridge” on 21 July. It does not identify the 1693 father, 1725 skipper or 1740 bailie; retain this as an earlier same-name occurrence only.<ref>''Muniments of the Royal Burgh of Irvine'', vol. II (1891), p. 272, no. 23, “The Town's Account to Janet Barclay,” begun 7 October 1669, [https://electricscotland.com/history/gazetteer/MunimentsoftheroyalburghofIrvine02.pdf#page=299 digitised page]. The 21 July line falls within the 1669–70 account.</ref>

=== Newly checked Irvine catalogue entries ===

* On 15 March 1729 a bond named “John Glasgow elder, skiller in Irvine,” as treasurer of the Sailors' Poor Box. The catalogue prints “skiller”; the underlying bond has not been inspected. His name, “elder” label, town and maritime association make him a strong candidate for the 1725 skipper, but the catalogue does not explicitly equate the men.<ref>Ayrshire Archives, ''Irvine Burgh Catalogue'' (2017), IB2/15/45, p. 160, 15 March 1729; [https://web.archive.org/web/20190919232657/https://ayrshirearchives.files.wordpress.com/2019/04/irvine-burgh-catalogue-2017-watermarked.pdf archived catalogue].</ref>
* On 30 January 1734 a ship share was sold from the heirs of the late John Glasgow, shipmaster. This man had died by that date. He is a plausible match for the 1725 skipper and 1729 sailors' fund treasurer, but those identities are not explicit in the catalogue.<ref>Ayrshire Archives, ''Irvine Burgh Catalogue'' (2017), IB2/14/52, p. 145, 30 January 1734; [https://web.archive.org/web/20190919232657/https://ayrshirearchives.files.wordpress.com/2019/04/irvine-burgh-catalogue-2017-watermarked.pdf archived catalogue].</ref>
* The 1740 legal-process entry calls its John Glasgow a bailie and merchant. He cannot be the shipmaster described as deceased by January 1734. Which of these men, if either, was the 1693 father or 1725 skipper remains to be established from the original records.<ref>Ayrshire Archives, ''Irvine Burgh Catalogue'' (2017), IB2/1/70, p. 70, 1740; [https://web.archive.org/web/20190919232657/https://ayrshirearchives.files.wordpress.com/2019/04/irvine-burgh-catalogue-2017-watermarked.pdf archived catalogue].</ref>

* [[Glasgow-1077|John Glasgow]], the later Irvine provost, has a documented 9 December 1690 Kilbirnie baptism and is a plausible candidate for the 1740 bailie entry. The same child cannot have been the adult father in the 1693 Irvine baptism attached as a separate proposition on this profile. The 1740 entry gives no parent, wife or birth identifier, so its assignment to Glasgow-1077 remains an identity hypothesis.<ref>Findmypast, Scotland Parish Births and Baptisms, record SCOT/OPR/BAP/3585655, Kilbirnie, 9 December 1690, John Glasgow; and Ayrshire Archives, ''Irvine Burgh Catalogue'' (2017), IB2/1/70, p. 70, 1740 bailie John Glasgow.</ref>

== Sources ==

44192425.Name: Glasgow-3023
44192425.bio:
{{Estimated Date}} == Biography == {{One Name Study|name=Glasgow}} '''Alan Glasgow''', recorded as '''Alan Glasgw''', was a man who had been killed by '''26 February 1495'''. No reliable evidence has been identified for his date or place of birth, residence, occupation, social status, parentage, spouse or children. The sole known record naming Alan appears in the proceedings of the justice ayre held at Jedburgh on 26 February 1495. James Pilmure, described as ''in Ednem'', produced a royal remission covering several offences. Robert Pitcairn printed the entry as follows:
JAMES PILMURE, in Ednem, produced a Remission for theftuously wasting of the goods of George Smythe, at the time he lay with his wife; Item, for the Slaughter of Alan Glasgw.—Ralph Ker became surety to satisfy the parties.Robert Pitcairn, ed., ''Criminal Trials and Other Proceedings before the High Court of Justiciary in Scotland'', vol. I, part I (Edinburgh, 1833), p. 19, [https://www.google.co.uk/books/edition/Criminal_Trials_and_Other_Proceedings_Be/LFAJAAAAQAAJ?gbpv=1&pg=PA19 Google Books scan]. Pitcairn’s printed date “1594–5” is a typographical error for 1494–5; the entry belongs to the second day of the Jedburgh justice ayre, 26 February 1495.
The entry establishes that Alan had been killed before the hearing and that Pilmure possessed a remission covering the killing. It does not state the date or place of Alan’s death, the circumstances or motive, or the precise nature of Pilmure’s involvement. The word ''Item'' identifies Alan’s killing as a separate matter within the remission. Nothing in the record connects the killing with the preceding offence involving George Smythe, Smythe’s goods and Smythe’s wife. Ralph Ker’s undertaking to “satisfy the parties” indicates that compensation was to be made to those legally entitled to claim following the killing. The record does not identify those parties and does not establish that Alan left a widow, child, heir or other particular relative. Ker’s role as surety does not imply kinship with Alan. == Research Notes == === Date === The date attached to Pitcairn’s entry is misprinted as 1594–5. The surrounding chronological sequence shows that the correct year is '''1494–5''', corresponding to 26 February 1495 in modern dating. There is no verified record of a separate Alan Glasgow killed in 1593. The earlier claim arose from a false or misattributed transcription and should not be repeated. === Name === Pitcairn prints the name as ''Alan Glasgw''. In digitised text, the long letter ''s'' may be incorrectly rendered as ''f'', producing ''Glafgw''. The form ''Glasgw'' appears to function as a personal surname or byname. The original manuscript should nevertheless be inspected before the absence of ''de'' in Pitcairn’s edited English text is treated as conclusive evidence of the exact Latin form. The surname alone provides no evidence of Alan’s birthplace, residence or ancestry. === James Pilmure === Pitcairn describes James Pilmure as ''in Ednem'', not “of Ednam”. This indicates residence or some other connection with Ednam but does not establish landownership or a territorial designation. No evidence has been identified that Pilmure was related to Alan. === Ralph Ker === The Ralph Ker named as surety may have been '''Ralph Ker of Prymsideloch''', who is independently recorded in the Jedburgh area in 1491 and later appears as a surety at the Jedburgh justice ayre of 1502.National Records of Scotland, GD6/592, procuratory dated 22 October 1491, naming Ralph Ker of Prymsideloch; compare Pitcairn, ''Criminal Trials and Other Proceedings before the High Court of Justiciary in Scotland'', vol. I, proceedings of the Jedburgh justice ayre of 1502. This identification remains provisional until the original 1495 manuscript entry is examined. === Original record === The underlying court book is held by the National Records of Scotland as '''JC1/1''', Court Books, old series, South Circuit and Edinburgh, covering 7 November 1493 to 13 August 1504.National Records of Scotland, JC1/1, Court Books, old series, South Circuit and Edinburgh, 7 November 1493–13 August 1504. A transcript of the court book is held by the National Library of Scotland as '''Adv. MS. 6.1.4'''. It was prepared circa 1809 under the direction of Thomas Thomson and is not a contemporary transcript.National Library of Scotland, Adv. MS. 6.1.4, transcript made circa 1809 of Scottish justiciary court records covering November 1493–August 1504. Inspection of the original entry may establish: * its exact manuscript folio; * the original Latin form of Alan’s name; * whether ''de'' appears before ''Glasgw''; * the precise legal term used for the killing; * whether the offence carried any omitted date, place or qualification; * Ralph Ker’s full designation. === Genealogical claims === No evidence currently identifies Alan’s parents, spouse, children or other relatives. No evidence connects him with Alan Stewart of Cardonald, the Stewarts of Minto or Gartnafuaran, the Cunninghams of Robertland, Sir Allan Smith, or later people bearing the Glasgow surname. Later marriage alliances and speculative naming patterns cannot establish Alan’s ancestry. No second independent record naming this Alan Glasgw has yet been identified. === Current research === Father assessment: '''father not identified; uncertain'''. This assessment draws on the cited records and public source material.[https://www.google.co.uk/books/edition/Criminal_Trials_and_Other_Proceedings_Be/LFAJAAAAQAAJ?gbpv=1&pg=PA19 www.google.co.uk]. == Sources ==

44193519.bio:
[[Category:Glasgow Name Study]]
== Biography ==
'''Helen Glasgow''' was born in 1652, recorded as a daughter of William Glasgow; the attachment to [[Glasgow-1556|William Glasgow]] does not by itself prove his identity.<ref name="Baptism1652">"Scotland Births and Baptisms, 1564-1950", database, FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:VQ4K-H58 : 16 September 2021), William Glasgow in entry for Hellein Glasgow, 1652.</ref>

== Research Notes ==
An Old Parish Register index records Helen Glasgow and James Hamiltoun at Kirknewton and East Calder on 21 June 1672.<ref name="Marriage1672">Scotland's People, ''Old Parish Registers: banns and marriages'', index entry for Helen Glasgow and James Hamiltoun, 21 June 1672, Kirknewton and East Calder, parish 690, reference 10/66, [https://www.scotlandspeople.gov.uk/ Scotland’s People] (original image not inspected; supplied index, reviewed 10 September 2026).</ref> The entry is compatible with this Helen by name, district and age. It does not name her father or residence, and its combined banns/marriages index cannot establish whether this was the wedding date. An original-register identity bridge is needed before a spouse attachment is justified.

=== Supplied parish index comparison ===

The supplied Scotland’s People index records '''HELLEIN GLASGOW''' on '''14/11/1652''' at Kirknewton and East Calder, with parent text “WILLIAM GLASGOW/”.<ref name="OPRBirth076">Scotland’s People, [https://www.scotlandspeople.gov.uk/ Old Parish Registers, births and baptisms], exact surname Glasgow through 1700, index text supplied 10 September 2026: HELLEIN GLASGOW, 14/11/1652, WILLIAM GLASGOW/, indexed gender F, Kirknewton and East Calder, parish 690, reference 10 / 29. Original register image not inspected for this review.</ref>

The profile’s structured birth date is 1652-11-11, whereas this index date is 1652-11-14. The two dates remain unreconciled. The combined births and baptisms collection does not establish whether the indexed date is a birthday or a baptism date. A parent’s name alone does not uniquely identify an attached historical person, and the index does not establish an unnamed parent. This date comparison does not resolve the possible later marriage identity discussed above.

== Sources ==

44194091.Name: Glasgow-3026
44194091.bio:
[[Category:Glasgow Name Study]]
{{Estimated Date}}

== Biography ==
'''Isabella Glasgow''' was an adult by 5 March 1600 and was married to [[Howe-15840|John Howe]], a dyer and citizen of Glasgow. On that date protocol 3637 records the spouses selling a workshop, waste ground and stable in a great Briggate tenement which John Hamilton had set in feu to the couple.<ref name="Howe1600">Robert Renwick, ed., ''Abstracts of Protocols of the Town Clerks of Glasgow'', vol. 11, protocol 3637, 5 March 1600, [https://archive.org/details/abstractsprotoc00renwgoog/page/144/mode/1up p. 145].</ref> This directly proves their marriage, John's occupation and their joint property, but it names neither of Isabella's parents.

== Research Notes ==

=== Parentage ===
The attached father, [[Glasgow-1097|Archibald Glasgow]], remains uncertain. A search of the published Glasgow protocols for 1530–1600 found no act calling Isabella a daughter, sister or heir of Archibald, Robert, William or another Glasgow. No present candidate has a demonstrated property, inheritance or personal link to her.

[[Glasgow-1096|Robert Glasgow]] was previously treated as the leading alternative because Robert Glesgw twice appeared with David Howe in 1557 and 1559/60.<ref>Renwick, ''Abstracts of Protocols'', vol. 2, protocol 372, 26 July 1557, [https://archive.org/details/abstractsprotoc08scogoog/page/n51/mode/1up protocol abstract]; protocols 525–526, 20 February 1559/60, [https://archive.org/details/abstractsprotoc08scogoog/page/n93/mode/1up protocol abstracts].</ref> A fuller Howe reconstruction removes most of that inference. On 25 August 1582 Peter Howie, dyer, and Isobella Maxwell expressly called a John Howee their son; the following act names their other son Umphrid. David Howie, expressly the son of the late William Howie, witnessed John's transaction.<ref name="Howe1582">Renwick, ''Abstracts of Protocols'', vol. 8, protocols 2448–2449, [https://archive.org/details/abstractsprotoc00scogoog/page/n78/mode/2up p. 64], 25 August 1582.</ref>

The 1582 John is probably Isabella's husband: exact name and city, suitable chronology, and the son of a dyer was himself styled dyer in 1600. A different contemporary John Howe is separately styled fisher and married to Marion Park. The probable parentage of Isabella's husband places him in Peter Howie and Isobella Maxwell's household, not David Howe's proved household. Robert Glasgow's association with David therefore does not materially support Robert as Isabella's father.

Robert Herbertson's appearance as a witness to the 1600 transaction does not establish that Isabella was related to [[Herbison-439|Margaret Herbesoun]].

== Sources ==
<references />

Spouses.Name: Howe-15840
Spouses.bio:
{{Estimated Date}}

== Biography ==

John Howe was a dyer and citizen of Glasgow. On 5 March 1600 he and [[Glasgow-3026|Isabella Glasgow]], his spouse, sold a workshop, waste ground and stable forming part of a great tenement on the south side of the Briggate which John Hamilton had set in feu to the couple.<ref name="Howe1600">Robert Renwick, ed., ''Abstracts of Protocols of the Town Clerks of Glasgow'', vol. 11 (Glasgow, 1900), protocol 3637, [https://archive.org/details/abstractsprotoc00renwgoog/page/144/mode/1up p. 145], 5 March 1600.</ref>

=== Probable parents ===

John was probably the John Howee whom Peter Howie, dyer, and Isobella Maxwell explicitly called their son on 25 August 1582. With Isobella's consent, Peter resigned to John a half-acre in Gallowmuir and Young's Croft. The immediately following protocol records another half-acre given to their son Umphrid Howee.<ref name="Howe1582">Robert Renwick, ed., ''Abstracts of Protocols of the Town Clerks of Glasgow'', vol. 8 (Glasgow, 1897), protocols 2448–2449, [https://archive.org/details/abstractsprotoc00scogoog/page/n78/mode/2up p. 64], 25 August 1582.</ref>

The parent-child wording is direct for the John of 1582; identifying him with Isabella's husband is strong circumstantial evidence. They share the exact name, Glasgow location, suitable chronology and the dyer occupation. A second contemporary John Howe is separately identifiable as a fisher married to Marion Park, so the occupational descriptions distinguish the two men.<ref>Renwick, ''Abstracts of Protocols'', vol. 5, protocols 1611 and 1724–1725, 4 February 1568/9 and 10 January 1570/1.</ref> Until a record names both Isabella and John's parents, the proposed parent links should remain uncertain.

John's stated birth year is an estimate derived from his adult property-holding in 1582.

== Sources ==
<references />

44209965.Name: Glasgow-3075
44209965.bio:
[[Category:Glasgow Name Study]]
{{Estimated Date}}

== Biography ==
'''William Glasgow''' was a mealmaker in Leith. His son
[[Glasgow-3078|Archibald Glasgow]] was baptised in 1618 and was described in
1639 as the son of William Glasgow, mealmaker in Leith, when apprenticed to
Thomas Park, cordiner.<ref>Francis J. Grant, ed., ''Register of Apprentices of
The City of Edinburgh, 1583–1666'' (1906),
[https://archive.org/details/scottishrecordso28scotuoft/page/71/mode/2up p.
71], 23 October 1639.</ref><ref name="Archibald1618">''Scotland Births and Baptisms, 1564–1950'', FamilySearch database, entry for Archbald Glascow, 1618.</ref> A mealmaker processed or sold grain meal within the urban food trade; the description does not necessarily mean that William was a miller.

William died in September 1644. His testament dative, confirmed 22 July 1646,
calls Archibald his lawful son and sole executor dative.<ref name="WilliamWill">National
Records of Scotland, Edinburgh Commissary Court, CC8/8/62, images 461–462,
testament dative of William Glasgow, mealmaker in Leith; [https://www.scotlandspeople.gov.uk/search-records/legal-records/wills Scotland's People wills search].</ref> Archibald's 1647
service of heir independently repeats the father-son relationship and both
men's Leith occupations.<ref>''Inquisitionum ad Capellam Domini Regis
Retornatarum... Abbreviatio'', vol. 2 (1811), Inquisitiones Generales no. 3278,
1 May 1647, original retour xix.128,
[https://archive.org/details/inquisitionumadc00grea_0 scan].</ref>

=== Parentage evidence ===

The identification of the Leith mealmaker with Niniane's son rests on several points:

* Niniane's 1613 testament directly names a son '''William Glasgw'''.
* The surname Glasgow was uncommon in this period.
* The age and generation fit the William later found in Leith.
* A possible Glasgow baptism record shows a William Glasgow already married and fathering a child in 1612.
* William was certainly the father of a child baptised in 1618.
* The movement from Glasgow to Leith is credible for a tradesman working in the meal and grain trade.

There is, however, no presently cited record which explicitly styles the Leith man:

:'''William Glasgow, son of Niniane Glasgow, flescher and burgess of Glasgow'''

The parent links should therefore be marked '''uncertain''' or '''probable''', rather than certain.

=== Marriage and children ===

William may be the '''William Glasgw''' recorded in the Glasgow High Kirk baptism register as husband of '''Christian Scot''' and father of:

* '''William Glasgw''', baptised 8 November 1612, lawful son of William Glasgw and Christian Scot. Witnesses were John Allassoun and Mathew Sympsoun.<ref name=Baptism1612>''Glasgow High Kirk Baptisms 1609–1777'', volume 1/962, baptism of William Glasgw, 8 November 1612.</ref>

This identification is plausible but not yet proved. The baptism places a man of the correct name in Glasgow immediately before Niniane's 1613 testament.

William was the father of:

* [[Glasgow-3078|Archibald Glasgow]], baptised in 1618.<ref name=Archibald1618>''Scotland Births and Baptisms, 1564–1950'', database, FamilySearch, entry for Archbald Glascow, 1618.</ref>

William was the father of [[Glasgow-3078|Archibald Glasgow]]. On 23 October 1639 the Edinburgh apprentice register described Archibald as the son of William Glasgow, mealmaker in Leith, when he was apprenticed to Thomas Park, cordiner. On 1 May 1647 Archibald was served heir to William; the retour abstract again described Archibald as a shoemaker in Leith and William as a mealmaker in the same town, expressly calling William his father. These independent occupational and residence identifiers confirm that the adult Archibald was the son of this William.<ref>Francis J. Grant, ed., ''Register of Apprentices of the City of Edinburgh, 1583-1666'', Scottish Record Society 28 (1906), [https://archive.org/details/scottishrecordso28scotuoft/page/71/mode/2up p. 71], 23 October 1639.</ref><ref>Great Britain Record Commission, ''Inquisitionum ad Capellam Domini Regis Retornatarum... Abbreviatio'', vol. 2 (1811), Inquisitiones Generales, no. 3278, 1 May 1647, original retour xix.128, [https://archive.org/details/inquisitionumadc00grea_0 Internet Archive].</ref>

The 1618 baptism alone would only require William to have been born by about the late 1590s. If the 1612 baptism also concerns him, a birth in the 1580s or early 1590s is more likely.

=== Occupation and residence ===

William later lived in '''Leith''', the port of Edinburgh, and worked as a '''mealmaker'''.

A mealmaker processed, prepared or sold grain meal, principally oat or barley meal. The occupation placed William within the urban food and grain economy rather than necessarily identifying him as a miller.

There may have been occupational links within the wider Meik surname:

* '''John Meik''', mealmaker and indweller in Niddrie, had a testament recorded in 1635.
* '''William Meik''', butterman in Whitburn, had a testament recorded in 1603.

These entries show that some people surnamed Meik worked in food-related trades. They do not prove that William Glasgow learned his occupation through his mother's family, or that either man was his relative.

=== Death and testament ===

William died in '''September 1644'''. His '''Testament Dative and Inventar''' was confirmed in the Edinburgh Commissary Court on '''22 July 1646'''. The original record describes him as William Glasgow, mealmaker in Leith, and says that the inventory was given up by '''Archibald Glasgow, his lawful son and sole executor dative'''.<ref name=Testament>National Records of Scotland, Edinburgh Commissary Court, CC8/8/62, images 461–462, testament dative and inventory of William Glasgow, mealmaker in Leith, confirmed 22 July 1646; [https://www.scotlandspeople.gov.uk/search-records/legal-records/wills Scotland's People wills search].</ref>

This corrects an earlier derivative transcription that gave William's death as September 1645 and called a John Glasgow his brother and executor. Inspection of the original testament shows that Archibald, William's lawful son, was the sole executor dative; it does not identify a brother John in that capacity.

=== Estate and financial connections ===

The inventory and debt account include the following working readings:

* '''£20 Scots''' owed by '''Andro Glasgow in Woodhead'''.
* '''£2 10s Scots''' associated with the late '''John Glasgow''' in England.
* '''£16 9s 4d Scots''' in debts owed by William and deductible from the estate.

These entries establish financial or commercial relationships. They do not by themselves establish that Andro Glasgow or the late John Glasgow was a relative.

The presence of several people surnamed Glasgow nevertheless suggests that William participated in a wider network of people bearing the surname across Leith, Glasgow, Lanarkshire and possibly England.

== Research Notes ==
=== Current evidence assessment ===

[[Glasgow-3188|Ninian Glasgow]] remains only a possible father. A William
occurs in Ninian's damaged 1613 testament material, but the formerly quoted
''his sone'' wording cannot be securely recovered and no record identifies that
William as the Leith mealmaker.<ref>National Records of Scotland, Glasgow
Commissary Court, CC9/7/9, images 142–145, testament of Ninian Glasgow; working
transcription reinspection supplied 6 September 2026.</ref>

William's own testament does not name a brother John. The earlier derivative
reading which made John his brother and executor is superseded by the original,
which names Archibald as sole executor.

If William was Ninian's son, [[Meik-14|Jonet Meik]] is a possible mother. Her 1607 testament names Ninian as her spouse and [[Glasgow-1027|Robert Glasgow]] as her son, but does not name William.<ref name="Meik1607">National Records of Scotland, Glasgow Commissary Court, CC9/7/5, images 82–83, testament testamentar and inventory of Jonet Meik, recorded 27 August 1607.</ref> An earlier unidentified wife therefore cannot be excluded. The manuscript surname is Meik; “Melk” in electronic indexes is best treated as a transcription error.

A separate Glasgow High Kirk entry records William Glasgw, lawful son of a William Glasgw and Christian Scot, baptised on 8 November 1612; witnesses were John Allassoun and Mathew Sympsoun.<ref name="William1612">''Glasgow High Kirk Baptisms 1609–1777'', volume 1/962, baptism of William Glasgw, 8 November 1612.</ref> The elder William is chronologically compatible with the later Leith mealmaker, but no residence, occupation or relative identifies them as the same man, so Christian Scot remains only a possible wife.

William's testament records £20 Scots owed by Andro Glasgow in Woodhead and £2 10s associated with the late John Glasgow in England.<ref name="WilliamWill" /> These are financial connections, not proof that either man was William's relative.

William's Leith residence and Archibald's apprenticeship to an Edinburgh cordiner make four women recorded in South Leith or Edinburgh—[[Glasgow-3182|Barbara]], [[Glasgow-3598|Margaret]], [[Glasgow-3302|Barbara]] and [[Glasgow-3336|Isobel]]—useful collateral candidates. Their marriages into cordiner or tailor households fit the same locality and craft network,<ref>Henry Paton, ed., ''The Register of Marriages for the Parish of Edinburgh, 1595–1700'', [https://www.tradeshouselibrary.org/uploads/4/7/7/2/47723681/register_of_marriages_for_the_parish_of_edinburgh_1595-1700_~_1898.pdf#page=277 printed p. 267].</ref> but none of their marriage records names a father. They should not be attached as William's sisters or daughters without a direct relationship record.

* This profile treats William as the probable son named in Niniane Glasgow's 1613 testament.
* The identification is based on name, generation, Glasgow association and chronology; there is no direct statement connecting the Leith mealmaker to Niniane.
* The parent links should remain marked uncertain.
* The correct manuscript and index spelling of the probable mother's surname is '''Meik''', not Melk.
* Jonet Meik's testament expressly names Robert Glasgow as her son but does not expressly name William as her son.
* If William was already a husband and father in 1612, he cannot have been a child of Niniane's later wife recorded in 1613.
* Jonet Meik is therefore the most likely known mother, but an earlier unidentified wife of Niniane cannot be excluded.
* The possible 1612 marriage to Christian Scot remains unproved.
* The 1618 Archibald baptism supports the generation but does not alone establish William's parents.
* A John Meik was a mealmaker in Niddrie in 1635, but this is not proof of a maternal occupational tradition.
* Andro Glasgow in Woodhead and the late John Glasgow in England should not be attached as relatives solely from debt entries.

=== Edinburgh-Leith collateral cluster ===
William's Leith residence and his son Archibald's 1639 apprenticeship to an Edinburgh cordiner provide the strongest geographic and trade bridge for [[Glasgow-3182|Barbara]], [[Glasgow-3598|Margaret]], [[Glasgow-3302|Barbara]] and [[Glasgow-3336|Isobel]].<ref>Francis J. Grant, ed., ''Register of Apprentices of the City of Edinburgh, 1583-1666'', [https://archive.org/details/scottishrecordso28scotuoft/page/71/mode/2up p. 71], 23 October 1639.</ref> Their South Leith or Edinburgh records and cordiner or tailor husbands fit possible sisters or nieces within William's branch.<ref>Henry Paton, ed., ''The Register of Marriages for the Parish of Edinburgh, 1595-1700'', [https://www.tradeshouselibrary.org/uploads/4/7/7/2/47723681/register_of_marriages_for_the_parish_of_edinburgh_1595-1700_~_1898.pdf#page=277 printed p. 267].</ref>

The repeated locality and craft are meaningful network evidence, but no marriage, testament or apprenticeship record names any woman's father. No exact relationship should be treated as proved.

A James Glasgow and [[Glessie-1|Annapill Glessie]], indexed also as Anabell Glass, were named as parents in three later St Cuthbert's entries:

* [[Glasgow-3076|James Glasgow]], recorded in 1661;<ref name="James1661">"Scotland Births and Baptisms, 1564-1950", database, FamilySearch, [https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:F316-KWL James Glesgow, 1661]; accessed 19 August 2026.</ref>
* [[Glasgow-3091|Thomas Glasgow]], recorded in 1663;<ref name="Thomas1663">"Scotland Births and Baptisms, 1564-1950", database, FamilySearch, [https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:F316-L74 Anabell Glass in entry for Thomas Glassgow, 1663]; accessed 19 August 2026.</ref>
* [[Glasgow-3338|Robert Glasgow]], recorded in 1665.<ref name="Robert1665">"Scotland, Births and Baptisms, 1564-1950", database, FamilySearch, [https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:F316-F84 Robert Glasgow, 1665]; accessed 19 August 2026.</ref>

== Research Notes ==

The two father profiles, formerly Glasgow-3077 and Glasgow-3337, were combined as the leading identification: the same name appears as a father in the same parish from 1658 to 1665, and the two household sequences do not overlap. Neither baptism explicitly identifies the 1658 father with the father in 1661–65. The change in named mother may reflect a second union, but no death or marriage record has been found to establish that sequence. The children’s mothers are recorded separately as each index names them. Search the original parish register and marriage or burial entries to test this identification.

The attached [[Glasgow-1103|Thomas Glasgow]] and [[Thomsone-70|Agnes Thomsone]] are uncertain parents. The children's baptisms name James as father but do not identify his parents. FamilySearch record F316-KWL is a 1661 event for James's son James, not this father's birth record.

44214123.Name: Glasgow-3103
44214123.bio:
[[Category:Glasgow Name Study]]
== Biography ==
'''James Glasgow''' was baptised at Edinburgh on 16 March 1679, a son of [[Glasgow-2682|James Glasgow]] and [[Duffe-18|Elizabeth or Isobell Duffe]].<ref>“Scotland, Births and Baptisms, 1564-1950,” FamilySearch database, [https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:VQC9-Q9N James Glasgow, 1679].</ref>

The same parents had another son named James, baptised on 18 April 1680.<ref>“Scotland, Births and Baptisms, 1564-1950,” index entry for James Glasgow, baptised 18 April 1680 at Edinburgh, son of James Glasgow and Elizabeth/Isobell Duffe.</ref> These are consecutive child records, so [[Glasgow-3368|James Glasgow]] remains a distinct same-name sibling. Reuse of the name suggests that the elder child may have died before the later baptism, but no burial or other survival record proves that conclusion.

An Edinburgh banns-and-marriages index records James Glasgow and [[Dobie-449|Jean Dobie or Wood]] on 28 July 1698.<ref>Scotland's People, [https://www.scotlandspeople.gov.uk/ Old Parish Registers], banns and marriages, Edinburgh parish 685/1, reference 450/47, 28 July 1698; index supplied 10 September 2026. The original entry has not been inspected.</ref> The index's “or Wood” is an alternative surname for Jean as indexed; it does not show whether it was an alias, prior surname or another convention.

This profile is attached to Jean, with sons [[Glasgow-3102|Peter Glasgow]] and [[Glasgow-2473|Robert Glasgow]], but those relationships remain uncertain. Peter's 1699 baptism proves an adult father James Glasgow at Edinburgh,<ref>“Scotland Births and Baptisms, 1564-1950,” FamilySearch database, [https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:F3BL-B2K Peter Glasgow, 1699].</ref> not whether he was the child baptised in 1679 or his 1680 brother. No inspected record bridges either infant to the adult marriage or proves Robert's parentage.

== Research Notes ==
Search Edinburgh burials from 16 March 1679 to 18 April 1680 and inspect the original 1698 marriage for residences, occupations, witnesses and Jean's stated name. Inspect Peter's original baptism to establish whether Jean Dobie is named as his mother. Treat this as a survival-and-adult-identity question, not a duplicate-profile question. Retain Jean Dobie or Wood, Peter and Robert as uncertain relationships pending that evidence.

The older profile gave James a birth year of 1670 at Kilwinning. No baptism or birth record for this adult has been found. The year and place are uncertain estimates from his adult presence there by 1689, not an independently recorded birth. His death is unknown.

== Research Notes ==
Compare both 1689 Kilwinning register entries, including residences, occupations, witnesses and whether the date represents birth or baptism. Search for a marriage to Margaret Park and for any later household records before treating the two children as proved siblings. The separate father's profile Glasgow-4178 was merged into this profile on 27 September 2026; its Anne citation and uncertain maternal status are retained.

44214274.Name: Glasgow-3107
44214274.bio:
== Biography == 

'''James Glasgow''' married '''Agnes Watt''' (recorded as Agnes Waitt or Waitte) on 18 June 1663 in Polwarth, Berwickshire, Scotland.<ref name="marriageRecordScotlandsPeople">“James Glasgow and Agnes Waitte,” Old Parish Registers - Banns and Marriages, National Records of Scotland (ScotlandsPeople), Parish Number 754, Ref 10/62, Frame 37, Polwarth, Berwickshire; marriage date 18 June 1663.</ref><ref name="marriageRecordFS">"Scotland, Marriages, 1561-1910", database, FamilySearch (https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:XTL8-X6D : 11 February 2020), James Glasgow, marriage to Agnes Waitte, 18 Jun 1663, Polwarth, Berwickshire, Scotland.</ref> His parentage remains unconfirmed. While some online trees suggest a birth year around 1640,<ref>See, for example, the FamilySearch profile GKWN-35S which associates this marriage with a 1640 birth year, though this profile demonstrably conflates individuals (see Possible Confusions section).</ref> this is an estimate likely based on his marriage date; he was probably born in the early-to-mid 17th century.

Polwarth is a parish located in the historic county of Berwickshire, near the town of Duns. Following their marriage, James and Agnes appear to have settled in the adjacent parish of Gordon, Berwickshire. A series of baptism records in Gordon list a James Glasgow (or Glascow) as the father of several children between 1666 and 1679. Given the proximity of Gordon to Polwarth, the consistent father's name, and the timing relative to the 1663 marriage, these children are very likely the issue of James and Agnes Watt:
*   '''[[Glasgow-3117|John Glasgow (1666-)]]''', christened 29 April 1666.<ref name="johnBaptismFS">"Scotland, Births and Baptisms, 1564-1950", database, FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:XTBS-Z9H : 16 September 2021), James Glascow in entry for John Glascow, christened 29 Apr 1666, Gordon, Berwickshire, Scotland.</ref>
*   '''[[Glasgow-1440|Patrick Glasgow (abt.1667-)]]''', christened 4 August 1667.<ref name="patrickBaptismFS">"Scotland, Births and Baptisms, 1564-1950", database, FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:XTBS-98Z : 16 September 2021), James Glasgow in entry for Patrike Glasgow, christened 4 Aug 1667, Gordon, Berwickshire, Scotland.</ref>
*   '''[[Glasgow-3364|Jean Glasgow (1671-)]]''', christened 16 April 1671.<ref name="jeanBaptismFS">"Scotland, Births and Baptisms, 1564-1950", database, FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:XYLM-Y4Z : 16 September 2021), James Glasgow in entry for Jean Glasgow, christened 16 Apr 1671, Gordon, Berwickshire, Scotland.</ref>
*   '''[[Glasgow-3106|Robert Glasgow (1673-)]]''', christened 1 April 1673.<ref name="robertBaptismFS">"Scotland, Births and Baptisms, 1564-1950", database, FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:XYHJ-3R9 : 16 September 2021), James Glasgow in entry for Robert Glasgow, christened 1 Apr 1673, Gordon, Berwickshire, Scotland.</ref>
*   '''[[Glasgow-3363|Agnes Glasgow (1676-)]]''', christened 29 October 1676.<ref name="agnesBaptismFS">"Scotland, Births and Baptisms, 1564-1950", database, FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:XYLM-Y4H : 16 September 2021), James Glasgow in entry for Agnes Glasgow, christened 29 Oct 1676, Gordon, Berwickshire, Scotland.</ref>
*   '''[[Glasgow-3365|Margaret Glasgow (1679-)]]''', christened 24 May 1679.<ref name="margratBaptismFS">"Scotland, Births and Baptisms, 1564-1950", database, FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:XYL9-Q32 : 16 September 2021), James Glasgow in entry for Margrat Glasgow, christened 24 May 1679, Gordon, Berwickshire, Scotland.</ref>

The christening of a daughter named Agnes in 1676 strongly supports the identification of this family unit with the 1663 marriage of James Glasgow and Agnes Watt, following common naming patterns. While the indexed baptism records from FamilySearch do not include the mother's name, the circumstantial evidence linking these Gordon children to James and Agnes (Watt) of Polwarth is compelling.

Further evidence of the family's presence in Gordon comes from the marriage record of their daughter, Jean. On 3 June 1702, '''John Smith''' married '''Jean Glasgow''' in Gordon, Berwickshire. The record explicitly names the bride's father as '''James Glasgow'''.<ref name="jeanMarriageFS">"Scotland, Marriages, 1561-1910", database, FamilySearch (https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:XTLH-1MB : 11 February 2020), James Glasgow in entry for John Smith and Jean Glasgow, 3 Jun 1702, Gordon, Berwickshire, Scotland.</ref> This confirms Jean survived to adulthood and indicates the family's continued connection to the Gordon parish into the early 18th century. The record identifies James as Jean's father but does not necessarily confirm he was still living in 1702.

Beyond these records, specific details about James's occupation or death date remain unconfirmed in contemporary Scottish sources.

== Research Notes ==

Likely a relative of the father of a William Glasgow, father of [[Glasgow-1605|William Glasgow (bef.1658-)]] in Polworth, Berwickshire. These are the first two Glasgow's to appear in this area. (brothers?) 

=== Possible Confusions with Ulster Glasgows ===
Genealogical research on this James Glasgow is complicated by the presence of other men with the same name in 17th-century records, particularly in Ulster, Ireland. Several online genealogies and collaborative trees (such as FamilySearch profile GKWN-35S, which attaches the Polwarth marriage, the Gordon baptisms, ''and'' a 1725 death date) have mistakenly connected James Glasgow of Polwarth and Gordon to the James Glasgow who settled in Kilwaughter Parish, County Antrim, Ireland. This Kilwaughter James appears in the 1669 Hearth Money Rolls for County Antrim and reportedly died in 1726.<ref name="kilwaughterInfo">This information regarding the Kilwaughter James is commonly cited in Glasgow family histories but requires primary source verification for the death date and details. Secondary sources often cite a James Glasgow in Kilwaughter, Co. Antrim, appearing in the 1669 Hearth Money Rolls and dying c. 1726. Primary source verification is recommended. This individual is considered distinct from James Glasgow of Polwarth/Gordon.</ref>

Crucially, there is currently no known documentary evidence directly linking the James Glasgow who married Agnes Watt in Polwarth (1663) and raised a family in Gordon, Berwickshire (c. 1666-1679+), to the James Glasgow recorded in Kilwaughter, County Antrim. The established family life in Berwickshire during the period the Kilwaughter James was documented in Ireland strongly suggests these were two distinct individuals. Researchers should treat them separately. The 1725/1726 death date often associated with James Glasgow belongs to the Kilwaughter individual, not the James of Polwarth and Gordon.
